levels: The walls grow to take in a new pine grove, and a carved timber hall with a double roof rises behind the moon gate.
A second moon-viewing terrace tower stands above the harbour, and a stone mole extends the port into the sea.

places.name: Đào Thanh Thành
places.look: A walled river city under endless pine, its quays set high up the bank on tall stone steps. Below them, at low water, a row of old drowned quay pillars stands in the current like a broken fence, marking where the city once met the river. When the wind turns, the forest above roars like surf, and the streets go quiet to listen.
places.lore: Tùng Đào Cung founded the city in 300 on the river below its forests, and named it for the sound of the pine waves heard from the seat above. Timber merchants, river traders and the families of Tùng Đào's outer disciples live here. On windy evenings the townsfolk climb the walls to hear the pines, and a child who sleeps through the first great wind of autumn is teased for a year.
places.history: Tùng Đào Cung took the river basin of Cửu Khúc Xuyên in the Age of First Gates, and in 300 founded Đào Thanh Thành on the river below its forests. The city grew as the palace's market and river gate, shipping timber and pine resin downstream. In 700 a great flood on the Nine-Bend River drowned three villages, and Tùng Đào moved the city's quays up the bank; the old pillars were left standing in the water. The city prospered through the long peace of the North Star Compact, and is said to have sent boats and grain north in the Long Lake War of the Age of Vein Wars. When the Ferry War burned Lãng Đào's ferries, its merchants felt it in their ledgers, and the split tolls still sour the wharf taverns. Today it is the busiest city on the river, and the pines above it are as loud as ever.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular walled river city among dark pines: tight rows of grey-tile roofs, green-glazed eaves on the city hall, and a three-storey gate tower as the tallest outline. Along the river edge, tall stone stair-quays climb the bank, and just offshore a line of broken old quay pillars stands in blue water, the signature element. Pine forest presses against the walls on the landward side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, pale glints on the river. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city and its strip of bank.
levels: A second row of wharf warehouses along the high quays and a pine-roofed listening terrace on the upper wall.
An outer wall reaching to the forest edge, a covered bridge over the river, and a five-roof bell pagoda that answers the pine waves.

places.name: Khai Dương Thành
places.look: A walled port city where the northern road meets a river mouth and the sea. Its east gate tower carries a great polished bronze disc that catches the first light before dawn, so the gate seems to burn while the streets below are still dark. Masts crowd the river quays under the walls.
places.lore: Thiên Xu Tông founded Khai Dương Thành on the northern road in 280, naming it for a star of the Northern Dipper. In 900 its gate was rebuilt to face the morning star, and travellers say the city wakes before the sun: bakers, porters and ferrymen are at work in the dark. Late sleepers are called guests here, even if they were born in the city.
places.history: A generation after Thiên Xu Tông extended its protection over Dao Quang Lĩnh, in 280, it founded Khai Dương Thành on the northern road where it reaches the sea. The city became the Pivot's northern port, shipping ore and timber by river and by sea. Through the Age of the North Star Compact it grew quietly rich, far from the wars of the south. When Thiên Xu founded Thanh Bách Thành on the same road in the first years of the Compact, Khai Dương became the road's harbour end. In the Phá Quân rebellion of the Age of Vein Wars, the city fed and shipped the Pivot's forces in the mountains above. In 900 its gate was rebuilt to face the morning star and the bronze disc was set over it; travellers say the city wakes before the sun.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular walled port city at a river mouth on the sea: grey-tile roofs in neat rows, river quays crowded with small masts, and a sea mole at one corner. On the east side, a tall gate tower crowned by a large polished bronze disc, the signature element and the tallest outline, flaring gold in the light. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, bright reflections on the water. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city and its quays.
levels: A stone sea mole with warehouses along it, and a second bronze disc on the river gate.
An outer harbour wall, a lighthouse tower on the mole, and a new walled quarter climbing the riverbank inland.

places.name: Trường Vân Thành
places.look: A walled harbour city at the edge of the desert, where a river reaches the sea under the snow mountains. A long roofed caravan gallery runs straight through the city from the land gate to the docks, so goods pass from camel to ship without seeing the sun. On cloudy days a faint shimmer of a ward formation hangs over the walls, and long clouds lie on the peaks behind.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các founded Trường Vân Thành in 470 at the edge of the desert, under the long clouds over the snow mountains, and it is still the sect's door to the sea. Caravan guards, ship chandlers and Băng Tâm's officers crowd the taverns of the gallery. Hạng Dạ Bôi was born here to a caravan guard's family in 870, and the guard families of the city have never let anyone forget it.
places.history: In 470, the year it claimed the ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, Băng Tâm Các founded Trường Vân Thành at the edge of the desert, under the long clouds over the snow mountains. The city became the sea gate of the desert road, and the sect raised a ward formation (trận pháp) over its walls. When Băng Tâm built Cô Thành on the caravan road half a century later, Trường Vân became its supply port. Through the Desert Road War the city sent water and swords to the lone fortress, until Cô Thành fell. In 870 Hạng Dạ Bôi was born here to a caravan guard's family; a century later Hạng Dạ Bôi founded Dạ Quang Môn and raided the caravans that fed the city. Since Dạ Quang Môn knelt to Băng Tâm, its raiders have guarded those caravans instead, and the gallery is busy again.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular walled harbour city of grey-tile roofs at a river mouth on the sea, with desert sand on its landward side. Straight through its middle runs a long continuous roofed caravan gallery from the land gate to the docks, the signature element. A gate tower of three roofs is the tallest outline; a faint translucent shimmer of a ward dome over the walls. Ships at the quays. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city.
levels: A second caravan gallery branching to a new dock, and a stone caravanserai inside the land gate.
An outer wall around the docks, a lighthouse on the river mouth, and a taller ward formation pagoda at the city's centre.

places.name: Liên Giang Thành
places.look: A grey port city where a cold river meets the sea, its walls running down both banks to the harbour. Across the river mouth stretches a long roofed bridge of dark timber and grey tile, its eaves hung with racks of silver ice-fish drying in the rain.
places.lore: The fishers of Hàn Giang Môn built the city and it still smells of their trade; under Băng Tâm Các its people pay their tax in ice-fish, as they have since the frost coast fell. Cold rain comes in off the sea at night and joins the river, and locals say a child born in such a rain will never drown; Đoàn Thanh Lãng, head of Trạc Anh Đài, was born on such a night. The city's line is the first of Băng Tâm's own poem: cold rain joins the river by night.
places.history: Hàn Giang Môn founded Liên Giang Thành in 350, where the cold rain joins the river, as the harbour of its fisher cultivators (tu sĩ). For a century and a half its boats worked the cold river and the frost coast under the Gate of the Cold River. In the last years of the Age of Seven Seats Băng Tâm Các made war on Hàn Giang for the coast, and in 498 Hàn Giang fell with its last head Liễu Cô Chu; the city passed to the Pavilion with the rest of Hàn Sương Châu. From 499 the old sect's fishers kept fishing the cold river under Băng Tâm's flag and paid their tax in ice-fish, a custom still kept. Old people say the roofed bridge was raised in Hàn Giang's time so the fishers could mend nets out of the rain. In 990 Đoàn Thanh Lãng was born here during a cold rain that joined the river by night, and grew up to lead Trạc Anh Đài. Today the city is the frost coast's oldest port and Băng Tâm's door to the sea.
places.art_brief: A city miniature at a river mouth on a forested coast: rectangular grey stone walls running down both banks, dense grey-tile roofs inside, a small harbour of fishing boats. The signature is a long, low roofed bridge of dark timber spanning the river mouth, its eaves lined with tiny silver racks of drying fish. Dark firs at the city's back, cold slate-blue water, a thin veil of rain over the sea edge. Warm golden light from the top left catching the wet roofs. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and the bridge.
levels: The roofed bridge is doubled with a second span, new ice-houses line the quays, and the walls take in the fishers' quarter on the far bank.
A tall grey drum tower rises over the harbour, the quays run out in stone piers to the sea, and both banks are walled to the forest edge.

places.name: Đàm Ảnh Thành
places.look: A low walled port city on the island's grassy shore where a river meets the sea. In its heart lies a large round pool, so still that the clouds and the city's roofs lie upside down in it, ringed with open pavilions where painters set up their easels.
places.lore: Cô Phàm Các built the city in 410 and it outlived the sect; now it is Lạc Hà Tông's, and lives by fish, trade and painters. Painters come from the mainland to paint the sky upside down in the pool, and a painting made here is signed at the bottom, not the top. The blind Đoạn Thương Hải, who survived the Hóa Thần tribulation (thiên kiếp) that killed his master, has lived beside the pool since 1062 and listens to it instead of looking at it.
places.history: Cô Phàm Các, the sailors' sect of Cô Vụ Đảo, founded only a decade before, built Đàm Ảnh Thành in 410, and below it the harbour of Bích Không Cảng, from which its sails vanished into the blue. At the close of the Age of Seven Seats the Strait Oath swore Cô Phàm Các to Lạc Hà Tông. Nearly three centuries after the city's founding a storm sank the whole Cô Phàm fleet with its head Mã Viễn Ảnh, and the city lost its masters in a night; Lạc Hà's stewards took it in hand. A year later the harbour below was abandoned, and the city turned to its river quay and its pool. By 800 the pool mirrored the clouds so clearly that painters came from the mainland to paint the sky upside down. In 1060 a Hóa Thần tribulation over the island sea killed the master of Đoạn Thương Hải, who survived it blind, holding the Thương Tang Kính. In 1062 he settled in Đàm Ảnh Thành, and he has listened to the pool ever since.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat grassy shore at a river mouth: low rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs, a small river quay. At the centre a large perfectly round pool, mirror-still, reflecting sky and clouds, ringed by small open pavilions with upturned grey roofs. Warm golden light from the top left, the pool a disc of pale gold and blue. No text, no people larger than specks, no seaward harbour quays, nothing outside the walls.
levels: A painters' hall with long open galleries rises on the pool's north side, and the river quay is rebuilt in stone.
A second walled ward takes in the river's far bank, and a tall pavilion over the water is built so its reflection completes it in the pool.

places.name: Nhạn Thanh Thành
places.look: A walled city where a river meets the sea on the dry steppe coast, its grey roofs crowded around wool warehouses. Over the main gate rises a tower whose two upswept roofs spread like the wings of a goose in flight, and the wild geese pass over it in long formations each autumn.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông founded the city in 450 where the wild geese fly in formation, and it is the wool market of the western plain; Kim Vạn Lý, the richest merchant of the west, made his name here. Since the cold year of 1120, when archers shot the low-flying geese from the walls, no one may shoot a goose in the city. Its scholars retire to Điền Viên Thôn to farm.
places.history: Lạc Hà Tông took the open grassland of Trường Thiên Nguyên in the Age of Seven Seats, and in 450 founded Nhạn Thanh Thành on the western plain where the wild geese fly in formation. The city grew on the plain's wool and grain, shipped from its river harbour. By the Age of Vein Wars its scholars were retiring to farm the gardens and fields of Điền Viên Thôn, which fed the city. In 1040 Kim Vạn Lý bought the wool of the whole plain in one season and became the richest merchant of the west. In 1120 the wild geese flew so low over the city in a cold year that archers shot them from the walls, and the city forbade it ever after. Kim Vạn Lý still lives here, and the goose gate is the first thing the herders see when they drive their flocks to market.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a dry, tawny steppe coast at a river mouth: rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs and long low warehouse roofs, a river harbour with boats. Over the main gate a tower with two broad roofs swept sharply upward like spread wings, the tallest outline. A thin V of tiny geese in the sky above it. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: A great wool exchange with a long grey roof rises by the harbour, and the walls take in the dyers' quarter.
A second winged tower is raised over the river gate, and stone wool warehouses line both banks to the sea.

places.name: Tử Điện Thành
places.look: A walled port city on the bay where a river meets the sea, its grey roofs packed tight inside strong walls. Above them rises a tall armoury tower roofed in violet-glazed tile, and on clear evenings the faint violet shimmer of its ward array (trận pháp) hangs over the whole city.
places.lore: Lạc Anh Phái founded the city on the bay side of the Petal Shore in 360; Lạc Hà Tông took it by the Pivot's judgement in 620 and renamed it Tử Điện Thành for its armoury, after the purple-lightning sword Tử Điện. Its smiths and guards are the most disciplined in the bay. Old families still plant a peach tree in the courtyard for Lạc Anh, though the city's first name is all but forgotten.
places.history: Lạc Anh Phái founded a city on the bay side of the Petal Shore in 360; it would bear another name before it bore its last. The same year Lạc Hà Tông forged twin swords for its armoury, Tử Điện and Thanh Sương, after the purple lightning and blue frost of an old general's blades. Two and a half centuries later Lạc Anh Phái split over its inheritance and its last head, Khương Vọng Nguyệt, vanished. Lạc Hà and Thính Vũ Lâu both claimed the empty Petal Shore, their disciples fought in the burning orchards, and Hồng Vũ Thành burned. In 620 the Pivot's judgement gave the bay to Lạc Hà and the forest to Thính Vũ, and Lạc Hà renamed the bay city Tử Điện Thành, for its armoury; it raised a ward array so the fire would not come twice. In the War of Broken Halberds Thanh Sương fell from its bearer's hand on Chiết Kích Nguyên, and no one has dared go back for it. Late in the Age of Vein Wars Tô Vãn Chiếu became head of Lạc Hà Tông and took the sword Tử Điện.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a bay shore at a river mouth: strong rectangular grey walls, dense grey-tile roofs, a busy harbour. Above them a tall square armoury tower with several roofs of glazed violet-purple tile, the tallest point; a barely visible pale violet dome of light over the walls. A few pink peach trees in courtyards. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: A second armoury hall with violet tile rises inside a new inner wall, and the harbour gains a war-boat slip.
The walls are doubled on the landward side with gate towers, and the ward array's shimmer brightens into a clear violet dome over the bay front.

places.name: Tinh Hán Thành
places.look: Thiên Xu's port on the inland sea sits where a river meets the shore, a walled grid of grey roofs behind a long curving breakwater. The breakwater is the reef itself: a line of great white arched ribs, the bones of the old sea-serpent, rising out of the water with stone packed between them. At night the harbour lamps and the Milky Way in the water make the city seem set among stars.
places.lore: Tinh Hán Thành, the City of the Star River, was founded by Thiên Xu Tông in 260 on the reef left by the sea-serpent a nameless swordsman killed in 15. A city formation (trận pháp) runs along its walls and the bone reef, and formation masters are common here; the freelance master Vệ Văn Cơ was born in the city and drew formations in the harbour sand before he could talk. Wheat comes from the mills of Thủy Đối and pearls from Châu Bạng, and sailors touch the nearest rib for luck before every voyage.
places.history: In 15 a nameless swordsman killed the sea-serpent of the inland sea, and its bones became a reef. In 260 Thiên Xu Tông founded Tinh Hán Thành on that reef as its port on the inland sea, packing stone between the ribs to make the breakwater. Its formation was laid along the walls and the reef against storms and sea beasts, and the Pivot's formation masters have kept it in repair ever since. In the Age of Seven Seats pearl oysters found in the shallows at Châu Bạng gave the port its pearl trade, and in the Compact years the water mills at Thủy Đối ground wheat for the whole city. Ore from Ngọc Hành Sơn and star iron from Thối Tinh Môn came down to its quays and went out across the sea. In 980 Vệ Văn Cơ was born here and drew formations in the harbour sand before he could talk.
places.art_brief: A walled port city in a rectangular wall where a river meets a calm sea on steppe coast: a grid of grey-tile roofs behind a long curving breakwater made of huge white arched bone ribs rising from the water with grey stone packed between them, a few boats moored inside. Sea and river mouth at the base. Warm golden light from the top left making the white ribs glow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: The wall runs the whole shore, a second stone quay reaches out from the bone reef, and a lighthouse tower rises at the reef's end.
A grand harbour hall with a three-roof pagoda faces the sea, the reef is armoured with dressed stone between every rib, and the formation's pillars glow faintly along the walls at dusk.

places.name: Lai Nghi Thành
places.look: A walled port city at a river mouth on the dry eastern steppe, its harbour mole curving out into the gulf. On the mole rises a terrace of nine stepped stone tiers, each crowned with a bronze bell frame, so that the whole stair glints at sunrise. A faint shimmer over the walls marks the city's guardian array (hộ thành trận).
places.lore: Phượng Minh Cung founded the city in 530 on the plain where, the old book says, the phoenix comes when the music is played nine times. Every dawn the city's musicians climb the nine tiers and play the same welcome nine times over, one tier at a time, whether or not anything comes. Harbour folk say the phoenix came once, long ago, and argue about which dawn it was. Ships of the gulf put in for rice from the plain and leave with lacquer and bronze.
places.history: Phượng Minh Cung founded Lai Nghi Thành in 530, soon after it took the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên, empty since the fall of Cửu Thiều. The name came from the old line about the Shao music played nine times, and the founders raised the bell terrace before the walls were finished. In the decades that followed the city became the Palace's door on the sea, and the guardian array was set over its walls. Once Hoàng Vân Thành was built upriver the grain barges came down to its quays, and in the great seven-year drought its harbour shipped the plain's rice to the hungry south. When Thôn Hải's pirates burned Châu Lệ Cảng, the city manned its walls every night until the Pirate Purge swept the gulf clean. It has grown quietly rich on the coastal trade ever since. Old musicians say Cửu Thiều's music was never truly lost, only scattered to the four coasts, and that some of it came home here.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature on a flat dry steppe shore at a river mouth: rectangular walls of pale stone, grey-tile roofs with a few red-lacquered halls, a curved harbour mole reaching into blue water. The signature, and the tallest element, is a terrace of nine stepped stone tiers on the mole, each tier topped by a small bronze bell frame catching the light. A barely visible golden shimmer over the walls for the array. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long shadows to the lower right. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: The nine-tier terrace gains a roofed musicians' gallery and the harbour a second mole lined with warehouses.
A second wall ring takes in the river quays; the terrace is faced in red-lacquered stone and a tall ceremonial gate opens on the sea.

places.name: Thu Trì Thành
places.look: A walled port city where a river meets the sea below wooded hills, built in steps so that tiers of square stone pools descend through its streets from the upper town to the harbour. After night rain on the hills every pool brims and spills into the next, and the whole city murmurs. Over the lower terraces hang the dark oiled-paper awnings of the Night Rain Market, and a guardian array (hộ thành trận) shimmers faintly on the walls.
places.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu founded the city in 400 and named it for the old poem of night rain on the mountain swelling the autumn pools. Since 1000 it has held the Night Rain Market, which sells ma đạo pills, poisons and arts that no other city allows; it opens only after dark and only in rain, and buyers come from as far as the desert. Innkeepers here learned long ago not to ask names. Nghê Hồng Đậu and the head's disciple Mạnh Lưu Ly were both born within its walls.
places.history: Thính Vũ Lâu founded Thu Trì Thành in 400, twenty years after its own founding, as its port on the southern sea. The stone pools were cut into the slope to catch the night rain off the hills, and the forest's honey, timber and grain went out from its harbour. In 800 Nghê Hồng Đậu was born here, and red beans grew from the cracks in her mother's doorstep. After the Night Rain Edict, strangers in black came up the forest road at night for the whole of 908, and the innkeepers learned not to ask their names. In 1000 the Tower opened the Night Rain Market in the city, and its treasury doubled within fifty years. By 1005 the market was known to open only after dark and only in rain, and it drew buyers from as far as the desert. In 1060 Mạnh Lưu Ly was born here, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ took her as his disciple.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature on a gentle slope between wooded hills and the sea at a river mouth: grey-tile roofs in stepped rows, and the signature, a descending stair of square stone pools brimming with water between the streets, spilling from tier to tier down to the harbour. Dark oiled-paper awnings over the lowest terraces; a faint shimmer of array light along the walls; a few boats at the quay. Wet surfaces after rain, warm golden-hour light from the top left breaking through. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: The pools climb higher up the hill as the upper town grows; a second harbour basin and a long covered hall for the Night Rain trade.
A walled upper city of dark halls looks down over the tiered pools; the market's awnings spread across three terraces and the harbour is walled in stone.

places.name: Không Mông Thành
places.look: A walled port city in a low valley mouth by the sea, almost always seen through fine hazy rain. Every street is roofed by long covered arcades of grey tile on red-painted posts, so that one can cross the whole city without getting wet. Above the arcades rise the older halls of Khải Lôi's time, their roof ridges capped in green bronze.
places.lore: Khải Lôi Môn founded the city in 200 in the hazy rain of its southern valleys, and Thính Vũ Lâu has held it since the Gate fell. Many of its families descend from the people of Lôi Trạch Thành, who came here after their own city burned. They still keep a thunder-day in spring, beating drums under the arcades when the first thunder is heard. The hills hazy in the rain are lovely too, the poem says, and painters come for it.
places.history: Khải Lôi Môn, the Gate That Opens the Thunder, founded Không Mông Thành in 200 in the hazy rain of its southern valleys, the same year Lý Thiên Cổ first beat the thunder drum Xuân Lôi Cổ. The city grew as the Gate's southern port, while Lôi Trạch Thành held the river mouth below the mountains. Nearly three centuries later Hầu Xuân Lôi was struck down by his own tribulation, and its lightning burned Lôi Trạch Thành. A year afterwards the people of Lôi Trạch moved up the valley to Không Mông Thành, and the arcades were raised over the streets to shelter the newcomers' stalls. The Gate never recovered, and Thính Vũ Lâu rose on its ground and took the city with the mountains. Through the Age of Vein Wars it has stayed a quiet trading port. Old families still whisper that the Gate's thunder inheritance lies sealed somewhere in the mountains above.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature in a low green valley mouth at the sea, seen through a soft veil of fine rain: rectangular walls, and the signature, long grey-tile covered arcades on red posts lining every street in a grid; above them a few older halls with green-bronze roof ridges as the tallest elements. A small harbour at the base. Warm golden-hour light from the top left diffused by the haze. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: The arcades reach the harbour quays, and a drum tower rises at the main crossing.
A second wall ring up the valley sides; covered bridges link the arcades across the river, and the harbour gains a stone breakwater.

places.name: Ngũ Thải Thành
places.look: A walled port city at a river mouth on the warm southern coast, its wards roofed in glazed tile of five colours, red, yellow, green, white and black, so that from the hills it looks like a bird's spread wing. A gate tower painted with a five-coloured bird faces the harbour.
places.lore: Xích Thành Môn built the city in 300 and named it for the five-coloured bird of Mount Đan Huyệt, the phoenix; Phượng Minh Cung has held it since 590. Each ward's guild keeps one colour of glaze, and quarrels between wards are settled by who repairs the most roofs. Hùng Phần Vũ, head of Phần Vũ Đường, was born here in 980, and a red feather fell on his cradle.
places.history: Xích Thành Môn built Ngũ Thải Thành in 300 on the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu as its port and market. Its potters glazed the roofs in five colours for the five-coloured bird of the old book, one colour to each ward. After Tôn Hà Khởi died, the city watched its own sect turn under Chu Liệt Nhật to burning villages. In 590 Phượng Minh destroyed Xích Thành Môn, and the city passed to the Palace with the rest of Đan Huyệt Châu. Through the pirate years it barred its harbour by night, and its ships sailed with Phượng Minh's fleet in the Pirate Purge. In 980 Hùng Phần Vũ was born here, and a red feather fell on his cradle. Since he grew up and founded Phần Vũ Đường in the old vents, the city's young walk inland to try themselves.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature at a river mouth on a flat warm coast: rectangular walls, and the signature, ward after ward of glazed roofs in bands of red, yellow, green, white and black, fanning out like a wing; a tall gate tower facing the harbour as the tallest element, with a painted bird on its face. Boats at the quay. Warm golden-hour light from the top left making the glazes shine. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A sixth ward of plain grey roofs for newcomers and a stone breakwater for the harbour.
A second wall ring up the river, and a five-roofed hall of the potters' guilds at the city's heart.

places.name: Lam Yên Thị
places.look: A broad stone stair climbs from the valley into the mountain haze below Thúy Vi Tông, lined on both sides with stalls under indigo cloth awnings. On misty days the awnings fade into the haze one step at a time, so the market seems to climb into cloud.
places.lore: The market grew at the foot of Thúy Vi Tông in the mountain mist and is named for it. Herbs, pill ingredients and scripture are its trade, and scholars from three sects come to buy the red-leaf bookmarks of Thu Diệp Thôn. Each stallholder hangs a small bell from the awning so customers can find the stall by ear in the fog.
places.history: Before the market, the foot of the mountain was only the place where Thúy Vi's disciples met the carters who brought up rice and herbs. In 600 a market had grown there in the mountain mist, and it took the name Lam Yên Thị. Its stair was paved step by step as each stallholder laid the stones in front of a stall, so no two steps quite match. It became the place where the sect sold the pills it did not need and bought what its herb terraces could not grow, and scholars climbed it for copied scripture. The custom of awning bells began on a fog day when two buyers searched for each other's stalls from morning to noon. Within living memory the red leaves of Thu Diệp Thôn came onto its stalls as bookmarks for scripture, and scholars from three sects now climb the stair to buy them.
places.art_brief: A market built along a broad stone stair that climbs a forested slope into haze. Signature element: two continuous lines of stalls under deep indigo cloth awnings flanking the stair, fading step by step into blue-green mist toward the top. A few low grey-roofed storehouses at the foot of the stair. At the base: a small paved square and the valley road. Warm light from the top left on the lower awnings. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, the sect seat itself, anything outside the stair's footprint.
levels: A second side stair of stalls branches off halfway up, and an inn with a double grey roof stands at the foot.
A covered market hall straddles the stair's midpoint, and a stone gate arch marks the market's lower entrance.

places.name: Tùng Hạ Thị
places.look: In a wide clearing under old pines, a market stands in a perfect ring: round stall-houses with low grey cone roofs set shoulder to shoulder around an open circle. A single gate in the ring opens onto the road through the pine sea.
places.lore: Tùng Hạ Thị began as a ring of tents pitched by pilgrims who came to hear the pine waves of the new palace, and it kept the ring when the tents became houses. It sells to caravans on the road through the pine sea and to travellers bound for the palace. The loose cultivator Lâm Dã Hạc was born here to a woodcutter's family, and the market still points out the roof where a crane landed on the day of his birth.
places.history: In 205 pilgrims who came to hear the pine waves of the newly founded Tùng Đào Cung stayed on, and Tùng Hạ Thị began as a ring of tents beneath the pines. As the palace grew, the pilgrims' ring became a market for the road through the pine sea, and the tents were rebuilt as round houses on the same circle. Caravans made it a resting place, and woodcutters' families settled behind the ring. In 1145 Lâm Dã Hạc was born here to a woodcutter's family, and a crane landed on the roof the day he was born. In 1190 wolves from the deep pines followed the caravans to Tùng Hạ Thị, and Tùng Đào doubled the road watch, posting guards at the ring's gate.
places.art_brief: A market in a clearing of tall old pines. Signature element: a perfect ring of small round stall-houses with low grey cone roofs set shoulder to shoulder around an open circular yard, with one gap for a gate. At the base: a forest road leading to the gate, a few carts as specks, woodcutters' houses just behind the ring. Warm light from the top left falling into the clearing. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, towers, anything outside the clearing.
levels: A second, outer ring of stall-houses is begun and a caravan yard is fenced beside the gate.
A round two-storey market hall rises in the centre of the ring, and a timber palisade with a roofed gate encloses both rings.

places.name: Đào Sa Thị
places.look: Where the river spreads its sand into the sea, a market sprawls across the flats on stilts. Rows of wooden washing cradles stand in the shallows, rocked by washers in wide straw hats, and at low tide the whole flat glitters with fine gold. Along the landing lie the charred ribs of burned ferries, left where they sank.
places.lore: Around 800 gold-washers learned that after a thousand washings the river sand gives up its gold, and Đào Sa Thị grew beside Lãng Đào Môn. It is a market of scales, sieves and quick hands under Tùng Đào's peace, where anyone who keeps their head down can find work at a cradle. The washers still tell how Triệu Huyết Y hid among them for two years after the hunt that killed her master, and lately some swear they have seen her again.
places.history: Before 800 the sand flats at the river mouth held little but gulls and driftwood. Around 800 gold-washers learned that after a thousand washings the river sand gives up its gold, and Đào Sa Thị grew beside the new ferry sect Lãng Đào Môn, which made its landing here. For three centuries the market lived on gold dust and ferry traffic under Tùng Đào Cung's peace. In 1090 Thiên Xu, Tùng Đào and Băng Tâm killed the demonic-path (ma đạo) master Mặc Huyết Sinh, and his last disciple Triệu Huyết Y escaped; in 1092 she hid for two years among the gold-washers here. A generation ago the Ferry War broke out, and in 1173 Lạc Hà raiders burned Lãng Đào's boats at the Đào Sa landing. For years afterward the washers fished nails from the river along with their gold. The burned ribs still lie at the landing, and the market washes on.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a sprawling stilt market on golden sand flats at a river mouth: low grey-tile and thatch roofs on posts, no wall, and one tall tarred signal mast as the tallest outline. Across the shallows, rows of small wooden washing cradles on stilts, the signature element, with gold specks glinting in the water around them. A blackened line of burned ferry ribs lies beside a timber landing at one side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the flats.
levels: A raised boardwalk links the stalls to a rebuilt landing, with a red-doored assay house at its head.
A market square on piles behind a timber palisade, a small customs pagoda flying Tùng Đào's colours, and washing cradles out to the far sandbars.

places.name: Tống Khách Thị
places.look: A forest market strung along the road on a gentle rise, its stalls tucked under dark fir eaves. At the eastern end stands a small eight-sided farewell pavilion over a stone table, where a single cup is always set out full.
places.lore: Travellers leaving the frost coast are seen off here at dawn, and the market lives on what they buy for the road: furs, dried fish and warm wine. Since a traveller seen off in 900 never returned, the market pours a farewell cup for him at the pavilion every year. The wandering sword sage Tư Không Hạc Niên, bound to no sect, has lived here since his duel of 1130 and teaches no one, however many come to ask.
places.history: Tống Khách Thị grew where the frost coast's road climbs inland, the last place travellers on Băng Tâm's roads took a cup before the long way south. Its name comes from the Băng Tâm poem: at dawn I see my guest off. In 900 a traveller was seen off from the market at dawn and never returned; the record keeps no name for him, and the market has poured a farewell cup for him every year since. The eight-sided pavilion at the eastern end was built, the stallholders say, to keep that cup out of the snow. In 1130, after his three-day duel with Thang Vô Tạ of Phất Y Cốc on Cùng Mục Phong ended with no winner, the wandering sword sage Tư Không Hạc Niên settled here. He teaches no one, though young swordsmen come up the road every year to ask. The market has grown used to him, and he to the market.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile stall roofs strung along a pale road on a gentle forested rise, timber posts and fur-hung awnings, dark firs close on both sides. At the eastern end a small eight-sided pavilion with an upturned grey roof sits over a tiny stone table, its single cup a speck of white. Light snow on the eaves, warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing beyond the road's edge.
levels: A walled inn yard joins the market, and the stalls double along the road under longer eaves.
The market gains a gate and a covered street, and a second, larger pavilion rises beside the old one, which is kept exactly as it was.

places.name: Tương Phùng Thị
places.look: A market built half on the water at the quay below Bình Thủy Môn: boats lashed side by side into a floating raft of stalls that rises and falls with the tide. Planks run between them, and faded green awnings drift like duckweed on the strait.
places.lore: The market grew beside Bình Thủy Môn in 525 and has never had a fixed shape; boats join and leave, and no stall sits in the same place two days running. It is said that anyone looking for a lost friend need only wait long enough at Tương Phùng Thị, and the strait ferries leave from its outer boats.
places.art_brief: A market miniature on calm coastal water: a loose, irregular raft of many small boats lashed together, joined by planks, each with a tiny faded green or ochre awning, against a short stone quay with a few grey-tile sheds. Turquoise water, warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, no sect halls, nothing outside the quay and the raft.
levels: A stone quay with warehouses anchors the raft, and the boats spread into two lashed arms.
A covered market hall stands on piles over the water, and the raft rings it in a wide floating crescent.

places.name: Vật Hoa Thị
places.look: A busy open market on the dry steppe below Thiên Bảo Trai, rows of awnings around a central square. In the square stands a great bronze steelyard on a stone frame, taller than a house, where any trader may have goods weighed in public.
places.lore: The market of the land's riches grew beside Thiên Bảo Trai in 500 and sells what the Trai refines and what the bay digs, grows and catches. Its public scale is the market's law: a deal weighed there cannot be undone. The famous alchemist Lạc Đan Thanh has kept a pill stall here since 1110 and charges whatever he likes.
places.history: In 500 a market for the land's riches grew beside Thiên Bảo Trai and was called Vật Hoa Thị. It sold the Trai's refinings and the red gold of Xích Kim, and drew traders from all round Thu Thủy Loan. In 1004, a year after Kim Cốc burned, Kim Cốc's merchants came begging here, and Thiên Bảo Trai hired the ones who could still count. The traders say the great scale was set up in the square after the crash, to keep the market honest. In 1105 Lạc Đan Thanh bought the Đào Nguyên Đồ, the only map of the way into the fisherman's lost valley, here for a pill no one else could make. In 1110 he set up his pill stall in Vật Hoa Thị, and he has charged whatever he likes ever since. Who sold him the painting is not recorded.
places.art_brief: A market miniature on a dry tawny plain: a low walled square of grey-tile stall roofs and striped ochre and dull red awnings, with a large dark bronze steelyard beam on a tall stone frame at the centre, the tallest element. A road leading off toward a rise. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the bronze. No text, no people larger than specks, no sect pagoda, nothing outside the market walls.
levels: A covered arcade rings the square and a caravan yard is walled in beside the road.
A stone exchange hall with a high double roof faces the scale, and the market's walls take in a second square.

places.name: Hạc Đinh Thị
places.look: Where the river spreads into shallows below Lạc Hà's seat, the market (phường thị) sits on a scatter of sandbar islets joined by plank causeways, its stalls under reed awnings. White cranes stand in the shallows between the islets and do not move for the crowds.
places.lore: Hạc Đinh Thị, the Market of the Crane Shoal, has traded since 320 in the sect's pills, river fish and the talismans of Nam Phố Đường. Cranes are never driven off; a stall a crane chooses to stand beside is thought lucky for the season. A talisman contest is held on the largest islet each autumn, and the market still talks of 1190, when the fourteen-year-old Tô Mộ Vân beat the scribes of Nam Phố Đường.
places.art_brief: A low market cluster on a river shoal in flat steppe: half a dozen small sandbar islets each carrying a few reed-awninged stalls and grey-tile sheds, linked by thin plank causeways over shallow silver water, with tiny white cranes standing in the shallows. Pale sand and reeds at the base. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the water. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: More islets are joined; a timber market hall on piles stands at the centre of the causeways, and a ferry landing serves the sect road.
The causeways become a raised stone walk on low arches across the whole shoal, with a two-roof market tower at its heart; the cranes still stand below.

places.name: Thiên Quyền Thị
places.look: At the foot of the Pivot's mountain, a square market of grey stone halls opens around a tall timber gantry from which hangs a giant bronze steelyard, its beam as long as a boat. Every large sale in the market is weighed on it in public view.
places.lore: Thiên Quyền Thị, the Market of the Heavenly Balance, opened beside Thiên Xu Tông in 200 as a market of weight and measure, and its scales are the fairest on the continent. The sect's standard weights are kept here in a locked hall and brought out each spring to test every scale in the market; a trader whose scale fails is barred until the next spring's test.
places.art_brief: A low market cluster of grey stone halls with grey-tile roofs around an open square on grassland at a mountain's foot, a tall dark timber gantry in the square holding a long horizontal bronze steelyard beam with a hanging weight, the tallest element. Paved square and a road at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the bronze beam. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second gantry and a covered arcade of money-changers' stalls ring the square, and a stone weights hall with bronze doors stands on its north side.
The market is walled and gated in stone, with a drum tower over the gantries and a long caravan yard on the road toward Thạch Kiều Thành.

places.name: Thiều Âm Thị
places.look: At the foot of Phượng Minh's ridges, a market of bamboo-roofed stalls lines a river among bamboo groves, and every lane is hung with curtains of bamboo flutes and pipes drying on strings, clicking and whistling in the wind. A raised music stage stands over the water.
places.lore: Thiều Âm Thị, the Market of the Shao Music, was opened by Phượng Minh's founder in 485 when he cleared the ridges for the new palace. It sells instruments, strings and lacquered drums, and its players are hired for rites all over the south. In 1195 a musician here played a tune no one taught him and every bird on the ridge fell silent; Phượng Minh's elders paid his passage far away, and players since are asked, politely, to name the teacher of any tune they perform.
places.art_brief: A low market cluster along a river in bamboo forest: bamboo-roofed stalls in narrow lanes with many thin hanging strings of pale bamboo flutes, a small raised timber music stage on piles over the water. Bamboo groves and the river at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the hanging flutes. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A covered market hall of bamboo and a second stage on the far bank join the lanes, with a footbridge between them.
The market is walled with a red gate tower, a drum tower and an instrument-makers' guild hall, and a stone landing takes the river boats.

places.name: Hạnh Hoa Thị
places.look: A market town on the river below the southern road to Thính Vũ Lâu, built of deep, narrow lanes between tall grey-tile houses. From every eave hang woven baskets of apricot blossom (hạnh hoa), so after rain the lanes are roofed in pink and white. Apricot trees crowd the river bank behind the stalls.
places.lore: The market grew up in 700 below Thính Vũ's southern road, and after a night of spring rain its lanes sell flowers, as the old poem of the small tower promises. It is also known for the healer Giả Hồi Xuân, born here in 1020, who cures what the alchemists of three sects would not touch. On mornings after rain the sick wait in the flower lanes alongside the buyers.
places.art_brief: A market town miniature on dry steppe by a river: rectangular walls around a tight grid of narrow deep lanes between tall grey-tile houses, the signature being woven baskets of pink and white blossom hanging from the eaves along every lane. Pink apricot trees along the river bank. Wet roofs after rain, warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A covered flower hall at the market gate and a stone quay on the river.
A second walled quarter of healers and herb sellers; the apricot grove is walled as a market garden.

places.name: Quy Điểu Trấn
places.look: A walled lakeside town of grey roofs whose shore is lined with rows of tall birch poles, each crowned with a straw nest-basket. In autumn every pole and roof ridge is crowded with returning birds; in winter the market tents stand out on the ice beyond the harbour wall.
places.lore: Quy Điểu Trấn began as a traders' camp named for the birds that return to the lake each autumn in great flocks, and townsfolk still raise a new nest pole for every child born. Lake pearls made it rich, and each winter its market moves out onto the ice, where pearl buyers walk from stall to stall over the frozen water. It is a Tùng Đào town, and much of what Hàm Nguyệt Trang's pearl beds yield passes over its scales.
places.art_brief: A small rectangular walled town of grey-tile roofs on a flat lake shore among birch and spruce. Signature element: long rows of tall, thin pale birch poles along the shoreline, each topped by a round straw nest-basket, a few with tiny birds as specks. A small stone harbour wall curves into the lake. At the base: a pebble shore, a few moored skiffs, a thin rim of pale ice. Warm light from the top left catching the pole tops. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, flocks that spill beyond the town, anything outside the town's footprint.
levels: The wall runs further along the shore and the nest poles stand in double rows; a stone pearl market hall rises by the harbour.
A second harbour basin is cut, and a tall grey-roofed bird-watching tower stands over the shore where the winter ice market is held.

places.name: Mục Ca Thành
places.look: A walled city of low grey roofs sits on open coastal grassland, hunched against the wind. Around its walls a ring of round dry-stone sheepfolds lies across the grass like beads on a string, and at dusk the herders' songs carry from fold to fold.
places.lore: Thúy Vi founded the city on its cape where herders sing to their flocks, and the songs are still how flocks are counted, called home and sold. Each herding family owns a fold in the ring and a tune no one else may sing at it. The city lives on wool, hides and the sea, and buys its grain, so a poor harvest anywhere on the cape hits it hard.
places.history: Long before any sect claimed the cape, herders drove their flocks along this grassy shore and sang to them. Thúy Vi Tông took Tuyết Hỏa Giác in the Age of the North Star Compact, and in 700 founded Mục Ca Thành on the cape where the herders sang. The city grew as the cape's wool and hide market, and its folds were added one by one around the walls as families settled. Its grain came from the cape villages and through the harbour of Yên Ba. In 1196 a poor harvest drove grain prices in the city so high that the herders went to sing their songs for coin in Yên Ba's streets. The songs came home with them changed, and old herders complain that the young now sing for strangers.
places.art_brief: A rectangular walled city of low grey-tile roofs on open green-gold coastal grassland, a modest gate tower its tallest roof and a small harbour on the sea side. Signature element: a ring of round dry-stone sheepfolds strung around the outside of the walls, each a pale stone circle on the grass. At the base: rolling grass, a shingle shore, a short stone pier. Warm light from the top left with long shadows from the fold walls. Avoid: text, people or sheep larger than specks, anything outside the city and its ring of folds.
levels: A second ring of folds is built and a long covered wool hall rises inside the walls.
A tall drum-and-song tower stands at the city's centre, and the harbour gains a stone mole for the wool ships.

places.name: Bạch Sa Trấn
places.look: A small walled town of whitewashed walls and grey roofs sits on a beach of dazzling white sand. Along the shore stand long rows of whitewashed net-drying frames, so many that from the sea the town seems fenced in white lattice.
places.lore: The Thẩm family, fishers of the white sands, built the first houses here, and the clan hall is still the town's court. Since a Thẩm daughter married into a merchant house of Yên Ba, the town trades as much as it fishes. A peach petal netted in midwinter is kept in a sealed jar at the clan hall; the elders say the hidden valley's stream has opened again, and strangers have begun asking which way the currents run.
places.history: In 380 the Thẩm family, fishers of the white sands, built the first houses of Bạch Sa on this beach. For centuries it was a fishing village, and once Thúy Vi Tông took the cape it owed its catch to that sect. When Thúy Vi founded the port of Yên Ba Thành a generation later, Bạch Sa's fish went to its markets. In 1040 a daughter of the Thẩm clan married into a merchant house of Yên Ba, and the white sands became a trading town. In 1120 a fisher of Bạch Sa netted a peach petal in midwinter, far from any peach tree, and the elders said the hidden valley's stream had opened again. Since then cultivators come through asking about tides and streams, and the Thẩm clan answers them politely and tells them nothing.
places.art_brief: A small rectangular walled town of whitewashed walls and grey-tile roofs on a broad beach of bright white sand. Signature element: long parallel rows of whitewashed net-drying frames running along the beach in front of the walls like white lattice. At the base: white sand, a few beached fishing boats, a short wooden pier into pale turquoise shallows. Warm light from the top left, the sand glowing. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, any peach tree, anything outside the town and its beach.
levels: A merchants' quarter of two-storey warehouses grows inside an extended wall and the pier is rebuilt in stone.
A tall double-roofed clan hall of the Thẩm stands at the town's heart, and a small harbour wall curves around the rows of net frames.

places.name: Bách Diệp Trấn
places.look: A walled town of grey roofs at a river mouth stands inside a vast grid of ancient cypresses planted in straight rows. From any approach the dark columns of the trees march out in lines, and the town sits at the centre of the pattern.
places.lore: Không Sơn Viện's students planted the cypress groves around Bách Diệp as a lesson in patience, and the trees have long outlived the academy. No townsman may cut a cypress, and a dead one is replaced by a seedling grown from its own cones. The town trades cypress incense and resin along the coast.
places.history: In the Age of First Gates the river mouth here was a fishing landing below the hills of Không Sơn Viện. In 240 the academy's students planted the cypress groves around Bách Diệp as a lesson in patience, setting each seedling on a measured line. The town grew up in the middle of the grid, its streets laid along the rows the students had drawn. When Không Sơn's last master gave the hills to Thúy Vi Tông, the town passed with them, and the new sect kept the old rule that no cypress may be cut. Over the centuries the groves grew taller than any roof, and the town learned to live by their resin and incense. Townsfolk say the trees are the academy's last lesson, and the only one anyone ever finished.
places.art_brief: A small rectangular walled town of grey-tile roofs at a river mouth on the coast. Signature element: a large, exact grid of tall, dark, spire-shaped cypresses in straight rows surrounding the town on the land side. At the base: a river mouth, a small wooden harbour, a sandy bank. Warm light from the top left casting long parallel shadows from the rows. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the town and its grid of trees.
levels: The grid is extended along the river and an incense workshop quarter is added inside a longer wall.
A tall cypress-wood hall of the incense guild rises at the town's heart, and a stone quay lines the river mouth.

places.name: Tiều Ca Trấn
places.look: A walled timber town of grey roofs sits on the coast below steep forested ridges. A long wooden log flume runs from the ridge tops straight down to the harbour, and logs rattle along it into the water.
places.lore: Woodcutters singing on the ridges below Không Sơn Viện were once asked to sing more quietly, and the town they founded is still called Tiều Ca. Its woodcutters sing to this day, but only below the old academy's boundary stones, out of habit rather than fear. Its timber goes by sea to the cape and to Yên Ba.
places.history: Woodcutters worked these ridges in the Wild Age, long before any sect stood above them. When Không Sơn Viện was founded on the mountain, its students found the woodcutters' songs too loud for their quiet. In 190 the woodcutters singing on the ridges below the academy were asked to sing more quietly, and the town they founded on the coast is still called Tiều Ca. They set boundary stones on the slope, and above those stones the woodcutters fall silent to this day. The log flume was built to bring timber down without the shouting of teams and oxen, and it became the town's pride. After the hills passed to Thúy Vi the timber trade grew, and Tiều Ca's logs now go by sea to the cape and to Yên Ba.
places.art_brief: A small rectangular walled town of grey-tile roofs on a narrow coastal strip below forested ridges. Signature element: a long raised wooden log flume running from the ridge top straight down the slope into the harbour. At the base: a log pond, a timber yard, a short pier with a cargo boat. Warm light from the top left along the flume. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the town and its flume.
levels: A second flume comes down a neighbouring ridge and a sawmill house stands over the log pond.
A stone harbour wall shelters the timber ships, and a tall woodcutters' guild hall rises inside the walls.

places.name: Lộc Minh Trấn
places.look: A walled town of grey roofs lies on a low river mouth at the forest's edge, every beam end of its timber houses carved. At the end of its ferry pier stands a life-sized stag carved from pine, head raised as if calling across the water.
places.lore: A deer called at the forest's edge every dawn for a year, and the Lâm family settled where it called and named the place Lộc Minh. The Lâm clan's woodcarvers are known across the pine sea, and they made the beams of a new hall in Tùng Gian Thành from a single fallen pine. The town is held by Lãng Đào Môn, the ferrymen's sect (môn phái) that carries the river trade, and its pier is one of their landings.
places.art_brief: A small rectangular walled town of timber houses with grey-tile roofs at a low, marshy river mouth on the edge of a pine forest. Signature element: a life-sized carved wooden stag standing at the end of a long ferry pier, head raised toward the water. At the base: reed banks, two flat ferry boats, a mud shore. Warm light from the top left on the stag. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the town and its pier.
levels: A carvers' quarter of open workshops spreads along the river bank and the ferry pier is doubled.
A tall carved timber hall of the Lâm clan rises over the town, and a stone ferry landing replaces the old pier with the stag moved to its end.

places.name: Cổ Độ Thành
places.look: A walled city stands among bamboo groves on the bank of the southern river, where a broad stone ferry stair runs down into the water. At the top of the stair, set upright on a stone plinth, stands a single huge rusted iron link from a sunken chain, taller than a man.
places.lore: Cổ Độ Thành stands at the old ferry on Tùng Đào's southern river, and its ferrymen still cross it as they did before the city had walls. In the War of the Pivot they carried the iron chain for Thiết Tỏa Quan link by link, and now they drag those links back out of the river and sell them to smiths. The great link at the ferry stair is said to be the first one raised, and no one has ever sold it.
places.history: Long before it had walls, a ferry crossed the southern river here, and the old ferry gave the city its name. In 320 Tùng Đào Cung founded Cổ Độ Thành at the crossing. In 506, during the War of the Pivot, the ferrymen of Cổ Độ carried the iron chain for Thiết Tỏa Quan link by link up the river road. Two years later Thiên Xu broke the fort, and the thousand-fathom chain sank to the river bed. For centuries the river kept it, until in 990 the people of Cổ Độ began dragging its links from the river, and smiths paid well for the old war iron. Smithies have grown up around that trade, and the clang of iron by the ferry stair is now as old a sound as the boatmen's calls.
places.art_brief: A rectangular walled city of grey-tile roofs among green bamboo groves on a river bank. Signature element: a broad stone ferry stair descending into the river, crowned by a single huge rusted iron chain link standing upright on a stone plinth. At the base: the river with two flat ferries, smithy smoke from a riverside quarter, bamboo along the bank. Warm light from the top left on the rust. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, any bridge across the river, anything outside the city's footprint.
levels: A smiths' quarter with tall chimneys grows outside the river gate, and a second ferry stair is built downstream.
A tall drum tower of the ferrymen rises over the stair, and the walls take in the smiths' quarter and a stone river quay.

places.name: Hà Bạn Trấn
places.look: A low riverside town whose fishing lanes all end at the water. At its upstream corner a great timber waterwheel turns beside a mill house, grinding roots from Thải Chi Cốc into powder, and its creak carries to the road. Herb sacks stand stacked on the short jetties, waiting for boats.
places.lore: Hà Bạn Trấn was a fishing hamlet until 290, when the river's new course ran past its door and it grew into a town on the new bank. It now answers to Thải Chi Cốc, grinding and shipping the valley's herbs downriver. The townsfolk have a saying for every stroke of luck: the river came to us, so we do not chase it.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a low town of grey-tile roofs inside a modest rectangular wall, open on the river side where short jetties reach into the water. At the upstream corner, a large dark timber waterwheel beside a mill house, the signature element and the tallest outline. Small boats along the bank and stacked herb sacks by the mill. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and its bank.
levels: A second waterwheel and a stone mill house, with a covered herb wharf along the bank.
The wall runs along the river with a water gate, and a row of mills turns in a cut channel beside the town.

places.name: Lâm Hạ Trấn
places.look: The town sits so deep in the shade of old beeches that its roofs are green with moss even in summer. Between the houses stand round timber granaries raised on squat stone staddles shaped like mushrooms, so that no rat can climb them. At noon the lanes are cool and dim, and smell of grain dust.
places.lore: In 600 Tùng Đào Cung set its northern granaries in the shade of Lâm Hạ Trấn, so the grain would keep, and the town has lived as a storehouse ever since. Its people are granary-keepers, coopers and rat-catchers, proud that their grain does not spoil. Felling a shade tree inside the town is the one crime the elders never pardon.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a low cluster of moss-green grey-tile roofs inside a small rectangular wall, almost hidden under the broad crowns of old beeches. Among the houses, several round timber granaries with conical roofs raised on mushroom-shaped stone staddles, the signature element. A river edge at one side with a grain jetty. Warm golden-hour light from the top left breaking through the canopy in patches. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town.
levels: More round granaries on staddle stones and a timber fence around the storehouse quarter.
A stone granary hall with a tall vented roof under the oldest beeches, and a full town wall with a grain gate on the river.

places.name: Bích Khê Trấn
places.look: A small walled town on a brook so green it looks dyed. Below the walls the stream runs over shallow stone weirs where jade-pickers kneel, sorting pebbles into baskets by colour. Polishing wheels hum in the workshops along the main street.
places.lore: A jade-green brook below the ridges gave Bích Khê Trấn its name around 300, and its trade in river jade. Pickers comb the brook bed after every flood, and the carvers in town turn the pebbles into seals and hairpins for Thiên Xu's officials. When a match is made, the bride's family gives an uncut pebble from the brook as its promise.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a low town of grey-tile roofs inside a small rectangular wall beside a brook of vivid jade-green water stepped by shallow stone weirs, the signature element. Baskets and tiny workshops along the bank; forest and ridges at the far edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, the green water glowing. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and its brook.
levels: A carvers' street with a covered market, and a stone footbridge across the green brook.
A larger wall, a jade hall with a green-glazed roof, and weirs stepping the brook far upstream.

places.name: Thanh Bách Thành
places.look: A walled city of grey roofs and dark, narrow cypresses on the northern road, a cypress standing over every courtyard. Outside its north wall lies a small round crater pond, glassy black at the rim, where a star fell in 980. Ore carts and officials' carriages pass through its gates all day.
places.lore: Thiên Xu Tông founded Thanh Bách Thành on its northern road in 520, and the city is named for its green cypresses. In 980 a star fell near the city; the fragment was sold to Thối Tinh Môn for three years of the city's taxes, and the crater filled with rain. Townsfolk toss a coin into the pond for luck, though the clerks say the city has paid that star enough already.
places.history: Thiên Xu Tông founded Thanh Bách Thành on its northern road in 520, in the first years of the North Star Compact, to guard the road between the heart and Khai Dương Thành. Cypress seedlings were planted in every courtyard, and the city took their name. It grew as a waystation for ore carts, officials and the Pivot's patrols in Dao Quang Lĩnh. In the Phá Quân rebellion of the Age of Vein Wars its gates stayed shut to the rebels, and it quartered Thiên Xu's troops. In 980 a star fell near the city; the fragment was sold to Thối Tinh Môn for three years of the city's taxes. The crater pond outside the north wall is all the city kept of it, and the old cypresses still stand over the courtyards.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular walled city with grey-tile roofs and many tall, narrow dark-green cypresses rising between them, a gate tower as the tallest roofline. Just outside the north wall, a small round crater pond with a glassy black rim, the signature element. A road runs through the gates. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, the cypresses casting long thin shadows. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city and its pond.
levels: A second market quarter inside the walls and a shrine pavilion on the crater pond's rim.
An outer wall enclosing the crater pond, and a tall tax hall with stacked roofs among the oldest cypresses.

places.name: Hòe Âm Trấn
places.look: A small harbour town where a river reaches the sea, and from its back gate an avenue of ancient locust trees climbs toward the mountains, their crowns meeting overhead in a green tunnel. Fishing boats and the hermitage's supply carts share one narrow quay. In early summer the locust blossom drops on the road like pale snow.
places.lore: Locust trees planted by the Tiêu family shaded the road into the mountains, and around 520 their village took the name Hòe Âm; it now answers to Lê Hoa Am. In 930 a hunter of the town found a sealed cave on the mountain with a sword's cold light behind the seal; he ran, and never found it again. Every hunter since has looked for that cave, and tavern talk names more dead swordsmen behind its seal than the mountain could hold.
places.history: In the first years of the North Star Compact the Tiêu family planted locust trees along the road from the river mouth into the mountains, to shade the carts that climbed to the ice. Around 520 the cluster of houses at the foot of their avenue took the name Hòe Âm, for the locusts' shade. The village fished, hunted the lower slopes and carried supplies up the mountain road, and grew into a small harbour town. After the hermitage of Lê Hoa Am was founded on the heights, the town came to answer to it and to carry its stores. In 930 a hunter of Hòe Âm found a sealed cave on the mountain with a sword's cold light behind the seal; he ran, and never found it again. Since then every hunter of the town has looked for that cave, and none has found it. Half a century ago the Tiêu clan sent a son to the hermitage's gate and saw him turned away, and he too took up the hunter's bow. The locusts still shade the road, older now than any house beneath them.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a low harbour town of grey-tile roofs inside a rectangular wall at a river mouth on the sea, a narrow quay with small fishing boats. From its landward gate, a double row of broad old locust trees runs uphill with their crowns meeting, the signature element. Mountains begin at the far edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and its avenue.
levels: A stone quay with a hunters' market, and the locust avenue extended further up the mountain road.
A larger wall with a harbour gate, a Tiêu family hall with a two-tier roof, and a waystation for Lê Hoa Am's pilgrims at the avenue's end.

places.name: Hồi Lan Thành
places.look: A harbour city on the desert coast, built behind a long curved breakwater that hooks out into the sea and turns the waves back on themselves. Sand-coloured walls enclose low warehouses under pale grey roofs. Ships from the south crowd the still water inside the hook.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các founded Hồi Lan Thành on the desert coast in 760, after the Desert Road War, so that trade with the south need not trust the desert alone. Its harbour filled with southern ships by 770, once the caravan road was safe. In 1160 a merchant of the city brought the first southern rice through the desert since the war, and Băng Tâm taxed it at half; the rice merchants still toast him at every new year.
places.history: The Desert Road War ended a generation before the city's founding with the border where it had been, and Băng Tâm Các looked for a road south that Phượng Minh's fire could not cut. In 760 it founded Hồi Lan Thành on the desert coast and raised the breakwater that turns the waves and gives the city its name. By 770 the harbour was full of ships from the south, now that the caravan road was safe. The city grew on salt, wool and southern goods, and on the trade that had once passed Cô Thành. In 1160 a merchant of Hồi Lan Thành brought the first southern rice through the desert since the Desert Road War, and Băng Tâm taxed it at half. The sea road and the rice road have both run through the city since.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular city of sand-coloured walls and pale grey-tile roofs on a desert coast, a gate tower as the tallest roofline. From its harbour a long curved stone breakwater hooks out into blue sea, the signature element, with white surf curling back along its outer face and small ships in the calm water inside. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city and its breakwater.
levels: A rice market quarter and warehouses along the inner breakwater.
A second hooked breakwater forming a full harbour ring, with a watch pagoda at its tip and a walled merchant quarter outside the old wall.

places.name: Mộc Lan Thành
places.look: A walled harbour city on the flat frost coast, its grey roofs low against the sea wind. A double row of old magnolia trees runs the length of the harbour wall, and in spring their white blossoms line the quay like snow that will not melt. Inland, the white cone of Sương Diễm Sơn stands over the city.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các's younger port on the frost coast trades furs, timber and live beasts from Vô Tung Lâm; hunters sell their catches on the magnolia quay, and buyers come from as far as Thiên Bảo Trai. The city remembers the week in the Age of the North Star Compact when Sương Diễm Sơn breathed fire and everyone slept on the beach; on that night each year, families still lay their bedding out on the sand.
places.history: Băng Tâm Các founded Mộc Lan Thành on the frost coast in 620, more than a century after taking Hàn Sương Châu from Hàn Giang Môn. Its builders planted magnolias along the new harbour wall, a southern tree coaxed to bloom in the cold, and the city took its name from them. Within a century of the founding, Sương Diễm Sơn breathed fire under the frost for a week, and the people of Mộc Lan Thành slept on the beach until it sank. The city grew as the coast's market for the furs and timber of Vô Tung Lâm, a forest only the coast's woodcutters and hunters dare. In 1180 hunters brought a white bear out of Vô Tung Lâm alive and sold it here to a buyer from Thiên Bảo Trai. The tale of that bear's long road south is still told in the harbour taverns. Today the city lives by the sea and the forest at once.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat, fir-edged coast: low rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs pressed close, a small harbour with a stone quay. Along the harbour wall runs a double line of small round trees covered in white blossom, the brightest white in the scene. A strip of pale beach to one side. Warm golden light from the top left, cool blue sea. No text, no people larger than specks, no volcano inside the footprint, nothing outside the walls and quay.
levels: A fur market hall with a high grey roof rises behind the quay, and the magnolia rows run on along a new sea wall.
The walls take in the beach quarter, a stone breakwater shelters the harbour, and a three-roofed gate tower faces the volcano inland.

places.name: Kê Minh Trấn
places.look: A small walled port town on the grassy frost coast, low grey roofs around a single harbour. Above its gate stands a tall pole topped by a bronze rooster, green with age, that turns with the wind.
places.lore: The cocks of Kê Minh crow even in the dark of winter, when the sun barely rises, and the town has kept the cock as its emblem since the Age of Seven Seats (Thất Tọa Kỷ). Its fishers set out at the first crow, not the first light, and a household whose cock falls silent fetches a new one before nightfall.
places.history: Kê Minh grew on the grassy frost coast as a fishing harbour in the days of Hàn Giang Môn. By 360 its cocks were known to crow even in the dark of winter, when the sun barely clears the sea, and the town took the cock as its emblem. Its fishers learned to set out at the first crow rather than the first light, and its boats were the first on the water all along the coast. When Hàn Giang Môn fell and the frost coast passed to Băng Tâm Các at the end of the Age of Seven Seats, the town changed its flag but not its emblem. The bronze rooster above the gate was cast, the townsfolk say, to go on crowing if every bird in the town ever fell silent. They boast that no bad news has ever reached Kê Minh before the first crow.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature on a grassy coast: a small rectangular wall of grey stone, a tight cluster of grey-tile roofs, a short harbour wall with a few boats. Over the gate a tall thin pole carries a tiny verdigris-green rooster, the highest point of the town. Pale winter grass, cold sea. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: The harbour wall is lengthened into a stone pier and a fish market roof rises by the gate.
A second ring of wall takes in the poultry yards and net sheds, and a covered gatehouse lifts the rooster pole higher still.

places.name: Xích Ngạn Trấn
places.look: A small walled town atop red cliffs on the island's east coast, its grey roofs bright against the rust-red rock. A long stair cut into the cliff face zigzags down to a cove where the boats are drawn up.
places.lore: The first mainland traders named the red cliffs Xích Ngạn in 330, and the town that grew on top kept the name. Its people grind the red rock into a pigment for the island's sails, and a Xích Ngạn boat is known far out at sea by its rust-coloured canvas.
places.art_brief: A town miniature on a grassy clifftop: a small rectangular grey wall and grey-tile roofs at the edge of a sheer rust-red sandstone cliff; a zigzag stair cut into the cliff face down to a tiny cove with boats with red-brown sails drawn up on the shingle. Warm golden light from the top left glowing on the red rock. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the clifftop and the cove.
levels: A pigment mill and drying yard sit inside the walls, and a second stair is cut to a new landing.
The town fills the clifftop, a stone pier runs out from the cove, and a tall grey-tile hall overlooks the sea from the cliff edge.

places.name: Hải Yến Trấn
places.look: A fishing town of low grey roofs on the flat island shore. Every house wears deep double eaves, and under them the sea swallows' nests cluster so thickly that the eaves look whitewashed; at dusk the air above the town is a whirl of birds.
places.lore: Since the Age of the North Star Compact the people of Hải Yến have sold swallows' nests to alchemists (đan sư), who prize them for pills that clear the breath. Families own eaves the way others own fields, and a daughter's dowry is counted in nests. Harvesters take only the nests the birds have left.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature on a flat grassy shore: a small rectangular wall, grey-tile roofs each with deep double eaves, the undersides crusted pale white with nests, a cloud of tiny dark specks of birds over the roofs. A small harbour of fishing boats. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: Tall nest houses with many tiers of eaves rise inside the walls, and the harbour gains a stone quay.
A ring of nest towers stands along the walls, and a nest market hall with a high grey roof faces the harbour.

places.name: Triều Âm Thành
places.look: A walled city on the island's western shore at a river mouth, grey roofs stepping up from the water. Along its sea front runs a stone breakwater bored with round holes that moan and sing as the tide pushes through.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông founded the city in 540 as its western foothold on Cô Vụ Đảo. Its people tell time by the breakwater's note, low at the ebb and high at the flood, and its watchmen call the tide instead of the hour. Musicians from the mainland come to tune to it, and the children call the sound the island breathing.
places.history: A generation before the city, Cô Vụ Đảo became Lạc Hà Tông's land under the Strait Oath. In 540 Lạc Hà founded Triều Âm Thành on the island's western shore, where a river meets the sea, as a harbour of its own beside the old Cô Phàm ports. Its builders bored the breakwater so the tide would pass through rather than break it, found that it sang, and named the city for the sound. When the Cô Phàm fleet was lost in the Age of the North Star Compact, Triều Âm's harbour took much of the island's sea trade. In the great storm of the Age of Vein Wars, while the fishing fleet sheltered at Nguyệt Loan Thôn, the breakwater is said to have shrieked all night and held. Lạc Hà's ships to and from the island still call here first.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat western shore at a river mouth: rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs stepping up gently from the water, a harbour of ships. Along the sea front a long curved stone breakwater pierced with rows of round holes, white spray bursting through them. Warm golden light from the top left, blue-green sea. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and breakwater.
levels: The breakwater is lengthened along the river mouth and a customs hall rises at the harbour gate.
A second harbour basin is walled in, and a tall bell-less listening tower stands on the breakwater's end, open to the sea wind.

places.name: Thanh Điền Trấn
places.look: A small walled market town in a sea of bright green fields that run to the horizon. Outside its gate stretches a long row of hitching rails where the farmers' horses wait, since the fields are too far to walk.
places.lore: The fields around Thanh Điền stretch so far that its farmers ride to work, and children learn to sit a horse before they can walk far. The town answers to Mục Vân Trang, whose head Khấu Mục Vân was born here in 940 on the same night as a spirit foal; the town still holds a horse fair on that night.
