places.art_brief: A low town miniature in flat, vivid green fields: a small rectangular grey wall and grey-tile roofs, and outside the gate a long straight row of timber hitching rails with tiny horse specks. Green field strips running out to the edges of the footprint, the coast just at one side. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and its near fields.
levels: A walled horse yard joins the town and the hitching rails double along the road.
A granary row and a fair ground with a viewing stand rise beside the walls.

places.name: Thảo Đường Thành
places.look: A walled city on the flat coastal plain, its grey roofs low among farms. Outside the walls lies a chequerboard of grass-banked ponds, each a square of sky, with fish and ducks raised in every one.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông founded the city in 680 among the farms of the western plain, and it lives by them: rice, fish ponds, ducks and hemp. Its name comes from the ponds the first farmers dug; each family owns a square, and the banks between are common ground. Its market day is the slowest and friendliest on the plain.
places.history: Farmers worked this stretch of the western plain long before the city, under Lạc Hà Tông's rule since the Age of Seven Seats. They dug grass-banked ponds for fish and ducks and to catch the plain's floods before they reached the fields. In 680 Lạc Hà founded Thảo Đường Thành among the farms, to gather their harvest and guard them. Through the wars of the Compact age its fields and ponds kept the western plain fed. During the War of Broken Halberds Lạc Hà built its western watch at Lô Cảng Thôn to guard the coast boats along this shore. Today the sect's stewards come here to count harvests, not swords.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat green coastal plain: rectangular grey walls, low grey-tile roofs, and outside the walls a regular grid of square ponds with green grass banks, each pond a small square of reflected blue sky, tiny white specks of ducks. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and the pond grid.
levels: A new granary ward is walled in and more ponds are dug in rows along the road.
A tall grain hall with a double roof rises at the city's heart, and canals link the pond grid to the sea.

places.name: Ngư Lương Trấn
places.look: A small walled town where a plain river spills into the sea. Across the river mouth runs a great zigzag weir of stone and bamboo, the largest on the plain, its traps glinting with fish.
places.lore: Lạc Hà's rule brought fishing weirs to the plain's rivers in 430, and the town grew around the largest. The weir is rebuilt piece by piece every year, the family that tends a stretch of it keeps that stretch's fish, and quarrels over the weir go to the town's oldest fisher.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature at a river mouth on a flat grassy coast: a small rectangular grey wall and grey-tile roofs on one bank; across the river mouth a long zigzag line of stones and bamboo fencing with small basket traps. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and the weir.
levels: A fish market roof and smoking sheds rise on the bank by the weir.
A second weir is built upstream and the walls take in both banks, joined by a footbridge along the old weir.

places.name: Liễu Ngạn Trấn
places.look: A small walled town on a river through flat grassland, set behind a high earthen levee. On the levee stands a tall stone flood-pillar cut with the marks of every great flood, the highest painted red; willows line the bank on either side.
places.lore: In 410 the townsfolk planted willows on the bank at Liễu Ngạn to hold the river where it floods, and the town has fought the river ever since. When the water climbs past the red mark on the pillar, the drum is beaten and every household sends someone to the levee.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature on a flat green riverbank: a small rectangular grey wall and grey-tile roofs behind a long raised earthen levee lined with willows; on the levee a single tall slim stone pillar with dark notches and one red band. The river running past. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and levee.
levels: The levee is faced with stone and a drum house is built beside the flood-pillar.
A stone river gate and a sluice tower guard the town, and the levee runs on past the walls on both sides.

places.name: Hòa Phong Trấn
places.look: A small port town on the open bay coast, its grey roofs low and airy. On every roof stands a tall woven wind-scoop turned toward the sea, so the whole town seems to lean into the breeze.
places.lore: In 900, the year of the southern plague, a gentle sea breeze kept Hòa Phong Trấn free of fever, and the town has built wind-scoops on its roofs ever since to keep the sea air moving through every room. Sick travellers are brought here to recover, and its healers swear by the breeze before any pill.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature on a grassy bay coast: a small rectangular wall, grey-tile roofs each topped by a tall woven straw-coloured scoop opening toward the sea, a small harbour. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: A house of healing with a long open veranda rises facing the sea.
The town grows a seaside terrace of guesthouses for the sick, each with its own tall wind-scoop, and a stone quay for the boats that bring them.

places.name: Ngũ Cốc Thành
places.look: A walled port city on the bay coast, its quay lined with granaries. Along the waterfront stands a row of tall round grain towers, each roofed differently for its grain, with wooden chutes running down to the ships.
places.lore: Ngũ Cốc Thành grew rich on the trade Kim Cốc lost when Kim Cốc Viên burned. It ships the grain of the bay and the western plain, and many of its merchants are Kim Cốc families who rebuilt their fortunes in grain. Each grain tower has its own guild, and their rivalry runs the city.
places.history: Before this city, much of the bay's trade went through Kim Cốc Thành, the merchant city around Kim Cốc Viên. A few years before this city was founded, Kim Cốc Viên collapsed in a market crash and a great fire, and Kim Cốc Thành burned. Its merchants were begging in Vật Hoa Thị the next year, and its trade looked for a new harbour. In 1010 Ngũ Cốc Thành was founded on the bay coast and grew rich on the trade Kim Cốc lost. Its builders raised the grain towers on the quay first and the walls after, so the trade would never wait. Under Lạc Hà Tông it is now the bay's grain port, and its guilds, remembering Kim Cốc's fire, keep their granaries in stone.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat bay coast: rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs, and along the quay a line of tall round stone-and-timber grain towers with conical roofs in grey tile, thatch and red-brown tile, wooden chutes slanting to ships at the quay. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and quay.
levels: A guild hall for the grain towers rises behind the quay, and a breakwater shelters the ships.
A second row of grain towers is built on a new pier, and the walls take in the barge canal from the plain.

places.name: Phong Lâm Trấn
places.look: A walled harbour town among red maples where a river meets the sea, its grey-tile roofs half hidden in leaves. At its centre stands the old Tạ clan hall, its deep eaves lined end to end with the mud nests of swallows, so that in spring the hall seems to breathe birds.
places.lore: Phong Lâm Trấn, Maple Wood Town, grew among the maples Lạc Hà's founder planted around the first hall, and is now kept by Nam Phố Đường. The Tạ family, once great in another land, arrived in 470 with nothing but their name, and the swallows of their old hall followed them; no one in town will knock down a swallow's nest. In 1000 the Tạ and their old rivals the Vương exchanged letters for the first time in four hundred years, and the letter is read aloud in the clan hall every New Year.
places.history: In 295 Lạc Hà Tông's founder planted maples around the first hall, and Phong Lâm Trấn grew among them as a landing where the river meets the sea. Townsfolk still point to a moss-grown stone plinth under the oldest maples and call it the first hall. Through the Age of First Gates and the Age of Seven Seats the town shipped timber and fish to the sect upriver. In 470 the Tạ family came with nothing but their name, and the swallows of their old hall followed them to nest under the eaves of the new one. The Tạ never regained their old greatness, but they became the town's clerks and harbour reckoners. Some four centuries later the new Nam Phố Đường took the town into its keeping, and its scribes began to buy paper and pine soot on the quay. In 1000 the Tạ and the Vương, old rival clans now far apart, exchanged letters for the first time in four hundred years.
places.art_brief: A low walled harbour town inside a rectangular wall at a river mouth on the sea: grey-tile roofs half hidden by red and orange maple crowns, a small timber quay with two boats, and at the centre one larger clan hall whose deep dark eaves are dotted along their whole length with small brown swallow nests. Sea on one side, river on the other, maple woods at the base. Warm golden light from the top left making the maples glow. No text, no people or birds larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: The wall reaches the waterline, a stone quay takes larger boats, and a second clan hall rises opposite the Tạ hall.
A curved harbour mole runs out under the maples, a two-storey gate tower stands on the sea wall, and the Tạ hall gains an upper storey whose new eaves the swallows fill within a spring.

places.name: Tang Ma Thành
places.look: A walled city on a river among endless rows of mulberry and blue-flowering hemp. Its river channels are crossed not by stone but by a lattice of swaying hemp-rope bridges slung between timber towers, which hum when the wind blows. Rope walks run along the outer wall, where long strands are twisted under open sheds.
places.lore: Tang Ma Thành, Mulberry and Hemp City, is Lạc Hà Tông's silk and rope city on the Ngư Ca plain. Its hemp ropes are so strong that Lãng Đào's ferrymen will buy no other, and its rope-makers swear no Tang Ma rope has ever parted under load. The talisman mistress Châu Phi Vân was born here and drew her first talisman in mulberry juice at four; children of the city still paint charms on their doors in purple juice each summer.
places.history: Lạc Hà Tông founded Tang Ma Thành in 330 among the mulberry and hemp fields of Ngư Ca Xuyên, the same year it took the bay of Thu Thủy Loan. Silk from its mulberry groves and rope from its hemp fed the sect's treasury through the Age of Seven Seats and the long Compact. The city lay far behind the front both when Lạc Hà lost the War of the Pivot and when it lost on Chiết Kích Nguyên, and its looms never stopped. In 930 Châu Phi Vân was born here, and at four she drew her first talisman in mulberry juice. By 1100 its hemp ropes were so prized that Lãng Đào's ferrymen would buy no other. In 1174, in the Ferry War, Tùng Đào raiders cut every rope bridge on the Ngư Ca border, and Tang Ma wove new ones in a month.
places.art_brief: A walled city in a rectangular wall on a grassland river: a dense grid of grey-tile roofs, the river channels through it crossed by many thin sagging rope bridges hung between small timber towers, long open rope-walk sheds along the outer wall. Neat green mulberry rows and blue-flowered hemp fields at the base. Warm golden light from the top left catching the rope lines. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: Weaving halls and silk-dyeing yards spill outside the wall, and a stone gatehouse rises over the main rope bridge.
A second wall rings the rope walks and dyeworks, a tall drum tower stands at the centre, and the lattice of rope bridges spreads over every channel, hung with silk pennants.

places.name: Thạch Kiều Thành
places.look: The first city of the heart sits astride a river in rolling steppe, a walled grid of grey roofs crossing the water on one great stone bridge. The bridge wears its age plainly: its old central arches are dark, almost black, while the wide new deck and outer arches added in 1050 are pale grey. Bell towers stand at both ends.
places.lore: Thạch Kiều Thành grew from the stone bridge where mortal traders from four coasts first met, and is the city where the North Star Compact was set in 510. Its people call the bridge the oldest thing in the heart, and the old stones taken out when it was widened are kept in the Pivot's hall. On the day the Compact was signed every bell in the city rang without being struck, and on that day each year the bells are left silent, so as not to answer. Both the head of Thiên Xu Tông, Doãn Ngọc Hành, and his disciple Doãn Hi Hòa were born here.
places.history: In 50 mortal traders began to meet at a stone bridge here, where the roads from four coasts cross. Under Thiên Xu Tông's protection the crossing grew into Thạch Kiều Thành in 150, the first city of the heart. In 270 Kỳ Tùng Ẩn and Chung Hoài Cực met here and drank for three days, and the Pine and the Pivot kept the peace for two centuries. In 510 Chung Hoài Cực set the North Star Compact before the seven sects in the city and stamped it with the Bắc Thần Ấn, and every bell in Thạch Kiều rang without being struck. On the night the founder died in 760, Doãn Ngọc Hành was born here under the fifth star of the Dipper. In 1050 the stone bridge was widened for the first time, and its old stones were carried to the Pivot's hall. In 1130 Doãn Hi Hòa was born here at sunrise, and Doãn Ngọc Hành took her as his disciple when she was five.
places.art_brief: A walled city in a rectangular wall on a steppe river: a dense grid of grey-tile roofs on both banks joined by one broad multi-arched stone bridge, its central arches dark near-black stone and its widened outer arches and deck pale grey, with a small bell tower at each end. Dry golden steppe and the river at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the pale stone. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second wall takes in the caravan yards on both banks, and a tall drum tower rises at the bridge's north end.
The city spreads across both banks in a double grid, with a three-roof Hall of the Compact beside the bridge, bell towers on every gate, and stone embankments lined with river barges.

places.name: Song Kiều Trấn
places.look: A walled town on the river road where two humpbacked stone bridges cross the river side by side, one for carts going in and one for carts going out, with a small toll house on a pier between them. In the square behind stands a row of open ore scales under a long tiled roof.
places.lore: Song Kiều Trấn, Twin Bridges Town, has weighed the miners' ore on open scales in its square since 235, when Thiên Xu's assayers first did it in public view; no miner of Ngọc Hành has rebelled since. The Ôn clan built the twin bridges in 900 and keeps the tolls, and an Ôn sits in the toll house every day of the year. Locals cross by one bridge and come home by the other; using the wrong one is said to bring a bad bargain.
places.art_brief: A low town inside a rectangular wall on a grassland river: grey-tile roofs, two small parallel humpbacked stone bridges side by side over the river with a tiny toll house on a pier between them, and a long open tiled shed in the square. River and grassy banks at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the bridge arches. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second wall takes in an ore yard beside the bridges, and an Ôn clan hall with a two-storey gate faces the toll pier.
The town spreads across both banks inside one wall, with a drum tower over the square and a stone assay hall raised over the open scales.

places.name: Mạch Điền Trấn
places.look: A walled town in flat wheat country where a river meets the gulf, dominated by one tall granary raised on a ring of mushroom-shaped staddle stones, its steep thatched roof the highest thing on the plain. Wheat barges tie up at a timber quay below.
places.lore: Mạch Điền Trấn, Wheat Fields Town, grew around its granary after 530, when its wheat fields were set to feed Phượng Minh's palace. The staddle stones keep out rats and high tides alike, and townsfolk boast that their granary never lost a sack in the hungry years.
places.art_brief: A low town inside a rectangular wall at a river mouth on a flat coast: grey-tile roofs around one tall granary with a steep golden thatched roof raised on a ring of squat mushroom-shaped stones, a timber quay with a barge. Golden wheat fields and the gulf at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the thatch. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second granary on staddle stones and a stone harbour wall join the town, and the town wall is extended to the quay.
A row of great granaries stands along the harbour, with a granary-master's hall and a drum tower over the gate.

places.name: Thanh Khê Thành
places.look: Phượng Minh's port on the gulf sits where a clear brook runs into the sea, a walled grid of grey roofs around a wide harbour. All along the harbour wall hangs an unbroken row of red lanterns, lit every night, so from far out at sea the city shows as a glowing line on the water.
places.lore: Thanh Khê Thành, Clear Brook City, was founded by Phượng Minh Cung in 560 as its port on the gulf. In the Cinnabar Vein War, in 1157, its harbour sheltered Phượng Minh's wounded and the city's lanterns burned all year; the custom stayed, and each family keeps one lantern on the harbour wall lit from dusk to dawn, for those who came home and those who did not. Its brook water is so clear that sailors fill their casks here before any long voyage.
places.history: Phượng Minh Cung founded Thanh Khê Thành in 560 as its port on the gulf, where a clear brook runs into the sea. In its first two centuries it shipped the palace's rice and wheat along the coast and drew in the trade of the south. When Thôn Hải Môn's pirates burned the pearl harbour Châu Lệ Cảng two centuries after the founding, Thanh Khê armed its boats and watched its harbour mouth by night. Soon after, Phượng Minh's fleet sailed in the Pirate Purge under the Pivot's writ, and the Purge ended at Thôn Hải Môn itself. When Thính Vũ Lâu attacked Đan Sơn Mạch and the war dragged on, the harbour became the palace's place of healing. In 1157 it sheltered Phượng Minh's wounded, and the city's lanterns burned all year; they are lit still.
places.art_brief: A walled port city in a rectangular wall where a clear blue brook meets a calm gulf: a grid of grey-tile roofs around a wide harbour, the harbour wall lined along its whole length with a continuous row of small glowing red lanterns, a few boats at anchor. Water and a sandy shore at the base. Warm golden light from the top left, the lanterns glowing softly against the dusk side. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second wall takes in shipyards along the brook, and a stone harbour arm doubles the anchorage under the lanterns.
A red gate tower stands at the harbour mouth, a three-roof harbour hall faces the gulf, and the lantern row runs round the whole enlarged harbour.

places.name: Hoàng Vân Thành
places.look: A broad walled city on the river where the rice plain lies flattest, crowned inside its walls by a ring of tall round granaries capped in yellow-glazed tile. At harvest a haze of rice chaff hangs over the roofs and turns gold in the low sun, which gives the city its name. Grain barges crowd the river quay below the granary gates.
places.lore: This is Phượng Minh Cung's granary city, and its keepers count grain the way other cities count gold. When the seven-year drought struck in 649 its granaries fed the whole south, and the Palace's power has rested on its rice ever since. In 1060 it opened its doors to Băng Tâm's desert in a famine year, and the old quarrel of the Desert Road was quietly let go. Every granary keeper swears an oath at the river never to sell the last basket.
places.history: Phượng Minh Cung founded Hoàng Vân Thành in 600 as the granary of the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên. Its first round granaries were raised along the river, where the barges of Thủy Điền and the inland villages could reach them. In 649 a drought began that lasted seven years; the granaries were opened and fed the south until the rains came back. That drought made the Palace's rice its strength, and granary after granary was added in the years that followed. In the Desert Road War, Phượng Minh and Băng Tâm Các fought over the caravan road between the desert and this plain, and the city's grain carts rolled to the front instead of the markets. The truce the Pivot imposed brought the caravans back, but the bitterness lasted for centuries. In 1060, in a famine year in the desert, the granaries were opened to Băng Tâm's people, and the quarrel was quietly forgotten. Its keepers still tell that story to every new apprentice.
places.art_brief: A broad, low walled city miniature on flat green-gold rice plain beside a river: rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs, and inside them a ring of tall round brick granaries with conical yellow-glazed tile caps, the signature and tallest element. A pale golden haze of chaff hanging low over the roofs; a river quay with a few grain barges at the base. Warm golden-hour light from the top left makes the yellow caps glow. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second ring of granaries rises outside the walls and a stone grain wharf runs along the river.
A walled granary district with a yellow-roofed counting hall at its heart; a canal basin is cut from the river for the barges.

places.name: Đạo Hương Trấn
places.look: A small walled town of grey-tile roofs in a sea of rice, the smell of ripening grain heavy on the river wind. Along the field road outside the east gate stands a long row of carved stone stakes, one for each generation of the Vương family, each beside the paddy that generation planted.
places.lore: The Vương family, rivals of the Tạ in another land, settled here in 520, and every generation since has planted one new field and set its stone, carved with the planter's name and the year's first rain. In the last days of 1199 the Vương sent a letter of betrothal to the Tạ of Phong Lâm. The town is still waiting for the reply, and its matchmakers are keeping very quiet.
places.art_brief: A small low town miniature inside rectangular earthen walls: a cluster of grey-tile roofs among flooded green rice paddies by a river. The signature is a long straight row of small carved standing stones along the field road outside one gate, each beside its own paddy. Water mirrors in the paddies; warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: The Vương build an ancestral hall facing the row of stones, and the town walls are faced in brick.
A second walled quarter for rice merchants and a stone-paved field road; the row of generation stones now runs to the river.

places.name: Lục Dã Trấn
places.look: A walled town in open green meadows, ringed by a chequer of square herb beds in a dozen shades of green, each bordered by a low stone channel of spring water. In the morning the beds steam faintly and smell of mint and bitter root.
places.lore: Since 662 the meadows of Lục Dã have belonged to Lễ Tuyền Phái, which grows its healing herbs here. Mai Lễ Tuyền, the school's head, was born in the town in 850, and the townsfolk say her first cry made the spring flow sweeter. Mothers still bring newborns to the spring channel at the town gate for a first wash, hoping for the same luck.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature on bright green meadow: rectangular walls, grey-tile roofs, and around them the signature chequerboard of square herb beds in many greens, edged by thin glinting stone water channels. A small gate with a spring channel running out of it. Warm golden-hour light from the top left; soft morning steam over the beds. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A drying pavilion for herbs and a walled seed garden of Lễ Tuyền Phái beside the town.
A brick-walled town with a healers' hall at the gate, and the herb chequer spread far across the meadows.

places.name: Bình Dã Trấn
places.look: A walled town in an open plain cleared from the forest, its grey roofs gathered around a huge paved yard of sun-baked brick. On dry days the yard is covered edge to edge with mats of drying tea, herbs, cloth and grain brought in from the wet country around.
places.lore: Bình Dã became a town in 410 on the one open plain in the south where it rarely rains. Forest folk carry their wet harvests here to dry, and the town lives on the fees. When rain does come, the yard-keepers beat a gong and the whole town runs out to roll up the mats.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature on a dry open grassland clearing with rain forest at its edges and a river nearby: rectangular walls and grey-tile roofs around the signature, a large square paved brick yard covered in a patchwork of drying mats in green, brown and ochre. A small gong frame at the yard's edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, a clear sky over the town and darker cloud at the forest margins. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second drying yard outside the walls and roofed sheds to store the mats.
A brick-walled town with a raised drying terrace on every rooftop and a merchants' hall facing the great yard.

places.name: Xuân Thảo Thành
places.look: A city on a river at the forest's edge, enclosed by thick earthen walls whose tops are capped with living turf, green even in the dry months. Inside, grey-tile roofs stand among young trees, and in the meadows outside the walls old blackened stumps lie grown over with grass.
places.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu founded Xuân Thảo Thành in 640 on the forest land the Pivot gave it after the Petal Shore fighting. Its people take their name from the old line that wildfire cannot burn out the grass, for the spring wind brings it back. Every spring the citizens recut and replant the turf on the walls together, and it is a festival day. The charred stumps in the meadows are left untouched.
places.history: The land of Xuân Thảo was once forest on the edge of Lạc Anh Phái's Petal Shore. When Lạc Anh split, Lạc Hà Tông and Thính Vũ Lâu both claimed the empty shore, and their disciples fought in the burning orchards. Fire swept the land, and Hồng Vũ Thành burned, its petals and ashes falling together like red rain. Then the Pivot's judgement gave the bay to Lạc Hà and the forest to Thính Vũ. Twenty years after the judgement, in 640, Thính Vũ founded Xuân Thảo Thành on ground the fighting had burned, where new grass had come up through the ash. The city grew as a market for the forest villages and a stop on the road from the Tower toward the coast. Its turf walls were never stormed, and through the Age of Vein Wars it has stayed one of the Tower's quietest cities.
places.art_brief: A walled city miniature on green grassland by a river at a forest edge: thick earthen walls with rounded tops capped in bright living turf, the signature; inside, grey-tile roofs among young green trees and a modest gate tower as the tallest element. In the meadow outside, a few blackened tree stumps half hidden in grass. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second turf-capped wall ring and a stone bridge over the river with a market at its foot.
A walled forest-trade city with a timber hall on a grassy mound at its heart, its own roof turfed like the walls.

places.name: Lãng Hoa Thành
places.look: A walled port city on a dry, wind-bitten steppe coast at the mouth of a river. Its sea wall is pierced with rows of carved stone blowholes, and when the waves strike, white spray bursts from them in plumes like flowers along the whole waterfront. Behind the wall, grey roofs climb a low rise toward a watch hall.
places.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu founded the city in 800 on the sea-spray coast, once the Pirate Purge had made it safe at last. Its people are mostly fishers and salt-boilers who came down to the shore when the pirates were gone. On storm days children run along the wall racing the spray, and the one soaked by the biggest plume is called lucky for the year.
places.history: For centuries this coast lay nearly empty, open to the raiders of the southern gulf. Once Thôn Hải Môn was founded on its islet its sails came often, and the watchtowers of Vọng Hải learned to see them a day before they landed. Then the Pivot called the Pirate Purge, and it ended with Ô Kình Hải dead on his islet. Two decades later, in 800, while the War of Broken Halberds held the Tower's strength in the north, Thính Vũ Lâu founded Lãng Hoa Thành on the sea-spray coast, safe at last from pirates. Its builders cut the blowholes into the sea wall to break the force of the storm waves. With the Tower's eyes on the war, the young city grew up largely on its own. Since the Age of Vein Wars began it has been a fishing and salt port, far from the quarrels over veins.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature on a dry ochre steppe coast at a river mouth: grey-tile roofs climbing a low rise to a modest watch hall, the tallest element. The signature is the sea wall along the waterfront, pierced with a row of carved stone blowholes throwing up white plumes of spray like flowers. Salt pans at one side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left catching the spray. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second harbour mole with its own blowholes, and stone salt pans along the shore.
A walled upper town around the watch hall, and a long spray wall running the whole bay.

places.name: Vọng Hải Trấn
places.look: A walled town in coastal bamboo at a river mouth, below a line of low sea cliffs. Along the cliff tops stand tall watchtowers with stone footings and bamboo upper storeys, each with a signal frame looking out over the gulf.
places.lore: Vọng Hải belongs to Xuyên Lâm Môn, whose people keep the watchtowers manned. In 780 the towers saw Thôn Hải's sails a day before they landed, and the warning is still told as the saving of the coast. The town keeps a watch on every tower though no pirate has come in centuries, and a watcher caught asleep must carry water to every house.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature among green coastal bamboo at a river mouth, grey-tile roofs below low rocky sea cliffs. The signature is a row of tall watchtowers on the cliff tops, stone bases with bamboo upper storeys and small signal frames. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, blue sea at the base. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A walled signal post joins the towers along the cliffs, and a fishing harbour is dug in the river mouth.
A brick-walled coastal town with a beacon hall and a covered stair from the harbour to the towers.

places.name: Phong Đăng Trấn
places.look: A walled harbour town in fertile river meadows by the sea, its fields heavy with grain. In its main gate hangs a huge wooden steelyard balance, its beam as long as a boat, where grain carts are weighed for the tax before they enter.
places.lore: The Lục family's harvests at Phong Đăng are so rich that since 600 Thính Vũ has collected its grain tax here first each year. The first cart weighed on the great steelyard is always the Lục family's, and the whole town turns out to watch the beam. The neighbouring villages grumble that the beam is honest only once a year.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature on rich green river meadows by the sea: grey-tile roofs inside rectangular walls, golden grain fields around. The signature is a massive wooden steelyard beam with a stone counterweight, hanging from a roofed frame over the main gate. A small harbour with grain boats. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A walled granary yard for the tax grain and a stone quay for the boats.
A brick-walled town with the Lục family's manor on a rise and a second steelyard over the harbour gate.

places.name: Thạch Cơ Thành
places.look: A walled harbour city on a flat stretch of coast, built around a long stone jetty that juts far out into the gulf. Most of the jetty is grey, sea-worn stone, but its outer end has been rebuilt in bright red stone that stands out against the water.
places.lore: Thạch Cơ Thành rose in 776 around the stone jetty where Phượng Minh's and Lạc Hà's fleets gathered for the Pirate Purge under the Pivot's writ. In 1190 a storm cracked the jetty, and Phượng Minh rebuilt it with red stone from the ruins of Xích Thành. Old sailors grumble that the red end is unlucky; young ones say it is the strongest part.
places.history: Before the Purge this was a quiet stretch of shore within sight of the pirates' gulf. In 776 Đỗ Tinh Hà called the Pirate Purge, Phượng Minh's and Lạc Hà's fleets sailed under the Pivot's writ, and Thạch Cơ Thành rose around the stone jetty where they gathered. Five years later the Purge ended at Thôn Hải Môn with Ô Kình Hải dead, and the fleets came home here. The captives freed from Thôn Hải's hold were landed at the jetty and walked home to villages like Lô Châu. After the war the city stayed on as a port and a station for the Palace's ships in the gulf. In 1190 a storm cracked the jetty, and Phượng Minh rebuilt it with stone from the ruins of Xích Thành. Its red end is now the first thing incoming ships see.
places.art_brief: A walled harbour city miniature on a flat grassy coast: rectangular walls with grey-tile roofs and a modest harbour hall as the tallest building, and the signature, a long straight stone jetty running far out into blue water, grey along most of its length and bright red stone at its outer end. A few ships moored along it. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second jetty beside the first and a walled shipyard on the shore.
A fortified harbour city with a stone lighthouse at the red end of the jetty and a sea wall around the anchorage.

places.name: Tang Điền Trấn
places.look: A walled coastal town on rust-red earth, surrounded by long rows of mulberry bushes. Among the rows stand low two-storey silkworm sheds with slatted wooden walls, and in season the whole town smells of boiling cocoons.
places.lore: Mulberry fields have been planted in the red soil of Tang Điền since 200, and they feed the silkworms of the south. The town now belongs to Phần Vũ Đường. Its silk women say the red soil puts fire in the thread, and some claim that Xích Thành's fire-silk began with their worms.
places.history: Mulberry was first planted in the red soil of Tang Điền in 200, in the Age of First Gates, and its silkworms soon fed the looms of the south. When Xích Thành Môn rose among the red cliffs a generation later, the town fell under its shadow, and its silk women still claim the sect's fire-silk banner began with their worms. Under the heir who burned villages, the town's elders say, it paid in silk to be spared. After Phượng Minh destroyed the gate under writ, Tang Điền passed with the rest of Đan Huyệt Châu to the Palace. The silk caravans that rest at Tang Âm carried its thread along the coast road. When Phần Vũ Đường was founded in the old vents, the town was given to the new hall, and its mulberry rows now feed the hall as well as the looms. The red earth and the slatted sheds are much as they were in the first planting.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature on a flat coast of rust-red soil: grey-tile roofs inside rectangular walls, surrounded by neat rows of green mulberry bushes, and the signature, long low two-storey sheds with slatted wooden walls among the rows. A small landing at the shore. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the red earth. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A reeling house by the shore and more silkworm sheds in the outer fields.
A brick-walled silk town with a dye works and a stone pier for the silk boats.

places.name: Tuyết Lộc Thôn
places.look: A handful of low log houses with grey tile and turf roofs sit on the snowy north shore of the lake, entered through a gate arch built entirely of shed reindeer antlers. Herds graze the lichen between the houses and the water's edge.
places.lore: Reindeer herders settled the lake's snowy north shore in 140, and their camp became Tuyết Lộc Thôn; each spring the herders add the year's finest shed antlers to the arch. A fisher of this village pulled from the lake the great pearl that started Hàm Nguyệt Trang's pearl farms, and the village answers to the manor. Since the Long Lake War, Băng Tâm fishers share the northern shore, and the herders trade them hides for salt.
places.art_brief: A tiny village of half a dozen low log houses with grey tile roofs dusted with snow, on a white lakeshore with dark spruce behind. Signature element: a tall, rough gate arch made of interlocked pale reindeer antlers at the village entrance. At the base: snowy ground, a fenced corral, a few reindeer as specks, the lake edge with a short plank jetty. Warm light from the top left on the antlers. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village footprint.
levels: The antler arch is doubled in height, and a row of smokehouses and a fenced winter corral grow along the shore.
A small stone shrine to the lake's first pearl stands beside the arch, and a longer jetty serves the fishers of the northern shore.

places.name: Hàn Yên Thôn
places.look: A huddle of grey-roofed houses with tall stone chimneys sits on the lake shore, where on still winter mornings the smoke hangs frozen in pale columns. At the ice edge stands a lone post with a bronze bell, rung at every dusk.
places.lore: The village takes its name from a winter so cold that smoke froze above its chimneys. When a snow-leopard spirit beast took a child from here, Hàm Nguyệt Trang's disciples tracked it for forty days across the ice; since then the bell at the shore calls the children in before dark. Villagers leave a fish on the bell post's stone base on the night the hunt set out, for the disciples who went.
places.art_brief: A small cluster of grey-tile houses with unusually tall stone chimneys on a snowy lakeshore, thin pale smoke columns standing straight up. Signature element: a single tall wooden post at the ice edge carrying a small bronze bell under a little grey roof. At the base: snow, a strip of grey lake ice, birch and spruce at the back. Warm light from the top left, the bell glinting. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village footprint.
levels: A palisade faces the forest and a second bell post stands at the village's back toward the trees.
A small stone watch-house for the lake patrol rises beside the shore bell, its single grey roof the tallest in the village.

places.name: Noãn Ốc Thôn
places.look: Domed stone houses, thick-walled and half sunk into the ground, cluster on the lake shore like loaves of bread, each capped with a small grey tile roof. Between them a timber bath-house stands over a hot spring, its steam visible far across the ice.
places.lore: Tùng Đào's first steward of the north built warm stone houses for the lake villages, and the hamlet beside them is still called Noãn Ốc. Since a hot spring was found under the snow here in 1015, old cultivators come every winter to soak their bones, and villagers rent bath hours by the burning of an incense stick. Locals say the steward's houses stay warm because he mixed a little of his own qi into the mortar.
places.art_brief: A small village of round, domed, thick-walled stone houses half sunk into a snowy lakeshore, each with a little grey tile cap. Signature element: the domed beehive houses themselves, clustered like loaves, with one plain timber bath-house among them giving off a soft steam plume. At the base: snow, a strip of lake ice, a few birches. Warm light from the top left rounding the domes. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village footprint.
levels: New domed houses ring the bath-house and a covered walkway links them against the snow.
A two-storey guest lodge for visiting cultivators rises beside the spring, and the bath-house gains a second, stone-walled pool.

places.name: Mạch Lãng Thôn
places.look: A few grey-roofed farmhouses stand among wheat fields that ripple like waves over dark volcanic soil. Low walls of black lava stone divide the gold fields into long strips running down to the sea.
places.lore: Wheat first grew here in the warm ash of the cape, and the fields of Mạch Lãng Thôn are still the oldest on it. Farmers say the ash remembers the fire and keeps the seed warm through the frosts. At harvest they leave the last strip standing for the wind to thresh.
places.art_brief: A tiny farming village of a few grey-tile farmhouses on a gentle coastal slope. Signature element: long strips of golden wheat over black volcanic soil, divided by low, dark lava-stone walls that run in parallel lines down to the shore. At the base: a narrow dark beach and one small boat. Warm light from the top left raking across the wheat. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village fields.
levels: The lava-stone walls extend up the slope over new strips and a stone threshing floor is laid by the houses.
A small granary barn with a double grey roof and a windmill on the slope serve the wider fields.

places.name: Phong Phàm Thôn
places.look: A village of grey roofs sits on a windy headland above its boat sheds. On the point stands a tall mast hung with long cloth streamers of many colours, which the sailors read before every launch.
places.lore: The sailors of Phong Phàm Thôn learned to read the cape's winds so well that their sails never go slack. Every family hangs its own streamer on the wind mast, and children learn the winds by watching how each one flies. Merchants of the coast hire Phong Phàm pilots whenever they can get them.
places.art_brief: A small village of grey-tile houses on a grassy headland, boat sheds and a slipway below on the shore. Signature element: a tall wooden mast on the very tip of the headland trailing long, many-coloured cloth streamers in the wind. At the base: grass, rocks, a few small sailboats drawn up. Warm light from the top left catching the streamers. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the headland.
levels: A second mast stands on the far point and the boat sheds grow into a small yard with a stone slipway.
A pilots' hall with a lookout gallery rises beside the mast, and a short stone breakwater shelters the boats.

places.name: Hòa Thử Thôn
places.look: Low farmhouses sit among millet and grain fields on the coast. Beside them stand rows of small granary huts raised on mushroom-shaped stone stilts, keeping the grain clear of damp and rats.
places.lore: Grain from Hòa Thử Thôn fed Yên Ba Thành through the long winter of 860, and the city has not forgotten. The village keeps one granary hut empty in every row in memory of that winter, filled only when another bad year comes. Its millet wine is poured at harvest feasts all along the cape.
places.art_brief: A small farming village of grey-tile houses among yellow millet fields near the shore. Signature element: neat rows of small square granary huts with grey roofs, each raised on mushroom-shaped stone stilts. At the base: field strips, a cart track, a small boat landing. Warm light from the top left casting short shadows under the raised granaries. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village.
levels: The granary rows double and a stone road links the village to the coast road.
A large stone grain store with a double roof rises at the end of the rows, and a small pier ships grain to Yên Ba.

places.name: Ẩn Loan Thôn
places.look: A few houses cling above a narrow cove hidden between cliffs, out of sight from the open sea. A steep stair cut into the rock leads down from the village to the mouth of a sea cave at the water's edge.
places.lore: One winter a pirate crew hid in the cove below the village, and the villagers fed them and said nothing. When Thôn Hải fell the pirates vanished in a single night, leaving a chest of salt and a child; some say the child's line still lives here. The villagers are polite to strangers and tell them very little.
places.art_brief: A tiny village of a few grey-tile houses on a cliff top above a narrow, hidden cove. Signature element: a steep stair cut into the cliff face zigzagging down to a dark sea cave mouth at the waterline. At the base: a small pebble beach, dark green water, one rowing boat. Warm light from the top left, the cove in partial shadow. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, ships, anything outside the cove.
levels: A rope hoist is rigged beside the stair and a few new houses climb along the cliff top.
A small stone harbour wall is built across the cove's mouth, and a grey-roofed watch-house stands over the cave stair.

places.name: Ô Đề Thôn
places.look: A small fishing village of grey roofs lies on the shore under a long ridge. On the ridge top a single huge bare oak stands black against the sky, its branches crowded with roosting crows.
places.lore: Crows gathered on the ridge in such numbers that the village beneath was named Ô Đề. Villagers feed them at the new year and believe the crows warn of storms by leaving the oak. Fishers look up at the ridge before they set out.
places.history: Fishers beached their boats under this ridge in the Age of First Gates, without a village to speak of. In 410 crows gathered on the ridge in such numbers that the village growing beneath was named Ô Đề. The great oak on the crest was already old then, and the crows have roosted in it ever since. Fishers learned that the birds leave the oak before a storm, and began to watch the ridge before setting out. The custom of feeding the crows at the new year followed, and no villager will harm one. The village passed with the hills to Thúy Vi Tông, and its boats now sell their catch to the sect's towns along the coast.
places.art_brief: A tiny fishing village of grey-tile houses on a strip of shore below a long wooded ridge. Signature element: one huge leafless oak on the ridge top, dark against the sky, its branches dotted with black crows as specks. At the base: a pebble beach, a few boats, drying racks. Warm light from the top left silhouetting the oak. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village and its ridge.
levels: A few more houses climb the slope toward the ridge and a small fish-smoking shed lines the shore.
A small shrine to the crows stands at the foot of the oak, and a stone pier serves the boats.

places.name: Lâm Tuyền Thôn
places.look: A coastal village of grey roofs lies under wooded slopes, with a long line of split bamboo pipes running down from the woods on wooden trestles. The pipes end in a row of stone troughs in the village square, always running.
places.lore: A spring in the woods above the village cured the coughing sickness of 760, and the village took its name from its woods and springs. The pipe line was built to bring the water down for the sick, and every family repairs its own length of it. Travellers still come to fill jars at the troughs.
places.history: Before it had its name, the village was a few fishers' houses on the shore below the wooded slopes. In 760 a coughing sickness spread along the coast, and a spring in the woods above the village cured those who drank from it. The village took its name from its woods and springs, and its families together built the long bamboo pipe line to carry the water down to the sick. Each family took one length of it to keep in repair, a duty passed from parent to child. Travellers and the sick of other villages came to fill jars at the troughs, and some of them stayed. The spring has never failed, and the villagers say that is because no one has ever sold its water.
places.art_brief: A small village of grey-tile houses on the coast below wooded hills. Signature element: a long line of split bamboo pipes on wooden trestles running down from the woods to a row of stone troughs in the village square. At the base: the shore, a few boats, a path into the woods. Warm light from the top left on the bamboo. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village and its pipe line.
levels: A small roofed spring-house is built at the top of the pipe line and a second line feeds a bath-house.
A healers' lodge with a double grey roof stands by the troughs, and the trestles are rebuilt in stone.

places.name: Thu Diệp Thôn
places.look: A small village of grey roofs by the shore stands in front of a grove of maples that burns crimson every autumn. Wooden frames of pressed leaves dry in rows along the house walls.
places.lore: Red leaves from Thu Diệp Thôn are sold in Lam Yên Thị as bookmarks for scripture, and scholars from three sects come to buy them. Each leaf is pressed between boards for a season. The villagers say a leaf picked by a cultivator turns brown, so only mortals may gather them.
places.history: For most of its life the village was a quiet fishing place on the shore, known only for the red maples behind it. Its people pressed the leaves for their own pleasure and for the little shrines of the coast. In 1140 red leaves from Thu Diệp Thôn began to be sold in Lam Yên Thị as bookmarks for scripture, and scholars came from three sects to buy them. The trade made the village busier than it had ever been, and drying frames went up along every wall. The rule that only mortals may pick the leaves grew with the trade, and the villagers keep it strictly. The grove is now tended as carefully as any herb terrace in the hills.
places.art_brief: A tiny village of grey-tile houses by the shore with a dense grove of red maples behind it. Signature element: the maple grove in full crimson, the brightest red on this coast, with small wooden leaf-pressing frames along the house walls. At the base: the shore, a footpath, a single boat. Warm light from the top left glowing through the red leaves. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village and its grove.
levels: The maple grove is extended up the slope and a long drying shed for pressed leaves is built.
A small hall for sorting and wrapping the leaves stands by the road, its double grey roof facing the grove.

places.name: Bạch Hoa Thôn
places.look: A small coastal village of grey roofs stands in a bright grove of white birches. Among the pale trunks the black stumps of old burned trees still stand, so the grove is pied black and white.
places.lore: White birches grew where a forest fire had burned, and the new village was named Bạch Hoa. Villagers strip birch bark for writing sheets and boxes, and will not pull up the old stumps, saying they hold the ground for the birches. Charcoal from those stumps is never burned in a house.
places.art_brief: A tiny coastal village of grey-tile houses inside a grove of slender white birches. Signature element: the white birch trunks mixed with tall black charred stumps, a striking black-and-white grove. At the base: a narrow beach, a small jetty, a bark-drying rack. Warm light from the top left on the white bark. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village and its grove.
levels: A bark workshop with long drying racks is built at the grove's edge and the jetty is lengthened.
A small double-roofed shrine stands among the oldest stumps, and a stone pier serves boats carrying bark goods.

places.name: Thanh Tùng Thôn
places.look: A river village of grey roofs sits beside a grove of tall pines planted in neat rows, each with a small flat stone at its foot. The rows run from the riverbank to the forest edge like ranks of soldiers.
places.lore: When a beast tide overran Hổ Khiếu Trấn, its survivors moved to Thanh Tùng Thôn and planted a green pine for each of their dead. The pines are tall now, and each spring families sweep the stones beneath their own trees. No one cuts or taps them.
places.art_brief: A small village of grey-tile houses on a river bank. Signature element: a grove of tall pines planted in exact rows beside the village, each tree with a small pale flat stone at its foot. At the base: the river, a ferry landing, a path between the rows. Warm light from the top left casting long ordered shadows. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village and its grove.
levels: A low stone wall is built around the memorial grove and a few new houses line the river path.
A small ancestral hall with a double grey roof stands at the head of the pine rows.

places.name: Tùng Phong Thôn
places.look: A small river village of grey roofs lies in the pines. Between two great pines at its edge long strings are stretched, and they hum and moan whenever the wind blows, a sound that carries over the whole hamlet.
places.lore: Vạn Hác Viện's zither students practise in Tùng Phong hamlet, and the villagers have learned to sleep through anything. A student once strung the wind strings between the two pines, and the village keeps them tuned in return for the students' quiet hours. Children here can name a note before they can name the stars.
places.art_brief: A tiny village of grey-tile houses beside a river in a pine forest. Signature element: two great pines at the village edge with long fine strings stretched between them, glinting in the light. At the base: a river bank, a shallow ford, a few garden plots. Warm light from the top left on the strings. Avoid: text, people larger than specks, anything outside the village.
levels: A small open practice pavilion for visiting students is built near the strings.
A second pair of pines is strung across the river, and a guesthouse with a double grey roof stands by the ford.

places.name: Tuyết Ốc Thôn
places.look: In winter the village almost vanishes: low turf-roofed houses sunk half into the ground, chimneys smoking through the drifts. Each house is marked by a tall red-painted door-pole so neighbours can find each other under the snow. In summer the poles stand oddly tall over a cluster of grassy mounds by the upper river.
places.lore: Winters on the upper river are so deep that the houses of Tuyết Ốc have been built half under the snow since at least 340. Families dig tunnels from door to door and visit underground all winter. A new bride paints her husband's door-pole fresh red on her first spring in the village.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a tight cluster of low, half-sunken houses with turf and grass roofs beside a narrow upper river, with patches of snow around them. Over each house rises a tall thin red door-pole, the signature element, a little forest of red lines taller than the roofs. Smoke from short chimneys. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the snow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A longhouse dug into the riverbank for winter gatherings, with snow-tunnels from every door.
A small timber stockade and a raised storehouse above the snowline, and door-poles crowned with carved finials.

places.name: Hàn Mai Thôn
places.look: A handful of grey-tile houses sits around a small snowy square, and in the middle of the square grows one gnarled winter plum behind a low bamboo fence. In the cold months its red blossoms are the only colour for days of travel. Villagers bow to it on their way down to the river.
places.lore: In 420 a winter plum bloomed through the snow above a buried child, and the diggers found her alive; the village was named Hàn Mai. The tree in the square is said to have grown from a cutting of that plum. Every child born in winter is carried to the tree before it is given a name.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a handful of low grey-tile houses around a little square on a snowy riverbank. In the centre of the square, one gnarled dark plum tree with bright red blossoms inside a low bamboo fence, the signature element. A narrow path down to the river. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, red petals glowing against white snow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A small shrine roof beside the plum and a few new houses facing the square.
A walled courtyard around the plum with a gate arch, and a second, younger plum planted at the village edge.

places.name: Bạch Lang Thôn
places.look: The village circles a hollow at its heart, ringed with white-limed boulders: the old den of the white wolf king. Children run between the houses with wolf-tooth charms clicking at their necks. A path from the hollow leads down to the river, where women beat laundry on flat stones.
places.lore: Thôi Khinh Hồng of Tùng Đào Cung slew the white wolf king of Cửu Khúc Xuyên, and in 456 the village built on its den was named Bạch Lang. Its children wear wolf-tooth charms. Each spring the boulders around the den are limed white again, and the village says that the year they are left grey, the wolves will come back.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a ring of low grey-tile and thatch houses around a central grassy hollow, the hollow rimmed by a circle of chalk-white boulders, the signature element. A footpath runs from the hollow to a strip of river with flat washing stones. Forest edge on one side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left making the white stones glow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A timber fence around the village and a small shrine at the lip of the den.
A stone wall with a gate carved with a wolf's head, and a hunters' lodge beside the den.

places.name: Ba Quang Thôn
places.look: A fishing village on the shore of a chain of small mountain lakes stepping down a grassy slope, its boats drawn up on the gravel. At midday the lakes throw so much light that the village seems to stand in a blaze. Flat reed rafts lie on the beach, ready for the evening nets.
places.lore: Light glints so brightly on the mountain lakes at Ba Quang that travellers have taken the village for a fire since at least 600, and more than one has run up with a bucket. Its people net lake fish and ferry Cửu Cao Phái's riders across the water. The elders squint their whole lives, and a squint is thought handsome here.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a few low grey-tile and reed-roofed houses on the gravel shore of a chain of small bright lakes stepping down a grassy slope, the signature element, each lake a mirror of gold light. Reed rafts and small boats on the beach. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, strong sparkles on the water. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and its lakes.
levels: A timber boat landing and a drying rack for nets along the lowest lake.
A small walled hamlet with a lakeside shrine and a crane perch for Cửu Cao's riders.

places.name: Hạc Quy Thôn
places.look: A quiet marsh-edge village of reed-thatched and grey-tile houses on a slow river. In the meadow beyond, the villagers keep a crescent-shaped landing pool dug in the turf and edged with flat grey stepping stones, where the cranes come down each year. They clear its weed by hand all summer.
places.lore: Cranes return to the marshes here on the same day every year, and since 700 the village where they land has been called Hạc Quy; Cửu Cao Phái rides the first of them. Ung Hạc Minh was born here in 1010, the year the cranes stayed a month longer. On landing day the whole village stands silent around the crescent pool until the last bird folds its wings.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a handful of reed-thatched and grey-tile houses on a slow river at a marsh edge. Beside them, in a green meadow, a crescent-shaped pool edged with flat grey stepping stones, the signature element. Reeds and still marsh water around. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people or birds larger than specks, nothing outside the village and its meadow.
levels: A reed-roofed watching shelter beside the crescent pool and a few new houses along the river.
A timber fence, a small shrine to the cranes, and a rest hall for Cửu Cao's riders.

places.name: Lộc Uyển Thôn
places.look: A hillside village of log houses above a high meadow where deer gather each spring. At the meadow's edge stands a black stone stele carrying Thiên Xu's ban on hunting, and shed antlers are heaped around its foot. A rail fence keeps the village goats off the deer's grass.
places.lore: Deer have gathered each spring in the high meadow of Lộc Uyển since before 380, when Thiên Xu forbade hunting there. Children collect the antlers the stags shed and lay them at the stele as a gift to the Pivot. Poachers from outside are rare; the villagers report them before the deer have even scattered.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a few log houses with grey-tile roofs on a forested slope above a high green meadow. At the meadow edge, a black stone stele with a heap of pale shed antlers around its foot, the signature element, its face blank in the art. A rail fence and a stream below. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people or deer larger than specks, nothing outside the village and meadow.
levels: A gamekeeper's lodge beside the stele and a fenced herb garden.
A small walled hamlet with a gate house of the Pivot's wardens and a covered antler hall.

places.name: Đỗ Quyên Thôn
places.look: A fishing village sits on a grey shore under steep slopes that turn blood-red with azaleas each spring. Its low houses are roofed with dark stone slabs against the wind, and its boats lie hauled up on black volcanic shingle. In bloom the slope looks like a fire about to come down on the roofs.
places.lore: Azaleas bloom red on the slopes above Đỗ Quyên Thôn each spring, and since at least 640 the villagers have said they are the dead of the eruption. No one picks them. On the first day of bloom the village leaves rice cakes at the foot of the slope and does not fish.
places.history: Fishers lived on this shore below the ice mountains while Hồ Thiên Phái still stood on the ice nearby, trading fish for the school's furs and salt. When Chúc Long Sơn erupted in the Age of Seven Seats and buried the school, ash fell on the village and the sea ran warm and grey for a season. The survivors stayed, and their dead were buried on the slope above the houses. Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice two generations later, and the village came under its rule. In time red azaleas covered the slope where the graves lay. By 640 the villagers said that the azaleas blooming red above Đỗ Quyên Thôn each spring were the eruption's dead, and the custom of leaving rice cakes at the foot of the slope had begun. No one in the village picks them, and when the mountain rumbled again in the last winter the azaleas were the first thing the fishers looked at in spring.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a few low houses with dark stone-slab roofs on a grey shore, small boats on black shingle. Above them, a steep slope blanketed in bright red azalea blooms, the signature element. Grey sea at the near edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left deepening the red. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and its slope.
levels: A small timber jetty and a shrine at the foot of the azalea slope.
A low stone sea wall, a boat shed, and a terraced path up through the azaleas to a lookout.

places.name: Hoàng Oanh Thôn
places.look: In a sheltered coastal valley, a ring of grey-tile houses stands among bare willows hung with woven straw bird shelters. All winter the shelters flash yellow with orioles, and their song carries down to the boats. Snow lies on the ridges all around.
places.lore: Orioles winter in the valley of Hoàng Oanh Thôn, the only birdsong in the ice mountains, and the village has woven shelters for them since at least 850. Nuns from the hermitage up the mountain are said to come down in winter only to listen. A child who throws a stone at an oriole must sleep one night with the goats.
places.history: The valley was a fishing cove long before it had a name, sheltered from the north wind by the ridges around it. Late in the Age of Seven Seats it came under Băng Tâm Các with the rest of the ice mountains. At some time no one recorded, orioles began to winter among its willows, the only birdsong anywhere in the ice mountains. By 850 the birds were known across Băng Tâm's land, and the village had taken the name Hoàng Oanh for them. The villagers began weaving straw shelters for the birds and hanging them in the willows each autumn. Nuns from Lê Hoa Am are said to walk down the mountain in winter only to hear them. The orioles have never failed to come, and the village takes their arrival as the true start of its year.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a ring of low grey-tile houses in a small coastal valley, with bare willow trees hung with round woven straw bird shelters, the signature element, dotted with tiny yellow specks. Boats at a short shingle beach, snowy ridges at the edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A timber boat landing and more willows planted along the stream.
A small walled hamlet with a listening pavilion among the willows and a stone jetty.

places.name: Ngư Đàm Thôn
places.look: Behind a bitter salt shore where nothing swims, a small oasis holds a grid of square fish ponds edged with mud brick and shaded by date palms. Low flat-roofed houses of the same brick line the dikes between the ponds. Children with wooden clappers chase the herons off the shallows.
places.lore: Since around 500, fish ponds dug in the oasis have given Ngư Đàm Thôn its name and Băng Tâm's desert its only fish; the sea beside it is too salt and barren to net. Carp travel from here to the seat in water jars. A fish dish at a Băng Tâm feast means it came from Ngư Đàm, and the village is proud of it.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a small oasis on a pale salt shore: a neat grid of square fish ponds with mud-brick edges, the signature element, a few date palms, and low flat-roofed mud-brick houses on the dikes between the ponds. A tiny landing for salt boats at the shore. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the still pond water. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the oasis.
levels: More ponds dug toward the dunes and a covered jar store by the landing.
A mud-brick wall around the oasis, a water tower, and a small shrine on the central dike.

places.name: Liên Đường Thôn
places.look: In the middle of the open steppe, a hollow of spring-fed ponds blooms pink and white with lotus all summer. A few mud-brick houses with reed roofs stand on the banks, and a wooden viewing pier reaches out over the leaves. Caravans halt on the rise above just to look.
places.lore: Lotus ponds have bloomed at Liên Đường since around 560, and caravans stop just to look. The village now answers to Dạ Quang Môn, whose riders water their horses here and leave the flowers alone. Lotus root and seed are its living, and a lotus seed is pressed into the hand of every traveller who asks the way.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a green hollow in golden steppe filled with ponds of pink and white lotus, the signature element, a few mud-brick houses with reed roofs on the banks and a small wooden pier reaching over the leaves. A caravan track on the rise. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the hollow.
levels: A caravan rest yard on the rise and a second viewing pier.
A low earth wall around the ponds, a lotus pavilion on an island in the largest pond, and a horse trough fed by the spring.

places.name: Mã Minh Thôn
places.look: Round corrals of piled dry stone ring a cluster of felt tents and mud houses on the steppe behind the range. The neigh of horses carries far over the grass. To the west a low hump of sand covers the old wells where the village once stood.
places.lore: Nomad herders drove their horses across the steppe behind the range as early as 100, and their camping ground became Mã Minh Thôn. In 1050 a sandstorm buried its wells, and the village moved a short way east, horses and all. Its herders sell remounts to Băng Tâm's caravans and to anyone else who can pay.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a few felt tents and flat-roofed mud houses on golden steppe, surrounded by several round dry-stone horse corrals, the signature element, with tiny horse specks inside. To one side, a low sand mound over old buried wells. Mountains at the far edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: New stone-lined wells and a long horse barn with a thatched roof.
A walled horse market, a herders' hall, and corrals spread out across the plain.

places.name: Tiều Lộ Thôn
places.look: A woodcutters' village where the forest comes down to the shore, its log houses under grey-tile roofs around a small timber jetty. At the forest's edge a fan of red-painted marker posts leads off among the trees, each one the start of a different path into Vô Tung Lâm.
places.lore: The woodcutters' paths into Vô Tung Lâm vanish under the snow every night, and only the people of Tiều Lộ Thôn can find them again; outsiders who need the forest hire a Tiều Lộ guide or go without. The village answers to Trạc Anh Đài, and it is said the poles of the terrace's drying lines are cut by Tiều Lộ hands.
places.history: Woodcutters settled this shore where Vô Tung Lâm comes down to the sea, cutting timber for the boats of the frost coast. By 540 their paths into the forest were known to vanish under the snow every night, and only the people of Tiều Lộ Thôn could find them again. They marked the start of each path with a painted post and kept the rest of the way in their heads, passed from parent to child. Hunters and timber buyers from the coast's towns learned to hire a Tiều Lộ guide or stay out of the trees. When the fishers and sea hunters of the coast founded Trạc Anh Đài, the village came under the terrace's hand, and it is said Tiều Lộ's woodcutters cut the poles for the terrace's drying lines. The elders boast that the village has never lost a guide in the forest, though it has lost many who went in without one.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a forested shore: a few log houses with grey-tile roofs, stacked cordwood, a short timber jetty into cold water. At the tree line behind, a spread fan of tiny red posts runs into the snowy firs. Warm golden light from the top left, snow on the roofs. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and its edge of forest.
levels: A sawpit and a log slide down to the jetty, and more houses climb along the posts toward the trees.
A palisade circles the village, a covered timber yard faces the water, and the red posts gain carved caps for each family's path.

places.name: Lâm Ẩn Thôn
places.look: A coastal village so deep in old firs that from the sea only its chimney smoke shows above the canopy. A single long plank jetty runs out of the trees into a quiet inlet.
places.lore: In the Age of the North Star Compact (Bắc Thần Kỷ) a hermit sheltered here and taught the village children to read tracks in the snow, and every child of Lâm Ẩn still learns tracks before letters. Hunters from Mộc Lan Thành come to hire them, and it is said no beast passes near the village without being named by its footprints.
places.history: Lâm Ẩn Thôn grew in a stand of old firs on the frost coast, so deep in the trees that passing boats saw only its smoke. Its people lived by fishing the inlet and hunting the forest edge. In 780 the village sheltered a hermit who taught its children to read tracks in the snow; the record keeps no name for him. He stayed until the children could tell a fox from a marten by a single print, and then, the villagers say, he walked into the forest and left no track at all. Every child of Lâm Ẩn has learned tracks before letters ever since. Hunters from Mộc Lan Thành come to hire them, and Băng Tâm's patrols ask a Lâm Ẩn tracker first when something goes missing in the woods.
places.art_brief: A natural-looking patch of dense, dark old firs on a coast, the grey-tile roofs only glimpsed between trunks; several thin threads of chimney smoke rise straight out of the canopy. A single long, narrow plank jetty runs from the trees into a still blue inlet. Snow on the fir crowns, warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, no clearings, nothing outside the stand of firs and the jetty.
levels: A tracking lodge is built under the firs and a second jetty reaches the inlet.
The village grows a hidden ring of houses under the canopy, a smokehouse row along the shore, and a small hall where the children learn the tracks.

places.name: Lô Hoa Thôn
places.look: A marsh village on the grassy coast, its stilt houses standing in a sea of reeds. In summer the reeds flower white and the whole marsh looks snowed over, with only grey roofs and winding boat channels showing through.
places.lore: The people of Lô Hoa cut reeds for thatch, mats and net floats, and sell the reed-flower down the coast to Liên Giang and Mộc Lan for stuffing winter quilts. Children are told the summer snow is the frost coast's reminder that winter is never far away.
places.history: Reed-cutters built their stilt houses in this coastal marsh, where the reeds grow tall enough to hide a boat and the spring thaw floods the ground. From the first they cut reeds for thatch, mats and the floats of nets. In 640 the reed flowers covered the marsh like snow in summer, and the sight drew travellers from along the coast. The village learned to sell the soft reed-flower for stuffing winter quilts, and the white summers made its name. Its reeds and down now go by boat to the ports of Liên Giang and Mộc Lan. Each summer, when the marsh first turns white, the children run the plank walks shouting that the snow has come early.
places.art_brief: A village miniature in a coastal marsh: a handful of small grey-tile roofs on timber stilts, joined by plank walks, standing in a dense field of reeds topped with soft white plumes, with dark winding water channels cut through it. Warm golden light from the top left makes the plumes glow cream. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the marsh.
levels: A reed-drying yard on stilts and a boat shed are added, and the plank walks reach a new row of houses.
A raised earth bank with a small grey-tile hall rises in the marsh, and the channels are lined with posts for the reed boats.

places.name: Bối Sa Thôn
places.look: A fishing village on a gleaming white beach on the island's grassy coast. On the sand above the tide line stands a small mound-shrine built entirely of white shells, with the village's drying mats spread around it.
places.lore: Since the Age of First Gates (Khai Môn Kỷ) the islanders have gathered shells on Bối Sa's beach to trade as coins on the mainland, long before any sect held the island. Old shell money is still taken in the village for small things, and every child adds a shell to the shrine on its first birthday.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a bright white beach: a few low grey-tile roofs behind the dune grass, rectangles of drying mats on the sand, and above the tide line a small rounded mound of white shells with a tiny roofed niche. Turquoise shallows. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the beach and village.
levels: A shell-sorting shed and a boat slip are added, and the shrine is given a low stone ring.
The village grows a short stone quay and a small hall for the shell traders, and the shrine mound rises higher every year.

places.name: Lãng Thạch Thôn
places.look: A small village behind a sea stack on the island coast. The stack, Wave Rock, stands split in two from crown to waterline, and through the gap shows the dark mouth of a sea cave.
places.lore: Wave Rock split in a storm in 960 and opened a sea cave full of old charts drawn by the lost sailors of Cô Phàm Các. The village answers to Bình Thủy Môn, and its fishers still row visitors into the cave; rumour says not every chart was carried out.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a grassy coast: a few grey-tile roofs and boats on the shingle, and just offshore a tall dark sea stack cleanly split into two halves, a black cave mouth visible in the gap at the waterline. White surf at its base. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and the stack.
levels: A landing stage is built at the cave mouth and a chart-copiers' hut rises in the village.
The village gains a small walled yard and a stone jetty reaching toward the split rock.

places.name: Dương Liễu Thôn
places.look: A village on the island's dunes, its grey roofs sheltered behind long rows of wind-bent willows planted along the sand ridges. Their roots bind the dunes, and from the sea the village looks hedged in green.
places.lore: Since 750 the villagers have planted willows on the dunes to hold the island's sand against the storms. Each household tends its own row, and a newborn's cord is buried at the foot of a new willow.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on pale sand dunes: a few grey-tile roofs in the hollows, with long parallel rows of leaning green willows on the dune ridges between village and sea. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the dunes.
levels: New willow rows run along the outer dunes and a boat shed is built in their lee.
A wattle sea fence stretches behind the willows, and a small grey-tile hall stands on the highest dune.

places.name: Tình Sa Thôn
places.look: A village of low grey roofs on a broad, sunny sandbar at a river mouth. On the bar lies a long driftwood effigy of a whale, built by the villagers and weathered silver.
places.lore: In 1190 a whale stranded on Tình Sa's sunny sands lived three days while the islanders worked to give it back to the sea. The villagers built the driftwood whale to remember it, and mend it from new driftwood whenever a storm takes a piece.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a golden sandbar at a river mouth: a few low grey-tile roofs, boats in the river channel, and on the open sand a long whale shape made of silver-grey driftwood. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the sandbar.
levels: A fish-drying frame and a jetty into the river channel are added.
