The village spreads along both banks of the river mouth, joined by a plank footbridge, and a small shrine roof shelters the whale's head.

places.name: Nguyệt Loan Thôn
places.look: A fishing village around a perfect crescent cove, its arms of rock nearly closing at the mouth. Inside rides a crowded fleet of island boats, their masts thick as reeds.
places.lore: In the great storm of 870 the moon-shaped cove sheltered the island's fishing fleet, and boats from every harbour on Cô Vụ Đảo still run for Nguyệt Loan when the sky turns. Captains who ride out a storm here hang a carved wooden moon on the village boat shed in thanks.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature around a crescent-shaped cove whose rocky arms almost close: grey-tile roofs along the curved shore, the still water inside crowded with many tiny boats and masts. Warm golden light from the top left, calm water inside, white surf outside. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the cove.
levels: A storm wall is built along the cove's curve and a long boat shed rises at its head.
Mooring piers ring the cove, and a small grey-tile storm shrine stands on the tip of one rocky arm.

places.name: Điền Viên Thôn
places.look: A village of gardens and fields on the plain coast, its grey roofs half hidden by orchard walls. In nearly every garden wall is a round moon gate, and through them show the small studies of retired scholars.
places.lore: Since 890 the gardens and fields of Điền Viên have fed the scholars of Nhạn Thanh Thành, who retire here to farm. The village answers to Mục Vân Trang, and its old scholars write letters for the herders and are paid in vegetables.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a green coastal plain: a few grey-tile roofs inside whitewashed garden walls, each wall pierced by a round moon gate, neat vegetable plots and fruit trees inside. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the gardens.
levels: A small library pavilion and a shared orchard are added.
A walled scholars' garden with a pond pavilion forms the heart of the village, and new moon gates open onto the fields.

places.name: Yến Quy Thôn
places.look: A small farm village on the plain coast, its grey roofs gathered around one old farmstead. The old farm's roof ridge is lined end to end with little clay swallows, and the real birds perch among them.
places.lore: Swallows returned to the same farm every spring for a hundred years, and by 300 the village was named Yến Quy, Swallows' Return. The farm still stands; each family adds a clay swallow to its ridge, and a year when the real birds are late is a year to plant carefully.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a green coastal plain: a few grey-tile roofs around one larger old farmhouse whose long roof ridge is lined with a row of tiny dark clay bird figures. Fields and a farm pond around it. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A new barn and a threshing floor are built beside the old farm.
The village grows a small walled yard and a shrine hall, its ridge also lined with clay swallows.

places.name: Chu Tân Thôn
places.look: A ferry village on the low, wet shore, below the level of the sea at high tide. Two tall carved ferry posts stand at the old ford, joined by a heavy rope across a narrow tidal creek, with a flat barge crawling along it.
places.lore: A ford on the plain's widest river became Chu Tân Thôn in 520; the river has since wandered from the village, but the old ford's posts still stand, and at high tide the villagers haul travellers across the creek on the rope ferry. The village answers to Mục Vân Trang, whose herds cross here every spring, and the ferrymen know each horse by name.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on low, wet coastal flats: a few grey-tile roofs beside a narrow tidal creek, two tall carved dark posts on either side of it joined by a taut rope, a flat barge on the water between. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, no river, nothing outside the flats.
levels: A ferry inn and a holding pen for herds are built by the landing.
A second rope and barge are added, and a small walled waystation stands on the far bank.

places.name: Lô Cảng Thôn
places.look: A village of reed-thatched boat sheds around a sheltered reed harbour on the plain coast. Out of the reeds rises a tall timber watchtower flying Lạc Hà's sunset-red banner, the sect's western watch.
places.lore: The reed harbour at Lô Cảng shelters the coast boats from the open sea, and in 800 Lạc Hà Tông built its western watch here. Watchmen and fishers share the village, and the tower lights a fire when strange sails are seen.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a reedy coast: a few grey-tile houses and long reed-thatched boat sheds around a small sheltered pool among tall reeds; one tall timber watchtower with a small red banner rising above it all. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the reed harbour.
levels: A walled barracks yard joins the watchtower and a jetty runs through the reeds.
A stone signal platform tops the tower, and a second harbour pool is cut into the reeds.

places.name: Diêm Điền Thôn
places.look: A village at the edge of a vast glittering grid of salt pans on the flat west coast. Between the shallow white squares stand rows of shining salt cones, raked up by hand.
places.lore: Salt pans dug at Diêm Điền in 200 made the continent's first sea salt, before any great sect held the west. The salt-makers keep the first pan unused and fenced, and pour a handful of new salt into it every year.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a flat coast: a few grey-tile roofs beside a wide grid of shallow rectangular pans, white and pale pink, with rows of small bright white salt cones on the dykes. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the salt. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the pans.
levels: A salt store with a high grey roof rises and the pans spread along the shore.
A walled salt yard and a stone loading jetty serve the pans.

places.name: Khê Thanh Thôn
places.look: A village on a clear grassland brook, its grey roofs strung along the water. Over the brook stand a row of small covered rinsing sheds on stilts, where the water chatters loudly over the stones beneath them.
places.lore: The brook at Khê Thanh runs so clear that since 700 Thiên Bảo Trai has washed its finest refinings in it. The Trai's apprentices come down with covered baskets, the villagers are paid to keep the banks free of mud and cattle, and the brook's chatter is said to sing the flaws out of the metal.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a clear, shallow, stony brook in green grassland: a few grey-tile houses along the bank and a row of small grey-roofed sheds standing on stilts over the water. Warm golden light from the top left sparkling on the brook. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the brook's banks.
levels: More rinsing sheds are built downstream and a small inspection hall for the Trai's stewards rises on the bank.
A walled storehouse for refinings and a stone footbridge join the village across the brook.

places.name: Khê Đầu Thôn
places.look: A small village at the head of a brook on the grassland, where the water rises from the ground. The spring pours from a stone spout carved as a carp's head into a round basin, and the brook starts from its overflow.
places.lore: Khê Đầu sits where the brook begins, upstream of Khê Thanh, and its water is the clearest of all; Thiên Bảo Trai washes its finest refinings at both villages. The villagers guard the spring like a shrine and let no one wash in the basin itself, only below it.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on gently rising grassland: a few grey-tile roofs around a round stone basin fed by a carved stone carp-head spout, the clear brook spilling out of it and away. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A low wall and a small roof are built around the spring basin.
A spring hall with a grey-tile roof shelters the carp spout, and a stone channel leads the brook toward Khê Thanh.

places.name: Hải Môn Thôn
places.look: A fishing village on the bay coast beside a great natural rock arch, the Sea Gate. Twice a day the tide runs through the arch in a white rush, and the village boats wait on the inner side for the slack.
places.lore: Since 450 the village has been named for its Sea Gate, the rock arch the tide runs through twice a day. Fishers time everything by it, and a bride and groom row through the arch at slack water for luck.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a grassy coast: a few grey-tile roofs and boats on the shore inside a sheltered pool, beside a large natural stone arch standing in the sea with white water rushing through it. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and the arch.
levels: A boat shed and a stone landing are built inside the arch's shelter.
A small grey-tile shrine stands on the arch's landward foot, and a jetty reaches out to the slack-water channel.

places.name: Tân Khẩu Thôn
places.look: A village at the mouth of a harbour on the bay coast, its houses all facing the sea. On the landward side they join into one long blank wall with no windows, turned against the plain.
places.lore: Refugees from Vô Định Thành founded the village in 805 after the battle on the plain, and never speak of it; the blank wall says it for them. Their children are less careful: not long ago children of Tân Khẩu dared each other to touch the edge of the miasma (chướng khí) by Vô Định Thành, and one did not come back.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature at a harbour mouth on a grassy coast: grey-tile roofs in a row, their seaward sides open with doors and boats on the shore, their landward sides joined into one continuous blank grey wall. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: The village lengthens along the shore and a small fish market roof is built at the harbour mouth.
A stone quay and a lantern post mark the harbour mouth, and the blank wall is raised and capped in grey tile.

places.name: Hoa Khê Thôn
places.look: A handful of grey-roofed cottages along a clear brook in open grassland, with wild plum and pear on its banks. Just below the last house a low fence of bamboo stakes crosses the brook, and in spring it catches a pink drift of petals and paper slips.
places.lore: Flower Brook Village has kept a custom since at least 560: every spring, when petals float down the brook, lovers write their names on slips and drop them in together. If the two slips catch on the bamboo fence side by side, the pair are thought bound for life; the village's old women sort the slips each evening and never tell what they find. The village pays its dues to Nam Phố Đường.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of five or six grey-tile cottages along a narrow clear brook in green grassland, flowering plum and pear trees on the banks, and below the last cottage a short fence of bamboo stakes across the brook with a pale pink drift of petals piled against it. Grass and a footpath at the base. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A small shrine to the brook's spirit stands beside the petal fence, and a tea house for spring visitors opens on the bank.
A cluster of inns and paper shops lines both banks, and a covered walk follows the brook down to the petal fence.

places.name: Ngân Than Thôn
places.look: A low village on a gravel bend of the river, its shallows lined with long wooden sluice boxes where flecks of silver glint under the moving water. Heaps of washed grey gravel stand in rows behind the houses.
places.lore: Since 400 the people of Silver Shoal Village have panned the river shallows for silver, which Lạc Hà Tông takes for its coin. Panners work in pairs, one rocking the sluice and one singing the count, so the river here is never quiet. A sluice that turns up a large nugget is retired and hung over the door of the family that worked it.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile houses on a gravel river bend in grassland: a row of long narrow wooden sluice boxes set in the bright shallows, small neat heaps of grey gravel behind the houses. Pebbled banks at the base. Warm golden light from the top left sparkling on the water in the sluices. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A weighing house with a sect clerk's office stands at the landing, and a small water wheel rocks the sluices.
A walled assay yard and a smelting kiln with a tall clay chimney stand behind the village, and a stone landing takes the silver barges.

places.name: Phương Thảo Thôn
places.look: A fishing village behind low dunes, where long swathes of golden-green sweet grass are laid out to dry in neat combed rows across the sea meadow. Open-sided weaving sheds face its small harbour.
places.lore: Phương Thảo Thôn, Fragrant Grass Village, cuts the sweet sea-meadow grass that has been woven into the mats of Lạc Hà Tông's meditation halls since 640. Its weavers say a good mat smells of the sea for a lifetime; a disciple who wears one through is sent here to cut the grass for its replacement.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile cottages and open-sided weaving sheds behind pale dunes by the sea, with a small harbour of two boats, and a broad meadow striped with long parallel rows of drying golden-green grass. Dune sand and sea grass at the base. Warm golden light from the top left raking across the grass rows. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A fenced mat-drying yard and a jetty for the sect's grass barge join the village.
A walled weavers' quarter with a guild hall and a stone harbour arm shelters the grass boats, and the drying rows cover the whole meadow.

places.name: Thủy Khẩu Thôn
places.look: Where a slow brook mouths into the main river stands a small village of grey roofs beside a dead-straight channel, dug by hand and banked with long ridges of spoil planted with willows. A stone tablet stands where the channel opens onto the river.
places.lore: Thủy Khẩu, Water's Mouth Village, lives on the boat trade where the brook joins the river. In 720 the mouth silted up, and Lạc Hà's disciples dug it out by hand in one winter; the tablet records the cut, and every winter the villagers walk the willow banks and each lift one spadeful so the river will remember.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile houses where a brook meets a broader river on grassland: a perfectly straight narrow channel running between two long low earth banks lined with willows, a small upright stone tablet at its mouth. River water and reeds at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the willows. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A small lock of timber gates closes the channel, and a boatyard grows on the willow bank.
A walled river station with a toll house and granary guards the cut, and the channel is faced with dressed stone.

places.name: Mộc Hương Thôn
places.look: A woodcutters' village of steep grey roofs under groves of tall incense trees on a river bank. Low clay curing kilns stand in a row along the water, and their thin blue smoke hangs over the river and smells sweet a long way downstream.
places.lore: Since 600 the scented wood of Mộc Hương Thôn's groves has been burned in the hall of the Pivot. The villagers cut only fallen or dying trees and plant a sapling for every log; logs are cured slowly in the kilns, and a log meant for the Pivot is wrapped in yellow cloth before it leaves.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of steep grey-tile roofs among tall dark-green incense trees on a forest river bank, a row of small domed clay kilns along the water with thin wisps of blue smoke drifting over the river, stacked logs beside them. Forest floor and river at the base. Warm golden light from the top left catching the smoke. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A walled yard of curing kilns and a timber landing for the wood barges stand by the river.
A small walled town of carvers and incense-makers grows around the kilns, with a gate pavilion on the forest road.

places.name: Thụ Âm Thôn
places.look: A village sheltering whole under the canopy of one vast old tree, its roofs dappled and its lanes always cool. From the far edge of the shade, on clear days, villagers can see a grey haze lying low over the plain beyond.
places.lore: Thụ Âm Thôn, Tree Shade Village, lives under its great tree near the edge of the poisoned plain left by the battle of Chiết Kích Nguyên. In 900 a boy of the village followed his goat into the miasma and walked out three days later, grey-haired and calm; the village tells it as a warning, and goats here are tethered to the tree's roots every night. The tree is never pruned, and a branch that falls is burned on the plain side of the village to keep the haze away.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile roofs almost entirely covered by the broad spreading crown of one enormous old tree, dappled light on the roofs, its thick roots showing between the houses, a small river at one edge. Forest at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the tree's crown. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A shrine is built into the roots of the great tree, and a walled goat fold and a waystation stand at the edge of the shade.
A small walled town spreads beyond the canopy, with a watch tower facing the miasma plain and a lodge for travellers bound for the battlefield.

places.name: Thủy Đối Thôn
places.look: A village on a fast stream where a row of waterwheels drives long wooden trip-hammers that rise and fall into stone mortars, thudding all day under open sheds. Flour dust whitens the roofs.
places.lore: Since 700 the water mills at Thủy Đối have ground the wheat of Thanh Mạch for all of Tinh Hán Thành. The hammers stop only on New Year's night, when the village stills the wheels and the silence wakes the babies.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of flour-whitened grey-tile roofs along a fast stream on grassland, a row of wooden waterwheels under open sheds, each driving a long wooden trip-hammer beam over a stone mortar. Stream and green banks at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the turning wheels. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: More wheels and a granary on stone piers line the stream, and a cart yard opens on the road to Tinh Hán.
A walled mill town with a sluice gate across the stream and a millers' guild hall grows around the hammer sheds.

places.name: Thanh Mạch Thôn
places.look: A farming village on a low rise above a river, its houses gathered around a round threshing floor of polished stone on the hilltop, with a heavy stone roller standing upright at its centre. Green wheat falls away on every side.
places.lore: Thanh Mạch Thôn, Green Wheat Village, grows the wheat the mills of Thủy Đối grind for Tinh Hán Thành. Its threshing floor is the village's meeting place, court and festival ground; the stone roller is laid down only for the harvest and set upright again when the last sheaf is in.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile farmhouses around a round pale stone threshing floor on a gentle hilltop, a single upright stone roller at its centre, green wheat fields sloping down to a river. Wheat and a cart track at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the threshing floor. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A granary and a shrine to the field spirit stand beside the threshing floor, and irrigation channels run down to the river.
A small walled town with a market lane grows around the threshing floor, and a waterwheel lifts river water to terraced fields.

places.name: Châu Bạng Thôn
places.look: A fishing village on the inland sea whose house walls are set all over with oyster shells, so the whole village glitters white and pearl-grey in the sun. Diving boats are drawn up on a beach of broken shell.
places.lore: Pearl oysters in the shallows gave Châu Bạng Thôn its name in 400 and Tinh Hán Thành its pearl trade. Every diver sets the shell of their first pearl into the wall of the family house, so a house's walls tell how many divers it has raised.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile cottages on a flat sea shore, their walls studded with shimmering white and pearl-grey oyster shells, small diving boats on a pale shell beach. Shallow turquoise water at the base. Warm golden light from the top left making the shell walls sparkle. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A walled pearl-sorting yard and a stone jetty for the Tinh Hán boats stand on the beach.
A small walled harbour town with a pearl guild hall grows behind the beach, with oyster beds fenced in the shallows.

places.name: Đào Khê Thôn
places.look: A small village beside a brook below the ridges, built at the edge of a wide terraced stone platform where wild peach trees grow straight out of the cracks between old paving slabs. Broken stone column bases stand in rows among the trees.
places.lore: Since 400, when wild peach trees grew over the empty palace grounds of the fallen Cửu Thiều Cung and gave the brook below its name, Đào Khê has lived beside the ruin. Villagers pick the peaches but will not cut a tree or lift a paving stone, and nobody sings in the orchard; the dead of the old palace lie in the hills nearby, and grief, the old people say, is still in the ground.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile cottages by a brook beside a broad stepped platform of old cracked grey paving, wild pink-flowering peach trees growing out of the cracks, rows of broken stone column bases among them. Grass and the brook at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the peach blossom. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A shrine to the dead of the old palace stands at the orchard's edge, and a peach-drying yard and a small inn join the village.
A walled village of peach farmers and wine makers spreads along the brook, with a gate pavilion facing the ruined platform, on which it never builds.

places.name: Hà Loan Thôn
places.look: A village on a wide river bend, every house raised high on timber stilts above the floodplain and joined by plank walks. Boats are tied under the houses, ready for autumn.
places.lore: The river bend at Hà Loan has flooded every autumn since at least 700, so its people build their houses on stilts. When the water comes the village simply moves into its boats, and the flood is a market season: traders row from house to house selling under the eaves.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile houses raised on tall timber stilts on a wide green river bend, thin plank walks between them, small boats tied below. Floodplain grass and the river at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the stilts. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A raised granary and a shrine on a stone mound join the stilt houses, and an earth dike begins along the bend.
A long earthen dike rings the bend, and a small walled market on a raised platform stands among the stilt houses.

places.name: Bích Lãng Thôn
places.look: A fishing village lying just below the level of the gulf behind a seawall of great woven bamboo baskets packed with stones, stacked in a long curve. Bamboo groves crowd the houses, and jade-green waves break against the baskets.
places.lore: Bích Lãng Thôn, Jade Waves Village, fishes the gulf, and its boatmen have long said the jade-green waves carry the fishing boats home. The village lies below the sea and lives by its basket wall, re-woven every winter from Trúc Thực Viên's bamboo; the garden keeps the village, and the village gives the garden fish meal for its beasts.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile cottages among bamboo groves on a coast, lying slightly below a long curved seawall made of large stacked woven bamboo baskets filled with stones, jade-green waves breaking on the seaward side, small boats beached inside. Green water at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the woven baskets. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second ring of baskets and a stone sluice gate guard the village, and a fish-drying yard opens on the wall.
The basket wall is faced with stone and topped by a walk, and a small walled harbour with a shrine to the waves stands at its end.

places.name: Thủy Điền Thôn
places.look: A handful of grey-tile houses on a low dyke between flooded paddies, beside the river. On the bank a great bamboo waterwheel, its rim strung with tube buckets, creaks round and lifts water into the oldest fields on the plain.
places.lore: Rice was first planted on this plain in 140, in the flooded fields of Thủy Điền, and its paddies are older than every sect but two. Farmers here measure age in harvests, not years. Each spring, before any other village plants, a child of Thủy Điền sets the first seedling, and the plain follows.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature: a few grey-tile roofs strung along a raised earth dyke between mirror-bright flooded paddies at a river bank. The signature is a tall bamboo waterwheel on the bank, its rim of tube buckets catching the light, spilling water into a channel. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second waterwheel and a stone sluice; a barn for seed rice stands on the dyke.
A walled hamlet with a small shrine to the first rice and a row of wheels along the bank.

places.name: Âu Lộ Thôn
places.look: A low marsh shore of the eastern gulf, where a stand of dead trees is white with nesting gulls and herons and loud from dawn to dusk. The village houses sit back from the waterline on the landward edge of the marsh, and on their walls hang old diving baskets and weighted ropes, dry for centuries.
places.lore: Fishers say the birds were here before the sects and will be after. In 763, after Thôn Hải's pirates burned Châu Lệ Cảng, the harbour's pearl divers settled here on the inland side of the marsh, away from the open sea, and never dived again. Their descendants fish only from the shore and hang an empty diving basket above every new door.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a flat salt-marsh shore: a few grey-tile roofs set back on the landward edge, reeds and mudflats between them and the sea. The signature is a stand of bare dead trees nearest the water, crowned white with nesting birds. Small dry wicker baskets hang on the house walls. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, a shimmer on the tidal channels. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A boardwalk across the marsh to a small fishing jetty; the divers' quarter gains a shrine to the pearl harbour.
A walled fishing hamlet with drying racks along the shore; the heron trees are fenced and left untouched.

places.name: Ngân Hạnh Thôn
places.look: A forest village on a small river among the oak woods at the plain's edge, its grey roofs gathered under one colossal ginkgo (ngân hạnh) that dwarfs them. In autumn the tree turns gold in a single night, and by morning the roofs are carpeted yellow.
places.lore: The ginkgo is older than the village, which grew up around it. Every autumn the villagers sit up to see the night it turns, and no one has yet managed it. Its roasted nuts are sold on the road, and children are warned that greedy eaters get bad dreams.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature in temperate woodland by a small river: a few grey-tile roofs clustered beneath one enormous ginkgo tree, the signature, its fan-leaf crown bright gold and taller than everything around. Yellow leaves scattered on the roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left makes the crown blaze. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A roofed bench ring around the ginkgo's trunk and a stone bridge over the river.
A walled hamlet with a small temple at the ginkgo's foot and an inn for the road.

places.name: Lý Hoa Thôn
places.look: A fishing hamlet on a sandy beach, its boats drawn up below an orchard of white plum (lý hoa) that runs right down to the high-tide line. In early spring the orchard is so white that beach and blossom are hard to tell apart, and grey snow geese sit among the branches.
places.lore: Plum blossom here is so white that snow geese land among it by mistake, a tale told since 560. The villagers leave the geese alone, and say a goose that wakes in a plum tree brings a good catch.
places.art_brief: A tiny coastal village miniature: a few grey-tile roofs and small boats on a pale sandy beach, behind them the signature, an orchard of white-blossoming plum trees running down to the waterline, with a few grey geese among the blossom. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, soft blue sea at the base. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A stone landing for the boats and a pickling shed for plums.
A small walled harbour hamlet; the orchard is terraced up the dunes behind it.

places.name: Hoàng Ngưu Thôn
places.look: A cattle village on the open plain, its grey roofs gathered beside a great round corral of piled fieldstone. Yellow oxen graze in loose herds all around, and the grass near the corral is worn to bare earth.
places.lore: Yellow oxen ran wild on the plain left empty after Cửu Thiều fell, and in 400 the village that tamed them took their name. Its oxen pull ploughs and barges across much of the rice plain. On the first day of spring the herders paint one ox's horns red and walk it round the corral to bless the year.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on open grassland: a few grey-tile roofs beside the signature, a large circular corral wall of piled grey fieldstone with a worn earth floor, a few yellow-brown oxen as specks inside and around it. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long grass shadows. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second corral and a roofed ox market beside the road.
A walled hamlet with a tannery and a shrine to the ox at the corral gate.

places.name: Kiều Bạn Thôn
places.look: Where the forest road crosses a slow river, a roofed timber bridge with deep eaves carries the traffic, and under those eaves hang rows of worn straw sandals. A cluster of grey-tile houses and an inn crowd its northern end.
places.lore: The village grew up around the crossing in 680 and took its name from the bridge. Travellers leave their worn-out sandals hanging under the eaves and buy new ones at the far end, so that their tiredness stays on the bridge. Once a year the village burns the old sandals on the bank.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature at a river crossing on grassland: a roofed wooden bridge with dark grey tile and deep eaves, the signature, rows of small straw sandals hanging under its eaves; a few grey-tile houses and an inn at one end. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, reflections in the slow water. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second inn and a stone pier strengthening the bridge's middle.
A walled hamlet at the bridgehead with a sandal-makers' row and a small shrine to travellers.

places.name: Bình Độ Thôn
places.look: A ferry landing on a wide, slow forest river, where a broad flat raft with a small thatched sleeping shelter on its deck is poled across from a village of grey-tile houses. The water here is glassy and barely moves.
places.lore: The ferry at Bình Độ has been famous since 460 for being so calm that sleeping passengers are carried over without waking. Ferrymen never raise their voices on the river, and the village forbids drums on the bank. Travellers who are carried over asleep are woken on the far side with a cup of tea.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a grassy bank of a wide, mirror-calm river: a few grey-tile roofs at a wooden landing, and the signature, a broad flat ferry raft mid-river with a little thatched shelter on its deck. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, perfect reflections. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second raft and a stone landing stair; a tea house on the bank.
A walled hamlet at the landing with a covered waiting hall, and ferry landings on both banks.

places.name: Hoa Điền Thôn
places.look: A river village set among sweeping fields of flowers in long strips of purple, yellow and white. Along the village edge runs a wall of stacked hollow-log beehives, humming loudly all summer.
places.lore: Since 540 the flower fields of Hoa Điền have fed the bees of the rain forest, and its honey is sold in Thu Trì Thành. Beekeepers tell their bees every piece of village news, births and deaths first, or the bees will leave.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature: a few grey-tile roofs by a river among long stripes of purple, yellow and white flower fields, and the signature, a low wall of stacked round hollow-log beehives along the village edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second hive wall and a honey-boiling shed by the river.
A walled hamlet with a wax-chandlers' row and a jetty for the honey boats to Thu Trì.

places.name: Yên Kiều Thôn
places.look: A river village in low meadows, where a long, narrow bridge of grey stone slabs on many low piers runs out across a misty river and fades into fog before it reaches the other side. On rainy days its far end cannot be seen at all.
places.lore: The misty bridge at Yên Kiều vanishes in the rain, and since 760 travellers who cross it have said it is longer than it looks. The village now belongs to Hồng Đậu Trang, whose guests pass this way. Locals cross only in pairs, holding a rope between them, and count their steps aloud.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature in low green meadow: a few grey-tile roofs on one bank, and the signature, a long low bridge of flat grey stone slabs on many small piers running out across the river and dissolving into a band of white mist. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the near bank, cool mist beyond. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A rope rail along the bridge and a small shrine at its near end.
A walled hamlet with an inn for Hồng Đậu Trang's guests; lamps of red glass on posts along the bridge.

places.name: Ương Ca Thôn
places.look: A hill village above a river, its grey-tile houses at the top of a stair of curving rice terraces. At the head of the terraces stands a round stone stage open to the sky, where the singers stand at planting.
places.lore: Farmers have sung as they plant the terraces here since 540, and the song is the oldest in the south. Since Thu Phần Các came, the villagers hear singing from the graves of Lôi Trạch every autumn, and they sing louder at planting to drown it. Nobody in Ương Ca sings the planting song in autumn.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a gentle hillside above a river: a few grey-tile roofs at the top of curving, water-filled rice terraces stepping down the slope. The signature is a round flat stone stage at the head of the terraces. Warm golden-hour light from the top left mirrored in the terrace water. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: More terraces cut down to the river, and a roof of thatch over the singing stage.
A walled hill hamlet with a hall of the planting song beside the stage.

places.name: Song Khê Thôn
places.look: A village where two brooks, one clear and one tea-brown from the forest, run together in a Y below the houses. On the point of land where they meet stands a tiny roofed shrine with two bamboo dippers tied together by a red cord.
places.lore: Lovers who drink from both brooks are said never to part, a belief recorded since 1000. Couples come from as far as Thu Trì to drink with the joined dippers. The village matchmaker keeps the cord and swears she has never had to replace it.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on grassland: a few grey-tile roofs above a Y-shaped meeting of two small brooks, one clear blue and one tea-brown. The signature is a tiny roofed shrine on the point of land where they join, with two small dippers joined by a red cord. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A pair of small stone bridges over both brooks and a wedding inn beside the shrine.
A walled hamlet with a lovers' pavilion over the confluence.

places.name: Thượng Độ Thôn
places.look: A ferry village on the upper river, where a ferry boat is hauled across on a rope strung between two tall carved stone posts. The post on the near bank is charred black to its top.
places.lore: In the Thunder Vein War of 1045, Phượng Minh's raiders reached the upper ferry at Thượng Độ before the Pivot's envoys stopped them. They burned the landing and scorched the stone post, which the villagers have never cleaned. The villagers say it is the nearest the Palace has come to the Tower's heart, and Thính Vũ's disciples stop here to look at it.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a grassy upland river bank: a few grey-tile roofs at a ferry landing, and the signature, two tall carved stone posts on either bank with a rope strung between them and a small boat on it; the near post blackened by fire. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A stone landing on both banks and a guard hut beside the charred post.
A walled hamlet with a small fort at the ferry, the charred post kept inside its gate.

places.name: Hà Châu Thôn
places.look: A river village of grey roofs on the bank, facing a raw new isle of grey mud and gravel that has risen in the middle of the river. Two rival boundary flags flap on the isle, one at either end.
places.lore: In 1199 an earthquake raised a river isle at Hà Châu out of the water, and Thính Vũ and Xuyên Lâm both claim it. Villagers row out each morning to see whose flag has been moved. Nothing grows on the isle yet, but everyone is sure something valuable will.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a flat river bank: a few grey-tile roofs and small boats, facing the signature, a bare new island of grey mud and gravel in midstream with two small differently coloured flags on poles at its two ends. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A jetty out to the isle and the first willows planted on it.
A walled hamlet across both bank and isle, joined by a wooden bridge.

places.name: Cúc Viên Thôn
places.look: A small harbour village on a flat coast, its grey roofs half hidden by banked beds of yellow and bronze chrysanthemums that fill every slope and yard. In autumn the gardens grow so thick that the paths between them cannot be seen.
places.lore: In the War of the Vermilion Caves in 586, the villagers of Cúc Viên hid Phượng Minh's scouts among the chrysanthemums. The Palace has not forgotten, and its people still buy the village's flowers for the autumn rites. Every household keeps one bed planted thick enough to hide a grown person, just in case.
places.history: The chrysanthemum gardens of Cúc Viên were already old when Xích Thành Môn held the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu. When the gate's heir turned to burning villages, Cúc Viên lived in fear of the red banners like every village on the coast. In the War of the Vermilion Caves, in 586, the villagers hid Phượng Minh's scouts among the chrysanthemums while the gate's patrols searched the shore. The scouts' reports are said to have helped the Palace bring the war to its end a few years later. When the coast passed to Phượng Minh, the Palace remembered the village and began to buy its flowers for the autumn rites. Through the pirate years the gardens were trampled more than once, but the beds always grew back. Every household still keeps one bed planted thick enough to hide a grown person.
places.art_brief: A tiny coastal village miniature: a few grey-tile roofs almost buried in the signature, banked mounds of yellow and bronze chrysanthemums filling every yard and slope; a few small boats at a shore landing. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A flower market under a roof by the landing and terraced beds up the dunes.
A walled hamlet with a small shrine to the hidden scouts amid the gardens.

places.name: Tang Âm Thôn
places.look: A harbour village on the coast road whose heart is a single vast old mulberry tree, its crown spread wide over a dusty caravan yard. Carts and pack animals stand in its shade, and the village houses face inward toward it.
places.lore: Since 600 the mulberry shade at Tang Âm has been the resting place of the silk caravans. Carters say the tree's shade is cooler than any roof, and that tying an animal to the trunk brings bad luck. The village lives on caravan inns and fodder.
places.history: The great mulberry at Tang Âm is older than the village, and herders sheltered under it long before any road ran along the coast. In 600, in the Age of the North Star Compact, the silk caravans of the south began to rest in its shade, and the village grew up around the yard to serve them. Its inns took in carters hauling thread from the red-soil fields of Tang Điền and goods bound for the port cities. In the pirate years the caravans ran fewer and under guard, and the villagers built their houses facing inward toward the tree. After the Pirate Purge the road filled again. The rule against tying an animal to the trunk is said to come from a carter whose mule tore down a limb, and whose luck went with it. Carters still touch the bark for luck before they leave.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a flat coast: a ring of grey-tile roofs facing inward around a bare earth yard, over which spreads the signature, one enormous wide-crowned mulberry tree; small carts parked in its shade. A small shore landing at one side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, dappled shade. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A long caravan inn with stables along the yard.
A walled caravan stop with a roofed gate on the coast road, the tree still at its centre.

places.name: Hồ Tâm Thôn
places.look: Behind the coastal dunes lies a round lake cut off from the sea, and the village sits on a small island in its middle, joined to the shore by a stone causeway. In the shallows beside the island stands a tall stone pillar notched with water marks, by which the villagers read the lake's strange tide. Their sea boats are dragged over the dunes to the beach.
places.lore: The lake at Hồ Tâm rises and falls with the tide though it touches no sea, and since 900 Phượng Minh's scholars have not been able to say why. The villagers do not mind; they set their fish traps by the pillar. Children are told the lake breathes with the sea through the gills of a sleeping creature.
places.history: The lake behind the dunes has fed fishers since before the sects came to the coast, and the island village is older than anyone can remember. Under Xích Thành Môn, and then under Phượng Minh Cung, it paid its dues in dried fish. In 900 Phượng Minh's scholars came to study the lake that rises and falls with the tide though it touches no sea, and they could not say why. They raised the notched stone pillar in the shallows to measure it, and their successors still come to read it. The villagers soon learned to set their fish traps by its marks. No explanation has ever been agreed on. The children's tale of a sleeping creature breathing with the sea is told more often than any scholar's.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature: a round calm lake behind pale sand dunes, a small island in its centre with a few grey-tile roofs, a narrow stone causeway to the shore. The signature is a tall notched stone pillar standing in the shallows beside the island. A few boats drawn up on the dunes. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A wider causeway and a boat slipway over the dunes.
A walled island hamlet with a scholars' tide hall built around the pillar.

places.name: Lô Châu Thôn
places.look: A river village on a low island of reed marsh, its houses raised on stilts with walls of bundled reeds lashed tight under grey-tile roofs. Paths of reed mats float between them, and the marsh around is cut into neat bays where reed is harvested.
places.lore: In 765 Thôn Hải's raiders carried off the whole village of Lô Châu; only the reed cutters hidden in the marsh escaped. In 782, after the Purge, captives freed from Thôn Hải's hold came home and rebuilt it reed by reed. Every family still keeps a reed bundle from that rebuilding hanging above the door, and the reed cutters are given the first seat at every feast.
places.history: Reed cutters lived on the marsh island of Lô Châu from the early ages, selling reed for thatch and mats up and down the river. In 765 Thôn Hải's raiders came up the river and carried off the whole village; only the reed cutters hidden in the marsh escaped. For years those few kept the island alive alone, cutting reed with no one to sell it to. When the Pirate Purge broke the pirates' hold, the captives held there were freed. In 782 they came home to Lô Châu and rebuilt it reed by reed. Every family hung a bundle from that rebuilding over its door, and the reed cutters were given the first seat at every feast. The custom has held ever since.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a low river island in a reed marsh: a few small stilted houses with pale bundled-reed walls under grey-tile roofs, the signature, linked by floating reed-mat paths; neat cut bays in the surrounding golden reeds. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A reed-weavers' shed and a timber jetty on the river.
A walled island hamlet on raised earth, its stilted houses joined by roofed boardwalks.

places.name: Bích Ngọc Khoáng
places.look: A stepped quarry face is cut into a forested hill, its terraces banded with bright green stone. A cart ramp zigzags down the cut to the road at its foot.
places.lore: Green jade was found in these hills when they belonged to Không Sơn Viện, but the academy forbade mining it, so the mountain stayed quiet. When the hills became Thúy Vi's, the mine was opened at last in 505. Today Hồng Lô Cốc works it under Thúy Vi, and its jade goes into pill bottles and furnace fittings.
places.history: The green hills of Thanh Loan Lĩnh kept their jade unseen through the Wild Age. In 300 green jade was found in the hills, but Không Sơn Viện forbade mining it, so the mountain stayed quiet. For two centuries the find was known and left alone, and the academy's students walked past the green outcrops on the way to their lessons. When the hills passed to Thúy Vi Tông, the new sect wanted stone for its furnaces and pill vessels. In 505 the green jade mine of Bích Ngọc Khoáng was opened at last. In time its working passed to Hồng Lô Cốc, the alchemists' valley sworn to Thúy Vi, which cuts the jade into pill bottles and furnace fittings.
places.art_brief: A stepped open quarry cut into the side of a green forested hill, its terraced faces showing bands of bright jade-green stone. Signature element: the green-banded stepped quarry face with a zigzag cart ramp down its middle. At the base: spoil heaps, two tiny plain sheds, a road. Warm light from the top left on the green bands. Avoid: any roofline beyond the two tiny sheds, text, people larger than specks, anything outside the quarry.

places.name: Vân Mẫu Khoáng
places.look: On a bare mountain slope a fan of glittering silver mica tailings spills down from a dark mine mouth, shining like a cloud resting on the rock. Above it thin seams in the cliff catch the light.
places.lore: The monks of Vân Khởi Quán opened this mine and say its stone is cloud made solid; they set it in the abbey's windows and lamps. When the mica ran thin, the abbot Tống Tọa Vân said that clouds, too, pass. The monks still dig a little each year, more for the lesson than for the stone.
places.history: The mica of this slope glittered unseen above the clouds until the monks of Vân Khởi Quán came up the mountain. In 560 they opened the mica mine and said the stone was cloud made solid. They set its thin sheets in the abbey's windows and lamps, so the halls glow pale at night. For five centuries the mine was dug by hand, a little at a time, as a practice as much as a trade. In 1080 the mica of Vân Mẫu Khoáng ran thin, and the abbot Tống Tọa Vân said that clouds, too, pass. The monks still dig a little each year, more for the lesson than for the stone.
places.art_brief: A bare grey mountain slope with one dark mine mouth. Signature element: a wide fan of glittering silver-white mica tailings spilling down the slope below the mine mouth like a resting cloud. At the base: scree and a narrow path. Warm light from the top left sparkling on the mica. Avoid: any roofline, text, people larger than specks, anything outside the slope.

places.name: Thạch Lục Khoáng
places.look: On a high slope of the pine sea, small mine mouths open between the exposed roots of giant old pines. Heaps of green malachite spoil lie below them, bright against the brown needles.
places.lore: Malachite was found under the roots of the oldest pines, and Tùng Đào let it be dug only where no tree must be cut. Miners tunnel between the roots and shore them with stone, never timber. Today Vạn Hác Viện holds the workings, and its malachite becomes green pigment for painters and inlay for zithers.
places.art_brief: A steep high slope under giant old pines with huge exposed roots. Signature element: small dark mine mouths opening between the great pine roots, with bright green malachite spoil heaps below. At the base: brown needle litter, a narrow mule path. Warm light from the top left on the green spoil. Avoid: any roofline, cut trees, text, people larger than specks, anything outside the slope.

places.name: Băng Lăng Khoáng
places.look: A mine mouth high on a bare grey mountainside, a timber headframe and spoil heaps under snow. Over the adit hangs a curtain of icicles thick as a man, which the miners walk through and never break.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các opened the mine in 580 for the cold metal in its rock; the shafts are hung with ice that never melts, even beside the miners' lamps. Miners wrap their boots in felt and speak softly underground, believing a shout can bring the ice down on them.
places.history: Băng Tâm Các took the frost land at the end of the Age of Seven Seats and searched its mountains for cold metal for its swords. In 580 it opened Băng Lăng Khoáng, a shaft hung with ice that never melts. The miners found that the ice grew back wherever it was broken, and learned to walk through the curtain of icicles at the mouth without touching it. Its cold metal went down the mountain to the Pavilion's sword smiths. The miners took to wrapping their boots in felt and speaking softly underground, believing a shout can bring the ice down. No one has ever seen the ice melt, even beside the lamps, and the mine is still worked today.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature on a steep grey mountain slope: a dark rectangular adit framed in timber, hung across its mouth with a dense curtain of long blue-white icicles; a timber headframe and grey spoil heaps beside it, snow on everything. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the ice. No text, no people larger than specks, no buildings beyond a small shed, nothing outside the slope.

places.name: Xích Kim Khoáng
places.look: An open-cut mine in the dry badlands, its terraces cut into rock banded with streaks of red gold. At sunset the whole pit glows the colour of Lạc Hà's evening sky.
places.lore: Red gold was found here in 360, and Thiên Bảo Trai bought the mine before Lạc Hà's stewards heard of it; the Trai holds it still. Its gold goes to the treasure market and the refining furnaces, and miners say the seam runs redder the deeper it goes.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature in eroded tan badlands: a stepped open pit with narrow terraces, its walls streaked with bands of glowing red-gold, a timber hoist and a couple of small grey-roofed sheds on the rim. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the pit and its rim.

places.name: Thần Sa Khoáng
places.look: In the red badlands, a hillside is cut into stepped terraces of bright vermilion spoil, with a shallow washing pool on each step where the cinnabar is rinsed. A low stone furnace house squats at the foot.
places.lore: Cinnabar was found in these red badlands in 300, and Thiên Xu's alchemists opened Thần Sa Khoáng to supply the alchemists' first stone. Miners wear cloth over their mouths and rinse their hands in a stone trough before eating; the old ones say the red gets into your dreams.
places.art_brief: A mine on a red badland hillside: a staircase of vivid vermilion spoil terraces, each with a small reddish washing pool, a dark adit at the top, and a squat grey stone furnace house with a short chimney at the foot. Cracked red ground at the base. Warm golden light from the top left deepening the reds. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Lưu Hoàng Khoáng
places.look: Flat pans of yellow sulphur crust spread across a grey badland floor, broken by steaming fissures, with low stone sheds where the crust is scraped and bagged. The ground around them is stained in rings of yellow, white and rust.
places.lore: Since 420 Thiên Xu has mined the sulphur crusts at Lưu Hoàng for fire powders, and the badlands smell of eggs for twenty li. Workers come in shifts and never sleep on site, and a gong is struck at the sheds whenever the fissures breathe harder than usual.
places.art_brief: A mine on flat grey badlands: shallow pans of bright yellow sulphur crust ringed with white and rust stains, thin steam rising from dark fissures, two low grey stone sheds with flat roofs. Cracked grey ground at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the yellow crust. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Vẫn Tinh Khoáng
places.look: On the high plain, a shallow round crater lined with dark, rust-streaked rock holds a timber headframe and winch over the deepest shaft at its centre. Small stone cairns mark the crater rim.
places.lore: At the end of the Wild Age stones fell from the sky on Thiên Tuyền Nguyên for nine days, and the iron at Vẫn Tinh is said to be from one of them. By 160 that star iron was being dug here, and Củng Tinh Quán keeps the mine still. The abbey's star-readers come each year to sight the crater rim against the stars.
places.art_brief: A mine on a high grassy plateau: a shallow round crater of dark rust-streaked rock with a timber headframe and winch wheel over a shaft at its centre, a ring of small grey stone cairns along the rim, a cart track leading out. Short highland grass at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the headframe. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Thiên Ngoại Khoáng
places.look: A sheer mountain face streaked rust-red, with a vertical line of square adits cut one above another and iron chains hanging from each down to the ore yard below. A sorting shed with a dark roof stands at the bottom by a stream.
places.lore: Thối Tinh Môn claimed the Mine of the Iron from Beyond the Sky in 335 and says its ore fell with the stars. Some star-readers quietly doubt it, but no smith who has worked the ore will hear a word against it.
places.art_brief: A mine on a sheer grey mountain face streaked with rust-red, a vertical column of small square adit openings one above another, thin iron chains hanging from them to a small ore yard and dark-roofed shed beside a stream. Scree at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the rust streaks. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Huyền Thiết Khoáng
places.look: Deep in the mountain a single great shaft opens under a massive stone winch house, and the ramp down to the road is worn into ruts a hand deep by carts that each carry one black ingot.
places.lore: Black iron was found deep under the mountain at Huyền Thiết in 280; it is so heavy that a cart carries only one ingot. Thiên Xu works it for armour and array anchors, and the oxen here are bred for the ramp and are the strongest in Ngọc Hành Sơn.
places.art_brief: A mine on a high mountain slope: a heavy square stone winch house over a dark shaft mouth, a steep stone ramp below scored with deep twin cart ruts, a single cart with one black ingot on it. Grey rock at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the winch house. No text, no people or oxen larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Can Tương Khoáng
places.look: High on a steep slope, two adits open side by side in the grey rock, one a little larger than the other, with a small stone shrine between them blackened by forge smoke. A narrow path zigzags down toward Phất Y Cốc.
places.lore: Named for Can Tương, the swordsmith of legend, this is where Phất Y Cốc digs the ore for its swords. The miners call the two adits the husband and the wife, after the legend of the paired swords, and ore from both is mixed in every blade; a sword of one ore alone, they say, will not keep its edge.
places.art_brief: A mine on a steep grey mountain slope: two dark adit mouths side by side, one slightly larger, a tiny soot-blackened stone shrine with a single small roof between them, a thin zigzag path descending. Grey scree at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the shrine. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Bạch Ngân Khoáng
places.look: Below a hillside stained red with cinnabar, a fan of pale silver-grey spoil spills from the adit mouths, so the slope looks dipped in two colours. A walled smelting yard with a squat chimney sits at the foot.
places.lore: Silver was found below the cinnabar slopes at Bạch Ngân in 450, and Thiên Xu's coin is struck from it. The mine lies close to Phượng Minh's border; in the Cinnabar Vein War its miners slept in the adits while the fighting at Đan Sơn Mạch lit the ridge above.
places.art_brief: A mine on a mountain slope whose upper half is red cinnabar rock and lower half a broad fan of pale silver-grey spoil spilling from two adits, a small walled smelting yard with a squat chimney at the foot. Rock and a road at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the red and silver slope. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Kinh Điện Khoáng
places.look: A mine on a bare ridge of Kinh Trập Sơn, where open-air forges stand on the rock beside the pit mouths, each with a tall iron rod raised above it to catch the lightning. The rock around them is streaked with burn marks.
places.lore: Lightning strikes the ore of Kinh Điện so often that since 220 Khải Lôi's smiths forged in the storm. Thính Vũ's smiths keep the old forges and still wait for storms to work. Miners wear wooden shoes and never carry iron tools in the rain.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature on a bare grey mountain ridge: a few dark pit mouths, low stone forge hearths in the open, and the signature, tall iron lightning rods standing above each forge. Scorch streaks on the rock, a storm cloud edge above. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Tử Kim Khoáng
places.look: A mine on a steep mountain slope, its tunnel mouths set in cliffs streaked purple and gold. Below them long fans of purple-tinted spoil spill down the hillside.
places.lore: Purple-gold ore, the colour of storm light, has been dug at Tử Kim since 300. The metal takes an edge well and is prized by Thính Vũ's sword smiths. Miners say a seam glows faintly before a storm, and they leave the tunnels when it does.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature on a steep high-mountain slope: timber-framed tunnel mouths in a cliff banded with purple and gold streaks, and the signature, long fans of violet-tinted spoil spilling down the slope below. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Vũ Hoa Khoáng
places.look: The highest mine in the thunder mountains, a stony upland where the stream beds have been dammed into long wooden sluices. In them lie heaps of smooth pebbles of every colour, red, agate-banded, green and white, gleaming wet in the rain.
places.lore: Rain-flower pebbles, said to be flowers that fell as rain while a master preached, were found here in 500, and Thính Vũ keeps the mine. It is held to be the richest mine ground in the Tower's mountains. Pickers sort the pebbles in the rain, when the colours show truest.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature on a high stony upland: no tunnels, but the signature, long wooden sluices and dammed stream beds filled with heaps of wet, multicoloured pebbles in red, green, white and banded agate. Low stone sorting sheds as the only structures. Light rain, warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Đan Thạch Khoáng
places.look: A quarry cut into a red mountain, its face stepped in tall terraces of raw vermilion rock. Rough-cut red blocks lie in rows on the quarry floor, waiting to be dragged down the road.
places.lore: Red stone from Đan Thạch was cut for Xích Thành's walls from 280. Phượng Minh still quarries it for its own builders. Quarrymen say the stone holds the day's heat long after sunset, and sleep against the blocks in winter.
places.history: The red mountain of Đan Thạch was known for its colour long before anyone cut it. In 280 Xích Thành Môn began to quarry it for its walls, and the halls of the red cliff-gate rose out of its blocks. Through the gate's long rule the quarry fed its builders, and the terraces of the face grew deeper with each generation. Under the heir who burned villages the quarrymen worked for war. When Phượng Minh destroyed the gate under writ, the quarry passed to the Palace with the rest of the coast. Phượng Minh's builders have cut it ever since, and its red stone stands in walls across Đan Huyệt Châu. Quarrymen still sleep against the warm blocks in winter.
places.art_brief: A small quarry miniature on a red mountainside: the signature, a stepped quarry face of raw vermilion rock in tall terraces, with rows of rough red blocks on the floor and a dirt road leading away. Warm golden-hour light from the top left deepening the reds. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Phụ Tinh Phong
places.look: A glacier peak stands beside taller neighbours, white ice over dark rock. Its broad shoulder holds a flat terrace cut into the ice, still bristling with rows of rusted iron stakes where weapon racks once stood. At night a single faint star hangs just above its summit.
places.lore: From 760 the disciples of Phá Quân Môn drilled here at night under the faint companion star beside the Dipper, as if to prove the small star could break armies too. Since the rebellion was crushed no one drills here; the stakes remain and the wind sings over them. Thiên Xu's patrols come up now and then only to look, and go down again.
places.history: Thiên Xu's protection reached Dao Quang Lĩnh in the Age of First Gates, and this glacier peak, too cold to farm or mine, was left to the wind. Late in the Age of the North Star Compact, Phá Quân Môn was founded in the mountains below it as a vassal of the Pivot. In 760, the year Chung Hoài Cực died, Phá Quân's disciples began to drill at night on Phụ Tinh Phong under the faint companion star, cutting a terrace into the shoulder and setting iron racks for their weapons. Whether the drills were meant for the Pivot's enemies or the Pivot itself, no one asked until a century later, when Hạ Lang Tinh led Phá Quân Môn against its lord. Within a few years Thiên Xu destroyed Phá Quân Môn, and the night drills ended. The racks rotted down to their iron stakes, which still stand in rows on the terrace. No sect holds the peak today.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a sharp glacier peak with no roofline: white ice and blue shadow over dark rock, a flat terrace cut into its broad shoulder holding rows of tiny rust-red iron stakes, the signature element. A faint pale star-glint just above the summit. Golden-hour light from the top left warming the snow, cold blue on the far side. No buildings, no text, no figures, nothing outside the peak.

places.name: Trích Tinh Phong
places.look: The roof of the heartland: a dark rock peak rising clear of the clouds, its summit ending in a thin stone needle. Strips of white cloth tied around the needle stream in the wind, and below it a pilgrims' road of a thousand rock-cut steps runs up the spine of the ridge. On clear nights the stars seem to rest on the needle's tip.
places.lore: Thiên Xu's first watchmen climbed Trích Tinh Phong in 260 and reported that one could pluck the stars by hand, and the peak has carried that name since. By 1100 the pilgrims' road up it had been cut into the rock in a thousand steps. Pilgrims tie a white strip at the needle and make a wish on a star; it is bad luck to say which one.
places.history: In 260, in the Age of First Gates, Thiên Xu's first watchmen climbed Trích Tinh Phong and came down saying one could pluck the stars by hand. The Pivot, founded under the stars of the Northern Dipper, kept the summit as a place to watch them. Two centuries later its patrols found the Star Marrow vein, Tinh Tủy Mạch, high near the peak, and posted a guard that has never been withdrawn. Through the Age of the North Star Compact pilgrims climbed to the needle by goat paths and tied their white cloths at the top. By 1100 the pilgrims' road had been cut into the rock in a thousand steps. Since Băng Tâm's claim to the vein was rejected by the Pivot, pilgrims climb under the eyes of a doubled guard and circling cranes.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a tall dark rock peak with no roofline, rising above a collar of cloud, its summit a thin stone needle wrapped with fluttering white cloth strips, the signature element. Snow in the gullies, and a faint thread of path along the ridge spine below. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the needle, deep shadow on the far side. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the peak.

places.name: Hồi Lộ Phong
places.look: A steep ice peak is wrapped in a switchback stair carved into its flank, the steps doubling back so often that the stair looks like white thread wound around a spindle. Wind-scoured snow fills the turns. From below, climbers on it seem to vanish and reappear at random.
places.lore: Hồ Thiên's disciples carved a stair of ice up Hồi Lộ Phong around 300; it bends so often that companions lose each other in plain sight. The school is long gone, but the cold has kept the stair. Băng Tâm's disciples climb it roped together, and quote the old line: the mountain turns, the road bends, and you are gone.
places.history: Hồ Thiên Phái was founded on the ice below Chúc Long Sơn in 210, and this peak above its ice fields became the school's training ground. Around 300 its disciples carved a stair of ice up Hồi Lộ Phong, bending so often that companions lost each other in plain sight. When Chúc Long Sơn erupted in 425 and buried the school, the stair stood high above the ash and lava. When Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn in the Age of Seven Seats, it found the stair still whole. Its disciples have climbed it roped together ever since, and have still lost one now and then. No sect holds the peak itself.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a steep ice peak with no roofline, its flank wound with a tight switchback stair of pale carved ice steps, the signature element, like a white thread around a spindle. Wind-blown snow in the turns, dark rock showing at the ridges. Warm golden-hour light from the top left catching the steps, cold blue shadows. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the peak.

places.name: Lê Hoa Am
places.look: The highest summit on the continent, a white glacier pyramid standing clear above a sea of cloud, with a cairn of pale stones on its very top. On a shelf of rock and ice on its flank a small hermitage of white-plastered halls hangs a bronze bell, ringed by frost-white stones.
places.lore: Lăng Tuyệt Phong is the Upper Hermitage of Lê Hoa Am, a hermitage (am) of women ice cultivators, a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) sworn to Băng Tâm Các. In 702 the founder Kỷ Hoa Ảnh raised it on the glacier, hung the bell cast from frozen lightning at the heart of the Pear-Frost Ring and planted ice pears round it; the white nuns live here under the abbess Thái Lê Tuyết, and the grey sisters hold the gate below. Băng Tâm's climbers reached the summit in 480 and left the cairn, and Băng Tâm's disciples still climb it before a long seclusion.
places.history: No climb of the continent's highest peak is remembered from the Wild Age or the Age of First Gates; even Hồ Thiên's disciples, who carved the stair on Hồi Lộ Phong, left no record of its top. Tần Ngưng Sương founded Băng Tâm Các in the Age of Seven Seats, and within a generation the sect had claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn. In 480 the sect's climbers reached the summit of Lăng Tuyệt Phong and saw all the mountains small. They left a cairn of pale stones at the top. In the centuries since, Băng Tâm's disciples have climbed it as a rite before long seclusion, and the sect has never set a building on it. No one claims the peak; the cold holds it.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a tall white glacier pyramid with no roofline rising out of a sea of soft cloud, clearly the tallest form on the map, a tiny cairn of pale stones on its point, the signature element. Blue crevasses on its flanks. Warm golden-hour light from the top left gilding the summit, the cloud sea below in pink and gold. No buildings, no text, no figures, nothing outside the peak.

places.name: Thanh Ải Phong
places.look: The highest peak of Ngọc Hành Sơn rises above bare grey ridges, its upper slopes wrapped in a band of soft blue haze that never burns off, so the summit is never seen. Climbers say the haze looks thick from below and is gone when walked into.
places.lore: Thanh Ải Phong, the Peak of the Blue Haze, is held by no sect; its name comes from the old line about blue haze that, walked into, is gone. Those who climb into the haze come down saying they found nothing but bare rock and their own footprints. In 1180 the haze lifted for a day for the first time in memory and a temple was seen on the summit; by evening it was gone, and the paths up the peak have never been busier.
places.history: Since the Wild Age the summit of Thanh Ải Phong has hidden in its blue haze, and the miners of the ranges below never could say what stands at the top. When Thiên Xu Tông took Ngọc Hành Sơn's ore mountains under its protection in the Age of First Gates, the peak was left unclaimed, for there seemed to be nothing on it to claim. Generations of hermits and treasure-seekers climbed into the haze and found only bare rock and their own footprints. The Pivot's surveyors left the summit blank on their mine maps and formation charts alike. In 1180 the haze lifted for a day for the first time in memory, and a temple was seen on the summit; by evening it was gone. Since then cultivators from across the heart have camped below the haze line, waiting for it to lift again.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a tall sharp grey peak above lower ridges, its upper third wrapped in a thick soft band of pale blue haze through which the summit is only a faint suggestion. Scree, snow streaks on the shaded side and stunted pines at the base. Warm golden light from the top left glowing on the haze band. No buildings (no temple visible), no text, no people, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Cùng Mục Phong
places.look: A narrow summit of pale granite stands above the ranges, so high that on clear days the plains and the shine of the inland sea seem to lie at its feet. Its flat top rock is criss-crossed with long, deep sword cuts that look as fresh as if they were made yesterday.
places.lore: Cùng Mục Phong, the Peak of the Farthest Sight, takes its name from the poem about climbing one storey more to see a thousand li further. In 1130 Tư Không Hạc Niên dueled Thang Vô Tạ of Phất Y Cốc here for three days; neither won, and Tư Không Hạc Niên left without a sect. Thang Vô Tạ will not speak of it, so Phất Y Cốc's disciples climb the peak to read the duel in the cuts; the summit winds are fierce, and not all of them come down.
places.history: In the Age of First Gates the peak was a lookout for the miners of Ngọc Hành Sơn, who watched from its spurs for beasts coming off the high valleys. Its name came from the old poem, and climbers took up the custom of adding one stone to the summit cairn to see a little further. After Phất Y Cốc was founded in the valleys below, its swordsmen used the summit for their trials, though no sect ever claimed it. In 1130 Tư Không Hạc Niên dueled Thang Vô Tạ of Phất Y Cốc on the peak for three days; neither won, and Tư Không Hạc Niên left without a sect. In 1131 Thang Vô Tạ would not speak of the duel, and Phất Y Cốc's disciples began to climb the peak to see the sword marks. The cuts have not weathered since, and climbers say the sword intent left in them still stings a careless hand.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a narrow pale granite summit thrusting above darker ridges, its flat top rock scored with a criss-cross of long straight bright cuts, a small stone cairn at one end. Bare rock and wind-bent juniper at the base. Warm golden light from the top left catching the cuts so they gleam. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Liệt Khuyết Phong
places.look: The highest summit of Kinh Trập Sơn, a sheer grey peak split from crown to shoulder by a deep vertical rift, as if cut by one stroke. The rock along the rift is fused black and glassy, and storm clouds gather on it more often than on any other summit.
places.lore: The peak takes its name from an old poet's line of lightning and thunder under which the ridges crumble. Khải Lôi's disciples once climbed it in storms to invite the lightning; Thính Vũ's disciples now drill on it in thunderstorms. The villagers below count the lightning and the disciples both, and lay a bowl of rice on the trail for each one who does not come down.
places.history: In the Age of First Gates, Khải Lôi Môn taught that a cultivator must invite the lightning, and this peak became its proving ground. By 440 the Gate's disciples were climbing it in storms, and only a third of them came down. The fused black rock along the rift is said to mark where the strongest strikes have landed. After Khải Lôi fell, the peak lay unused, and the mountain folk said its storms were waiting. Thính Vũ Lâu, whose arts lean toward Thunder, took up the old practice in its own way. By 1166, as the Tower rebuilt its strength after Đan Sơn Mạch, its disciples were drilling on Liệt Khuyết Phong in thunderstorms. The villagers below count the lightning and the disciples both.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline, the tallest summit of its range: a sheer grey rock peak split by a deep vertical rift from its crown, the rift's edges fused black and glassy. Snow streaks on the high ledges, a dark storm cloud pressed against the summit with a faint thread of lightning. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the lit face. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Chúc Long Sơn
places.look: A black cone rises out of the ice fields, its flanks streaked with old lava under a skin of snow. In its crater a dull red glow shows through a lid of ice, like the half-open eye of something asleep. Steam drifts from cracks around the rim and freezes into feathers of rime.
places.lore: Ice hunters have said since the Age of First Gates that the Torch Dragon sleeps under Chúc Long Sơn and lights the mountain when it dreams. In 425 the mountain erupted under the ice and buried Hồ Thiên Phái with its founder Khúc Hồ Già. In 1199 it rumbled for the first time since that eruption, and the nuns of Lê Hoa Am prayed all winter.
places.history: In 120 ice hunters already told that the Torch Dragon slept under Chúc Long Sơn and lit the mountain when it dreamed. In 210 Khúc Hồ Già founded Hồ Thiên Phái on the ice below the fire mountain, where snow flies in the eighth month. In 425 Chúc Long Sơn erupted under the ice and buried the school with its founder, and Ngọc Hồ Sơn lay empty for forty-five years. Băng Tâm Các claimed the ice after those empty years and built nothing near the cone. For centuries the mountain slept, and only the red glow in its crater showed it was alive. In 1199 it rumbled under the ice for the first time since the eruption, and the nuns of Lê Hoa Am prayed all winter.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a black volcanic cone with no roofline rising from white ice fields, its flanks streaked with dark lava under thin snow. In the crater, a lid of ice with a dull red glow beneath it, the signature element, like a sleeping eye. Thin steam wisps at the rim, frosted white. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, the red glow answering it from below. No buildings, no text, no figures, nothing outside the mountain.

places.name: Sương Diễm Sơn
places.look: A broad snow-capped volcanic cone rising alone out of the forest. Down one flank runs a crimson fissure that never freezes, glowing through the snow and trailing a thin plume of steam.
places.lore: No sect holds the mountain; the fire under its frost draws cultivators of both fire and water to its slopes, each sure the other side's qi is the danger. The people of Mộc Lan Thành watch its steam the way sailors watch the sky.
places.history: Sương Diễm Sơn smoked under its snow long before any sect came to the north-east, and the fishers of Hàn Giang Môn called it the mountain of frost and flame.
