It stood outside every border when Băng Tâm Các took the frost coast in 498, and the Pavilion has never claimed it. In the Age of the North Star Compact Băng Tâm founded Mộc Lan Thành on the coast below it. In 700 the mountain breathed fire under the frost for a week, and the people of Mộc Lan Thành slept on the beach until the fire sank. Ash fell on the snow that winter, and the forest at its foot grew thick and dark in the years after. The crimson fissure on its flank has never closed since. Wandering cultivators climb to it to temper fire and water arts together, though few stay long.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a broad, solitary volcanic cone with a white snow cap, ringed at its base by dark firs; one flank split by a narrow glowing crimson fissure from which a thin white steam plume drifts. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left on the snow, the fissure glowing against the shadow side. No text, no people, nothing outside the cone and its forest skirt.

places.name: Hạo Nguyệt Hồ
places.look: The long lake runs pale silver between dark forest shores, the largest water on the continent, its far end lost in haze. On one shore a thin stone causeway leaves a small fishers' shrine and runs straight out into the lake, stopping in open water.
places.lore: Fishers say a man once walked across this water into the moon, and they built a shrine where he set out; the causeway was laid later, stone by stone, by those who wanted to follow as far as they dared. The lake's pearls feed Hàm Nguyệt Trang and the shore towns, and once brought two great sects to war. Its water is cold and deep with qi, and the lake villages say the master who left the world here never quite took his home with him.
places.history: In the Wild Age fishers on the long lake saw a man walk over the water into the moon, and in 45 they built a shrine on the shore where he had set out. In 470 a fisher of Tuyết Lộc pulled a pearl the size of a fist from the lake; Hàm Nguyệt Trang bought it and began to farm pearls, and the pearl trade later made the shore towns rich. In 748 Hạo Nguyệt Hồ froze to its bed for one winter, and the spirit fish of Hàm Nguyệt Trang lived through it in the moon's reflection. Its pearls drew Tùng Đào Cung and Băng Tâm Các into the Long Lake War in 940. In 944 Đỗ Tinh Hà arbitrated: the lake stayed Tùng Đào's, and Băng Tâm won the right to fish its northern shore. In 1192 a white moon-fox was seen on the lake three nights running, and the villagers say a blessed land is waking somewhere in the north.
places.art_brief: A long, narrow lake of pale silver water lying between dark conifer and birch shores, seen from above at an angle, its far end fading into haze. Signature element on the near shore: a thin grey stone causeway that leaves a tiny grey-roofed shrine and runs straight out over the water, ending abruptly in open lake. At the edges: reed beds, a few lines of pearl-farm stakes, thin rims of pale ice. Warm low light from the top left laying a gold path across the water. Avoid: text, people, boats larger than specks, any roofline other than the tiny shrine, anything beyond the lake's own shores.

places.name: Phiến Băng Hồ
places.look: A small round lake set in a hollow of the forest. In winter it freezes as clear as glass, so the stones and weed of its bed show through the ice, and the dark specks of meditating disciples sit scattered across it like drops of ink.
places.lore: The lake lies near Băng Tâm Các, and its name comes from a line of the Pavilion's poem: one piece of ice heart. Since the winter of 1065, when it froze clear as glass and disciples who meditated on it saw their own hearts, Băng Tâm disciples walk out onto it each winter to sit. Its qi runs to wood and fire, strangely warm for a frozen lake, and the elders say that is why it shows a heart and not a face.
places.history: The lake has no recorded name from before Băng Tâm Các came to the cold north-east in the Age of Seven Seats. The Pavilion named it Phiến Băng Hồ after a line of its poem, one piece of ice heart. For centuries it froze white and cloudy like any forest lake. In 1065 it froze as clear as glass, and Băng Tâm disciples who meditated on it saw their own hearts. Since that winter disciples have gone out onto the ice every year; some come back calmer, and some come back and leave the sect. No one holds the lake, but no one fishes it. Elders of the Pavilion hold that the clear ice comes only in winters when the Pavilion's own heart is steady.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a small round lake in a forest hollow, frozen perfectly clear so the brown stones and green weed of its bed show through glassy ice; a few tiny dark specks of seated figures scattered on the ice. Dark firs and snow on the rim. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left glancing off the ice. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the hollow.

places.name: Tinh Lạc Hồ
places.look: High on the plain beside Củng Tinh Quán lies a dark, perfectly round lake so still it reads as black glass, rimmed by a single ring of pale stones. At night the whole Northern Dipper lies in it, star for star.
places.lore: Tinh Lạc Hồ, the Lake Where the Stars Fall, is a high lake that holds the Dipper at night as clearly as the sky. The star-readers of Củng Tinh Quán read it alongside their armillary, and they forbid boats, fishing and even skipping stones, lest a ripple spoil a reading. Herders believe a wish whispered at the water's edge on a windless night is heard by the stars themselves.
places.history: At the end of the Wild Age stones fell from the sky on Thiên Tuyền Nguyên for nine days, and the herders of the high plain came to believe the round lake was where the first of them had struck. When Củng Tinh Quán was founded nearby in the Age of First Gates, its star-readers studied the lake from the shore. In 155 they found that Tinh Lạc Hồ holds the Dipper at night as clearly as the sky. They set a ring of pale stones around the water to mark where readers may stand, and banned boats and fishing. When the abbey's armillary was finished a generation later, the abbey began to read sky and lake together, trusting a sign only when both agreed. No sect holds the lake itself, but no one has broken the abbey's ban in living memory.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a small perfectly round lake of very dark, mirror-still water on a high grassy plateau, rimmed by a single thin ring of pale stones, faint star-like glints in the water. Short highland grass and grey rock at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the stone ring, the water staying dark. No text, no people, no buildings, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Lễ Tuyền Phái
places.look: A wide shallow lake lies so still at dawn in the open grassland that the first clouds lie doubled on it, a rose mist lifting off the water. On its shore stands the Dawn Hall, pale timber halls at the water's edge with herb terraces behind, and in the eastern shallows lies a low flat platform of weathered stone, half awash.
places.lore: Lễ Tuyền Phái, a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) of healers under Phượng Minh Cung, keeps its Dawn Hall (Triêu Đường) on this shore, where in 950 Mai Lễ Tuyền delivered Hoa Triêu Dương, now head of Phượng Minh Cung, at dawn as the clouds turned red. Mai Lễ Tuyền raised the hall in 1141 with a gift from the palace head and moved the healers and the inner gate down from the spring, while the brewers kept the Spring House. A bronze mirror that came with the gift hangs under the hall's eaves and gathers the lake's dawn light. The plain folk say the east's dawn clouds answer Lạc Hà's sunset clouds in the west, and pilgrims of the Palace come at dawn to watch them.
places.history: In the Age of First Gates the musicians of Vân Môn Thành, Cửu Thiều Cung's city on the plain, came to this lake to play to the rising sun. By 200 it was said that the dawn clouds took the colour of their music, and the players built a low stone platform in the shallows to stand on. After the War of the Nine Shao the musicians were gone, and for nearly two centuries only herders saw the dawns here. When Phượng Minh Cung took the plain, its people came back to the shore. In the Age of the North Star Compact healers founded Lễ Tuyền Phái beside the lake, at the sweet spring. In 950 Hoa Triêu Dương was born at dawn on the shore as the clouds turned red; a century and a half later she became head of Phượng Minh Cung. Since then pilgrims of the Palace come at dawn to watch the clouds, and some bring flutes.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a broad, calm, shallow lake in flat grassland, its surface mirroring rose and gold clouds, a soft pink mist lifting off the water. The signature is a low, flat, square platform of weathered grey stone, half awash in the eastern shallows, with rose light reflected on its wet surface. Reeds at the margins. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Tàn Hà Hồ
places.look: A grey lake at the foot of the Tower's cone, its surface crowded with withered lotus: tall brown stalks, curled dry leaves and empty seedpods that are never cut and never cleared. Even in summer the lake looks like the end of autumn.
places.lore: Phó Tiêu Tương kept the withered lotus on the lake below her tower to listen to the rain on it, and the lake took the name Tàn Hà Hồ. Disciples of Thính Vũ sit on its shore in storms, learning to hear each drop on the dry leaves apart. No one may cut a stalk, and any lotus that blooms is left to wither.
places.history: Phó Tiêu Tương founded Thính Vũ Lâu above this lake, and in 382, two years after the founding, she kept the withered lotus standing on the lake below her tower so that she could listen to the rain on it, and the lake was named Tàn Hà Hồ. From then on the Tower's sword disciples were sent to its shore to listen to the rain before they were taught the sword. When the founder died five centuries later the lotus was left as she had kept it. After the Night Rain Edict the lake shore became the place where new masters were first received, by night. In 1158, after the Tower's defeat at Đan Sơn Mạch, Mạnh Dạ Vũ did not leave the Tower for a year, and in all that year the rain on Tàn Hà Hồ never stopped. Disciples still call a long rain a head's mourning.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a small grey-green lake in rain forest at the foot of a volcanic slope, its whole surface crowded with brown withered lotus, the signature, dry upright stalks, curled leaves and empty seedpods. Rain dimpling the water. Banana and forest leaves at the shore. Warm golden-hour light from the top left breaking under rain cloud. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Phù Chử Đảo
places.look: A low wooded isle off the plain coast, its trees dark against the water. Around it floats a thick, shifting raft of wild ducks, so dense the water looks feathered.
places.lore: The isle takes its name from the old line about crane shoals and wild-duck isles. Since the Age of Seven Seats boats have had to wait for the ducks to move before they can land, and fishers say anyone who forces a way through will have no luck all season. No sect holds it, and only egg-gatherers go ashore in spring.
places.history: The isle had no name in any record before the fishers of the western plain began to row out to it. When Lạc Hà Tông took the grassland of Trường Thiên Nguyên early in the Age of Seven Seats, the isle was left outside its rule, too small to claim. By 470 wild ducks crowded Phù Chử so thickly that boats had to wait for them to move. Egg-gatherers from the coast villages row out every spring and take care to leave most nests. Hunters who shot into the flocks, the coast says, found the ducks gone the next year, and no one hunts there now. No sect has claimed the isle in any age.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a small low island covered in dark temperate trees, with a narrow pale shore, ringed on the water by a dense brown-and-white mass of tiny duck specks. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left, calm blue water. No text, no people, nothing outside the isle and its ring of birds.

places.name: Tịch Chiếu Đảo
places.look: The westernmost island, a low grassy hump in the open sea. On its western cliff stands a single long stone bench facing the sunset, and behind it the grass is dotted with small cairns of grey stones.
places.lore: Tịch Chiếu is the last land to see the sunset of Lạc Hà, and since the Age of the North Star Compact the sect's elders have gone there to die. They sit on the bench at evening; the cairns mark those who did not come back. The boats that bring them out do not wait.
places.history: Tịch Chiếu Đảo lies west of all other land, the last to see the sun go down over Lạc Hà Tông's western lands. No settlement has ever stood on it. Lạc Hà, founded late in the Age of First Gates in the western lands where the sun goes down, named it for the evening glow. By 600 the sect's elders had begun to go there to die, sailing out at the end of their lives to watch the last sunset. Each leaves a small cairn of grey stones on the grass. The island is held by no one, and fishers give it a wide berth out of respect. Elders who feel their time near still ask for a boat to Tịch Chiếu.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a small low grassy island with a short western cliff, a single long grey stone bench at the cliff edge facing away to the west, and scattered tiny cairns of grey stones on the grass behind. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left, the sea turning amber. No text, no people, nothing outside the island.

places.name: Tương Phi Đảo
places.look: A small steep island off the coast, covered from shore to crown in dense bamboo whose canes are flecked with purple-brown spots, like old tear stains. There is no landing and no roof; the bamboo comes right down to the rocks.
places.lore: The spotted bamboo on Tương Phi Đảo, the Isle of the Xiang Consorts, is said to be stained by the tears of two consorts mourning their lord, as in the old legend. Phượng Minh forbids cutting it, and boatmen passing at dusk fall silent out of respect. Flutes of the spotted bamboo made before the ban are said to play sadder than any other.
places.history: The island stood in the gulf long before any sect came south, and the coast people cut its spotted bamboo for flutes and brushes. In the Age of Seven Seats the legend took hold that the spots were the tears of two consorts mourning their lord, and pilgrims began to sail out to see them. In 500 Phượng Minh Cung, newly risen on the ridges, forbade cutting the bamboo. The island has never been settled or claimed, and Phượng Minh keeps its ban by custom rather than by holding the land. The instrument makers of Thiều Âm Thị treasure the old flutes made before the ban and will not sell them lightly. Boatmen of the gulf like to say that the ribs of Thính Vũ Lâu's famous umbrella were cut here long ago, though no one in the Tower has ever said so.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a small steep rocky island in jade-green water, covered entirely in dense bamboo whose pale canes are flecked with purple-brown spots, the bamboo crown rounded like a cushion. Dark wet rocks and a ring of white surf at the base, no landing, no buildings. Warm golden light from the top left on the bamboo crown. No text, no people, no boats larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Dục Nhật Đảo
places.look: A forested island in the far south-eastern sea, its eastern shore facing open ocean where the sun rises straight out of the water. On that shore stands a great ring of sea-worn rock, an arch open to the sunrise, by which the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh opens. A single thatched hut sits under the trees above it.
places.lore: The first fishers of the gulf believed the sun bathed here every night before it rose. On this island Mạc Quy Khư entered the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh, the Realm of the Sunrise Mulberry, at its first recorded opening, and the Thiên Nguyên calendar (Thiên Nguyên lịch) counts its years from that day. Since 700 he has lived here by the gate, the oldest living person, and has never left. Pilgrims come by boat to ask him about the world before the sects, and he answers one question a year.
places.history: In the year 0 of the Thiên Nguyên calendar, Mạc Quy Khư entered the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh on Dục Nhật Đảo at its first recorded opening, and the calendar counts its years from that day. In 5 the first fishers of the gulf saw the sun rise out of the sea here, and believed it bathed at the island every night. Through the Wild Age and the ages of the sects, cultivators sailed here when the realm opened and went home again, and no sect ever held the island. Mạc Quy Khư's name grew with every age, until he was the oldest living cultivator in the world. In 700 he came to live on Dục Nhật Đảo by the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh, and he has never left it since. By 1100 pilgrims were coming by boat to ask the hermit about the world before the sects, and he answers one question a year. The island is still unclaimed, and the fishers of the gulf still bow to its sunrise.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a small forested island in deep blue sea, its eastern shore of dark rock facing the rising sun. The signature is a great ring-shaped arch of sea-worn rock on that shore, open to the horizon, with a faint warm glow within it. Under the trees above, one tiny thatched hut no larger than a speck. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, a gold path on the water. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Đồ Nam Đảo
places.look: A low grassy island in the southern sea, its crown pressed into a vast shallow hollow, as if something enormous had lain there. The grass in the hollow grows in long swirled streaks like the print of feathers, and seabirds wheel over it in their thousands.
places.lore: The great Bằng is said to rest on Đồ Nam Đảo before its flight to the south, as the old book tells of the bird that rises beyond the clouds and sets out southward. Fishers say the hollow is its bed, and that the wind there always blows toward the south. No one lives on the island; sailors land only to leave fish in the hollow for a fair wind.
places.history: Fishers of the southern gulf knew the island from the earliest ages, a bare grassy hump with no spring and no harbour. By 350, in the Age of Seven Seats, the tale was told that the great Bằng rested on Đồ Nam Đảo before its flight to the south, and the hollow on its crown was called its bed. Sailors began to leave fish in the hollow for a fair wind southward, a custom that has never stopped. In the pirate years of the Age of the North Star Compact, Thôn Hải's ships are said to have anchored off the island but never landed, holding it unlucky. After the Purge the fishers came back to its waters. No sect has ever claimed it, and no one has ever dug the hollow.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a low green island in blue sea, its crown pressed into a broad shallow oval hollow, the signature, with grass inside it combed in long swirling feather-like streaks. Small white seabirds circling as specks. Warm golden-hour light from the top left raking across the grass. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Phản Cảnh Lâm
places.look: From outside it is a dark sea of old spruce and larch rising gently to a low crown. At its heart a hollow ringed by giant trees holds a patch of amber evening light that lingers long after the rest of the forest has gone grey.
places.lore: Lost travellers have walked out of Phản Cảnh Lâm by the light at its heart, which stays until dawn, and the forest is named for that returning light. Woodcutters tie a strip of bark to the last tree they pass, so the next lost walker can follow the light out. The forest belongs to no sect; Tùng Đào's patrols skirt its edge, and hunters leave the inner hollow alone.
places.history: In the Wild Age and the Age of First Gates the northern forest was only a hunting ground for the lake villages, unnamed and unmapped. Late in the Age of First Gates its region passed under Tùng Đào Cung, but the palace never fenced or settled the deep heart of the wood. By 530 travellers knew that the evening light lingered in the heart of the forest so long that the lost could walk by it until dawn, and the forest took the name Phản Cảnh Lâm. The custom of tying bark strips to the trees grew from those walks, and the strips now mark several faint ways out. In 870 hunters found footprints in the snow leading into the forest and never out, and no one followed them. Since then the heart has been left alone, and the lake villages tell children that the light is someone waiting.
places.art_brief: A broad, gently rising dome of dense dark conifer forest seen from above at an angle, no clearings at its edges. Signature element: a sunken hollow at the centre ringed by a few giant old larches whose crowns glow amber-gold as if lit from within, while the canopy around them lies in cool blue-green shadow. At the base: patches of snow, a faint hunters' trail that stops at the forest edge. Warm light from the top left, with the hollow's glow slightly warmer than the sun. Avoid: any roofline, text, people, paths into the heart, anything outside the forest's footprint.

places.name: Vô Tung Lâm
places.look: A dark, rolling forest of spruce and fir under deep snow, its crowns bowed white. Through it runs a frozen stream like a white ribbon, and not one track crosses it or the snow on either bank.
places.lore: The Forest Without Tracks takes its name from the poem: on ten thousand paths, no human trace. Snow fills every path by morning and only the woodcutters of Tiều Lộ Thôn can find the ways again; white bears, snow foxes and stranger beasts live deep inside. Hunters who go in alone notch the trees behind them, and still come back mostly by luck.
places.history: No sect has ever claimed the forest, and no road crosses it. In the Age of Seven Seats the fishers of Hàn Giang Môn cut wood at its edge but never went deep. Early in the Age of the North Star Compact the woodcutters' paths into it were known to vanish under the snow every night, and only the people of Tiều Lộ Thôn could find them again. After Băng Tâm Các founded Mộc Lan Thành on the coast, the forest's timber and furs fed the city's market. Late in the same age a hermit sheltering at Lâm Ẩn Thôn, on the coast at the forest's edge, taught the village children to read its beasts' tracks in the snow. In the last generation of the Age of Vein Wars hunters brought a white bear out of Vô Tung Lâm alive and sold it in Mộc Lan Thành to a buyer from Thiên Bảo Trai, and the forest's beasts have had a price on the coast ever since. Still, no map shows its heart.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a dense, rolling mass of dark spruce and fir with snow-laden crowns, no clearings, cut through by a single winding frozen stream that lies like a smooth white ribbon with untouched snow on both banks. No buildings, no roofline, no paths. Warm golden light from the top left on the crowns, deep blue shadow between trees. No text, no people, nothing outside the forest.

places.name: Đả Diệp Lâm
places.look: A grove of tall green bamboo on low hills, so dense that rain on the leaves roars like surf. In its heart is a clearing filled with cut bamboo stumps of different heights, standing in rows like a field of posts.
places.lore: The forest gives its line to Xuyên Lâm Môn nearby: pay no heed to the rain piercing the forest and beating the leaves. The school's young disciples train their footwork on the stumps in downpours, learning to keep their footing as the rain hammers the grove. Woodcutters who come for poles must leave the clearing alone.
places.history: The bamboo of Đả Diệp Lâm was old long before any sect came to Kinh Trập Sơn, and in Khải Lôi's day it was a wild grove that the Gate's people crossed on their way to the sea. After the Gate fell the grove passed into Thính Vũ Lâu's land, and woodcutters from the villages took its poles for houses and ferries. When Xuyên Lâm Môn was founded nearby in the Age of the North Star Compact, its staff fighters took the forest's line for their own and began to train in it. The clearing of stumps was cut in the school's early years, and every generation of disciples has recut it. In the year after the Night Rain Edict, while their head walked the forest road in protest against the Night Rain Edict, the disciples are said to have trained here through the whole rain in silence. A guide of Xuyên Lâm is still not trusted to lead travellers until they have crossed the stumps in a storm without falling.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a dense grove of tall green bamboo on low rounded hills, rain streaking through the leaves. The signature is a clearing at its heart filled with rows of cut bamboo stumps of many different heights, like a field of posts. Warm golden-hour light from the top left slanting through the rain. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Viên Đề Hạp
places.look: A narrow gorge cuts through the high mountains, its walls hung with vines and its river loud below. A timber plank road pinned to the cliff face runs the length of one wall, and gibbons swing above it, crying on both banks without end. Mist fills the gorge floor at dawn.
places.lore: The gibbons of Viên Đề Hạp cry on both banks without end, and since at least 600 caravan drivers have stopped their ears with wax to cross. Old drivers say the cries are worst for the homesick. No sect holds the gorge, and the plank road is mended by whoever needs it.
places.history: The river cut this gorge through the high mountains of Cô Yên Mạc long before any record was kept. Mortal caravaneers pinned the first planks to its walls to shorten the road between the desert and the lands beyond, though no one remembers when. By 600 caravans used it often, and the gibbons crying on both banks without end had taught the drivers to stop their ears with wax. In the Desert Road War, more than a century later, the plank road is said to have served as a back way for messengers, and both sides burned stretches of it. The planks were renewed after the Pivot's truce. No sect has ever claimed the gorge, and the gibbons have outlasted every war.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a narrow gorge with no roofline between steep grey mountain walls draped in green vines, a white-water river at the bottom. Along one wall, a thin timber plank road on pegs pinned to the cliff face, the signature element. A few dark gibbon specks in the vines, mist at the gorge floor. Warm golden-hour light from the top left lighting the upper walls, the depths in cool shadow. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the gorge.

places.name: Vạn Trùng Hạp
places.look: A deep, twisting gorge where the river races white between ranks of steep ridges folded one behind another like stacked screens. A narrow plank road on timber beams socketed into the cliff runs along one wall above the rapids.
places.lore: Vạn Trùng Hạp, the Gorge of Ten Thousand Mountains, takes its name from the poem of the light boat that has passed ten thousand mountains. Boats in the gorge pass ten thousand mountains in a day, and the river is the fastest road to the sea. Travellers going upstream take the plank road; boatmen going down never look back, since a pilot who turns his head is said to lose the river.
places.history: The river cut Vạn Trùng Hạp through Ngọc Hành Sơn long before any cultivator came to the heart. When Thiên Xu took the ore mountains and founded its port Tinh Hán Thành on the inland sea in the Age of First Gates, the gorge became the quickest way to bring ore down toward the coast. Ore boats ran the rapids, and the wrecks of the reckless still lie in the deep pools. By 620 it was said that boats in the gorge passed ten thousand mountains in a day, and that the river was the fastest road to the sea. A plank road was socketed into the cliff for those going upstream, and it has been rebuilt beam by beam ever since. No sect holds the gorge, and its pilots answer to no one but the river.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a deep winding gorge seen from above at an angle, white-water river at the bottom between steep layered ridges stacked one behind another, a thin timber plank road on beams clinging to the left cliff wall, a single tiny boat on the rapids. Grey and ochre rock with dark pines on the ledges. Warm golden light from the top left on the upper ridges, the gorge floor in cool shadow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Tinh Tủy Mạch
places.look: High on a black rock face near Trích Tinh Phong, seams of silver-white star marrow thread through the stone and glitter like frost even at noon. A low stone breastwork and a guards' fire pit sit on a ledge in front of the face. Cranes wheel over it in slow rings.
places.lore: Thiên Xu found the Star Marrow vein (linh mạch) high near Trích Tinh Phong in 470 and posted a guard that has never been withdrawn. Its qi (linh khí) runs to Metal and Earth, heavy and cold as iron. In 1188 Băng Tâm Các claimed it before the Pivot and was refused; since then the guard has been doubled, and Cửu Cao's cranes circle it day and night.
places.history: At the end of the Wild Age stones fell from the sky on Thiên Tuyền Nguyên, and the star iron in them drew the first cultivators to the heart; some say the marrow in this mountain is kin to that iron, though no one has proved it. In 470 Thiên Xu found the Star Marrow vein high near Trích Tinh Phong and posted a guard that has never been withdrawn. Through the long Compact the vein lay quiet near the border of Băng Tâm Các, never fought over. In 1188 Băng Tâm claimed Tinh Tủy Mạch before the Pivot; the claim was rejected, and Sở Ngọc Hồ withdrew in silence. In 1189 Thiên Xu doubled the guard, and Cửu Cao Phái's cranes began to circle the vein day and night. The silence from the desert seat has not yet been broken.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a black high-mountain rock face with no roofline, seamed with bright silver-white glittering veins, the signature element. On a ledge before it, a low curved stone breastwork with a tiny glowing fire pit. Snowfields above, tiny white crane specks circling. Warm golden-hour light from the top left making the veins flash. No roofs, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the rock face and ledge.

places.name: Thương Tùng Mạch
places.look: On a high summit above the pine sea stands a grove of pines with bark the colour of ash, older and paler than any around them. An old fence of stone posts and timber rails rings the grey grove, and the air inside is still even when the forest below is roaring.
places.lore: A wild spirit vein runs under the grey pines, close to the heart and the Pivot's border. Tùng Đào fenced it and still guards it, and its disciples cultivate there in turns. Foresters say the pines turned grey from drinking the vein's metal and earth qi.
places.history: Before it had a name, the grey grove on the summit was known to woodsmen only as a place where the wind fell silent. Tùng Đào Cung held the pine sea from its founding, but only in 470 did its disciples fence the grey pines over an old spirit vein near the heart and name it Thương Tùng Mạch. Under the North Star Compact, the vein could change hands only by a fall, a gift, an oath or a war licensed by the Pivot's writ, and it has stayed Tùng Đào's. In the Age of Vein Wars, when neighbours fight short wars over the wild veins near their borders, Tùng Đào set a standing watch on the grove, for it lies close to Thiên Xu's land. Its disciples cultivate there in turns, and the stillness under the grey pines is said to help a cultivator hear his own meridians.
places.art_brief: A high, rocky summit rising above an endless dark pine sea. Signature element: a grove of pale, ash-grey pines on the summit, ringed by an old fence of stone posts and weathered timber rails. At the base: bare rock, a narrow guarded path climbing from the forest. Warm light from the top left on the grey bark. Avoid: any roofline, text, people larger than specks, anything outside the summit.

places.name: Trường Hà Mạch
places.look: A high bare mountain on the border, its slope split by a long seam of amber-gold rock that winds down the face like a river. In the setting sun the seam glows as if the river ran with fire.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông found this spirit vein (linh mạch) on its new border with Thính Vũ Lâu in 620, the year the Petal Shore was divided, and named it for the line about the long river and the round setting sun. Its qi runs to earth and metal. Lạc Hà's disciples cultivate on its ledges with one eye on the far ridges, where Thính Vũ's land begins.
places.history: The mountain lay in no sect's reckoning until 620, when the Pivot's judgement divided the Petal Shore, the bay to Lạc Hà and the forest to Thính Vũ. That year Lạc Hà found the Long River vein on its new border with Thính Vũ and named it Trường Hà Mạch. On the eve of the War of Broken Halberds the founders of the two sects met on the Petal Shore and swore to end the Pivot's oversight, and through that war this border lay at the allies' backs, not their front. After the truce that ended it renewed the Compact, the two sects went back to watching each other. In the Age of Vein Wars, when neighbours fought short wars over the veins near their borders, Lạc Hà set a standing watch on the ridge; no war over this vein is recorded. Since Thính Vũ rebuilt its strength after Đan Sơn Mạch, the watch has been strengthened.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a steep, bare grey-brown high mountain face with a long winding seam of glowing amber-gold rock running down it like a river, a few tiny cultivation ledges cut beside it. No roofline. Warm golden light from the top left setting the seam alight. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the mountain face.

places.name: Kinh Lôi Mạch
places.look: High on a bare black ridge of Kinh Trập Sơn, seams of violet light run through the rock like veins under skin, brightening whenever thunder rolls. Nothing grows on the ridge, and the air above it smells of a struck flint.
places.lore: Kinh Lôi Mạch is a spirit vein (linh mạch) that carries Thunder from the storm peaks, the richest prize in the mountains and close to Thiên Xu's border. Lệ Tiêu Hồn, master of the Tower's soul vaults, has kept it since 1010. Phượng Minh Cung fought for it from 1040 to 1046 and lost; the south remembers.
places.history: The vein runs within reach of the storm peaks of Kinh Trập Sơn, and its qi has carried Thunder for as long as anyone has drawn on it. Khải Lôi Môn's cultivators knew the ridge in the Age of First Gates, and after the Gate fell it passed with the mountains to Thính Vũ Lâu. In 1010 Lệ Tiêu Hồn broke through in the Tower's soul vaults, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ made him keeper of Kinh Lôi Mạch. In 1040 Phượng Minh Cung went to war with Thính Vũ Lâu for the vein. In the war's last year the Palace's raiders reached the upper ferry at Thượng Độ before the Pivot's envoys stopped them. In 1046 the Pivot ended the Thunder Vein War: Thính Vũ kept the vein, and the south remembers. A century later the Tower struck at Phượng Minh's own vein, Đan Sơn Mạch, and lost.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a bare black rock ridge high in grey mountains, its surface split by glowing violet seams of light like veins. The signature is the branching violet seams themselves, glowing through the black rock like veins under skin. Storm cloud above. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the rock. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Băng Phách Mạch
places.look: Below the ice mountains, a round cave mouth opens in a cliff, rimmed with ice so white it glows faintly blue, like the moon seen through mist. Inside, pillars of ice give off a cold light of their own. Frost feathers grow on the rocks for a long way around the entrance.
places.lore: Băng phách, the ice soul, is an old name for the moon, and Băng Tâm opened this spirit vein (linh mạch) below the ice mountains in 760. Its qi (linh khí) feeds the sect's ice cultivators and is fierce enough to freeze a careless breath in the throat. The storm peaks loom close, and beasts drawn to the vein's cold make the approach perilous.
places.history: Hồ Thiên Phái held these mountains from 210, but the deep cold under them was never tapped before the eruption of 425 emptied the land. Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn in the Age of Seven Seats, and for nearly three centuries searched the ice mountains for a vein worthy of its arts. In 760, the year it also founded Hồi Lan Thành on the desert coast, the sect opened the Ice Soul vein, Băng Phách Mạch, below the ice mountains, and named it for the moon. Since then the vein has fed the sect's ice cultivators far from the desert seat. Its approach, close under the storm peaks, remains one of the most feared roads in Băng Tâm's lands.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a dark cliff below snowy ice mountains with no roofline, a round cave mouth rimmed in glowing moon-white and pale blue ice, the signature element, faint ice pillars glimmering inside. Frost-covered rocks around the entrance. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the snow, the cave giving off its own cold blue glow. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the cliff.

places.name: Hỏa Ngọc Mạch
places.look: Far out in the western sea a black volcanic island rises in a steep cone, steam leaking from its flanks. Down the cone's sides run seams of fire jade that glow red-green through the rock at dusk, as if the mountain were cracked over a lamp.
places.lore: A spirit vein (linh mạch) of fire jade lies under the volcano, charted by Thúy Vi's surveyors and kept on a sealed chart. It sits at the edge of the cape's waters, where Lạc Hà's waters begin, and few ships come so far. Thúy Vi sends no settlers; those who go are alchemists and miners on short, guarded voyages.
places.history: In the Wild Age the island was only a smoking mark on the horizon for the cape's fishers. A few years before the find, Thúy Vi Tông took the cape of snow and fire and set its surveyors to chart the coast and the sea beyond. In 565 they found a pocket of fire jade under a volcano far out at sea, named it Hỏa Ngọc Mạch and kept the chart sealed. The vein became Thúy Vi's quiet treasure, worked in small voyages rather than settled. In the Age of Vein Wars it lies on the edge of Lạc Hà's waters, the kind of wild vein neighbours fight over, yet no war has been fought for it. The cape's sailors say the sealed chart is the reason: no one fights for what they cannot find.
places.art_brief: A steep black volcanic cone rising alone from deep blue sea, a thin steam plume from its crater and wisps from its flanks. Signature element: branching seams of fire jade running down the cone's sides, glowing red and green through the dark rock. At the base: a narrow rim of black sand and white surf, at most one tiny cove. Warm light from the top left on the cone's shoulder. Avoid: any roofline, text, people, ships, anything beyond the island's shore.

places.name: Đan Sơn Mạch
places.look: A steep mountain flank of vermilion rock is split by a long seam that glows a deeper crimson at dusk, where the vein's qi runs close to the surface. Along the ridge above stand the scorched stone footings of watch platforms from the last war.
places.lore: Đan Sơn Mạch, the Vein of the Cinnabar Mountain, is Phượng Minh's spirit vein (linh mạch) near its border with the heart, named after the cinnabar mountain of the old classics where the phoenix is born. Thính Vũ Lâu attacked it in 1150 and was beaten in 1158 with Thiên Xu's help; Mạnh Dạ Vũ swore the Pivot would answer for it, and the palace has kept a guard on the ridge ever since. Alchemists of the south say cinnabar from the seam needs no grinding.
places.history: Cinnabar and silver had long been dug from the slopes around this mountain, and since the Age of Seven Seats Thiên Xu has struck coin from the silver at Bạch Ngân below it. In 900 Phượng Minh found the vein near its border with the heart and named it Đan Sơn Mạch, after the cinnabar mountain where the phoenix is born. The palace guarded it closely, for a vein so near another sect's border was exactly what the Age of Vein Wars was fought over. In 1150 Thính Vũ Lâu attacked Đan Sơn Mạch. In 1154 Doãn Ngọc Hành brought Thiên Xu Tông into the war on Phượng Minh's side, to enforce the Compact. In 1158 Thính Vũ Lâu was beaten at Đan Sơn Mạch and withdrew, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ swore the Pivot would answer for it. The watch platforms burned in the fighting still stand in ruin on the ridge, and the palace has not left the vein unguarded since.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a steep vermilion rock mountain flank seen at an angle, split by one long seam glowing deep crimson, a few small scorched grey stone footings of ruined watch platforms along the ridge above. Red scree and sparse dark pines at the base. Warm golden light from the top left deepening the reds. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Cao Cương Phong
places.look: A high bare ridge-top above the wutong hills ends in a flat crest of pale gold stone that takes the first light of dawn before anything else in the south. A single stone pillar stands on the crest, worn at its top into the shape of a perch.
places.lore: Cao Cương Phong, the Peak of the High Ridge, takes its name from the old ode in which the phoenix sings on that high ridge, and it is a sacred summit where the light gathers. Phượng Minh's disciples have climbed it at dawn since at least 600 and say the phoenix sang there. Pilgrims leave nothing on the crest, and what is left anyway is gone by the next dawn.
places.history: It is said that the court musicians of Cửu Thiều Cung named this crest after the ode of the phoenix singing on the high ridge, and played their dawn tunes toward it. After Cửu Thiều fell in the War of the Nine Shao the ridge went quiet for well over a century. When Phượng Minh Cung rose on the empty lands, its disciples took up the dawn climb. By 600 they said the phoenix had sung there, on that high ridge, and the climb became a rite of the palace. Light gathers on the crest at dawn more than anywhere else in the south, and cultivators of light come from far away to sit on it. No sect holds it; Phượng Minh says no one can hold a place the phoenix chose.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a tall bare ridge-top rising above green hills, ending in a flat crest of pale gold stone with a single slender stone pillar on it, its top worn into a curved perch. Light scree and a few wind-bent wutong trees at the base. Strong warm golden light from the top left making the crest glow brighter than everything around it. No text, no people, no birds larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Không Sơn Viện
places.look: High on a ridge above the haze a cluster of old halls stands silent, their doors open, the roof of the great lecture hall sagging and its small pagoda missing its top tier. Beside the path a raw landslide scar runs down the slope, and in it a stone gate carved with lines of poetry stands half-buried, its opening blocked with newer stone.
places.lore: The Academy of the Empty Mountain was so quiet that, as its poem says, on the empty mountain no one is seen. Its last master gave it away and died here, and Thúy Vi has left it unlocked and unlooted ever since; no visitor takes so much as a brush. Travellers who sleep here tell of someone reading aloud in the next room.
places.history: In 180 Bùi Lộc Trại founded Không Sơn Viện in the hills of Thanh Loan Lĩnh, an academy so quiet that, as the poem says, on the empty mountain no one is seen. The woodcutters of Tiều Ca were asked to sing more quietly below it, and its students planted the cypress groves of Bách Diệp as a lesson in patience. When green jade was found in its hills the academy forbade mining it, and in the Age of Seven Seats fishers and ferrymen built Hàn Tân Thành under its protection. Bùi Lộc Trại died in 460, and Thôi Bất Kiến became master and took no disciple but one boy, Tống Tọa Vân. In 500, with no heir, Thôi Bất Kiến gave the hills, his whisk and his only student to Phùng Yên Hà, and the empty mountain became Thúy Vi's. He died in the empty academy in 520, and Phùng Yên Hà left it as it was, unlocked and unlooted. In 830 a landslide on the ridge uncovered a stone gate carved with Không Sơn's poem, and Thúy Vi sealed it again. In 1195 a traveller who spent a night in the empty halls swore he heard someone reading aloud in the next room.
places.art_brief: A ruin of broken verticals high on a bare ridge above the mist: old academy halls of grey stone with weathered grey tile roofs, doors standing open, a small pagoda missing its top roofs and the great lecture hall's roof sagging at one end. Signature element: a raw brown landslide scar down the slope beside the halls with a carved stone gate half-buried in it, its opening blocked with paler new stone. At the base: bare rock, a few old pines, haze below. Warm light from the top left with long, quiet shadows. Avoid: text, people, signs of looting or fire, anything outside the ridge.

places.name: Băng Tâm Các
places.look: Băng Tâm Các's white halls climb a black lava mountain on a sheet of blue glacier ice, raised on the ruin of Hồ Thiên Phái, with a great Vessel Hall on the summit and a tall white pagoda behind it. At the mountain's foot the green-tiled tip of one old pagoda roof still stands out of a bare field of black lava, and a ring of jade-green light glows up through the ice.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các, the Pavilion of the Ice Heart, is a great sect (đại tông môn) of sword cultivators (kiếm tu); its name comes from the old line that the ice heart sits in the jade vessel. In 470, when the sect claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, Tần Ngưng Sương moved it onto the ruin of Hồ Thiên Phái and laid the Jade Vessel Array into the ice over the buried vent; the steam stopped and the birds came back. Sở Ngọc Hồ has led the sect since 1010 as keeper of the Jade Vessel, with Tiết Hàn Mai as first elder. Hồ Thiên Phái, buried by Chúc Long Sơn in 425 with its founder Khúc Hồ Già, lies beneath the halls, and the sect leaves the ruin as it lay.
places.history: In 210 Khúc Hồ Già founded Hồ Thiên Phái on the ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, below the fire mountain Chúc Long Sơn, where snow flies in the eighth month. In 230 Khúc Hồ Già forged the sword Phi Tuyết from ice that never melts. In the school's best years its disciples carved the winding ice stair of Hồi Lộ Phong. In 425 Chúc Long Sơn erupted under the ice and buried the school with its founder, and Ngọc Hồ Sơn lay empty. A year later steam still rose from the ice where Hồ Thiên had stood, and no bird sang there. Two generations later Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice and left the ruin as it lay. The villagers of Đỗ Quyên Thôn still say the red azaleas on their slopes are the eruption's dead.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of broken verticals on a flat tundra shore: a field of black frozen lava with frost in its cracks, and rising from it only the green-tiled, curled-eave tip of one buried pagoda roof, the signature element, with a few broken roof ridges nearby. Grey water at one edge. No intact buildings. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the green tiles. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Xích Thành Môn
places.look: On the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu, cliffs of deep red rock rise in rounded tiers like banks of rosy cloud above the sea. Into them are cut the broken terraces and gutted halls of the old gate, their fire-blackened walls open to the sky, with fresh pale quarry scars where stone has lately been taken away.
places.lore: Tôn Hà Khởi founded Xích Thành Môn here in 250, among red cliffs and vents where the rock rises like a rosy cloud. Its banner Xích Hà Kỳ was woven from fire-silk spun in the vents. Under his heir Chu Liệt Nhật the sect burned villages to feed its fire arts, and Phượng Minh destroyed it under the Compact's first writ. Herders do not graze here; they say the cliffs are still warm at night.
places.history: Tôn Hà Khởi founded Xích Thành Môn in 250 among the red cliffs and vents of Đan Huyệt Châu, and in 260 the sect wove its war banner, the Xích Hà Kỳ, from fire-silk spun in the vents. Within a generation its walls were cut from the red stone of Đan Thạch, and soon after it built Ngũ Thải Thành on the coast. Tôn Hà Khởi died in 560, and his heir Chu Liệt Nhật turned the sect to burning villages to feed its fire arts. After eleven villages had burned, Phượng Minh Cung asked the Pivot for a writ, and the first writ of the North Star Compact was granted. In 590 Phượng Minh destroyed Xích Thành Môn with Chu Liệt Nhật, and the Xích Hà Kỳ went to hang in the Palace's hall. Four centuries later the banner was lent to Phần Vũ Đường, which revived the fire arts in the vents inland. In the last years of the Age of Vein Wars, Phượng Minh took stone from these ruins to rebuild the cracked jetty of Thạch Cơ Thành.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature of broken verticals on a steppe coast above the sea: deep red cliffs in rounded stacked tiers like rosy cloud banks, the signature, with broken terraces and roofless, fire-blackened stone halls cut into them; a few pale fresh quarry scars on the red rock. No roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left turning the cliffs crimson. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Hàn Giang Môn
places.look: A broken sect seat on the frost coast: a stone gate arch fallen on its side and half buried in snow, behind it the stumps of halls stepping up a low bank. A fishing rod carved along the fallen lintel shows where the wind has swept the snow away.
places.lore: Here the Gate of the Cold River taught its fishers to cultivate alone in the snow beside holes cut in the river ice, sitting for days without moving. It fell to Băng Tâm Các in 498 with its last head Liễu Cô Chu. The coast's fishers still leave a fish on the fallen gate after a good catch, and no one, not even Băng Tâm's disciples, takes it.
places.history: Liễu Thoa Lạp founded Hàn Giang Môn on the frost coast in 300, a sect of fishers who cultivated alone in the snow on the cold river. By 330 its fishers were known for cutting holes in the river ice and sitting beside them in the snow for days without moving. A generation later the sect founded Liên Giang Thành where the cold rain joins the river. When Băng Tâm Các came to the cold north-east in the Age of Seven Seats, the two sects shared the ice uneasily. Half a century later Băng Tâm, under Tần Ngưng Sương, made war on Hàn Giang for the frost coast. In 498 Hàn Giang Môn fell with its last head Liễu Cô Chu, and Hàn Sương Châu passed to Băng Tâm Các. Its fishers stayed and fished the cold river under the Pavilion's flag, but the seat was never rebuilt, and the snow has had it since.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature on a low snowy coastal bank: broken stone stumps of halls in small terraces, a few jagged wall ends and one leaning timber post as broken verticals; in front, a large stone gate arch lying on its side, half buried in snow, a long carved rod visible along its lintel. Dark firs behind, grey sea in front. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people, no intact roofs, nothing outside the ruin's footprint.

places.name: Thôn Hải Môn
places.look: A small forested islet in the southern gulf, ringed by rocks. At the waterline gapes the black mouth of a sea cave large enough to take a ship, its rim scorched and the stumps of a broken log boom still standing across it. Charred timbers of the old hold lie heaped inside the entrance.
places.lore: Ô Kình Hải gathered pirates on this islet in 640 and founded Thôn Hải Môn, the Gate That Swallows the Sea, and for over a century its ships raided the southern coasts. The Purge ended here in 781 when he died on his islet, and his sabre Kình Nha was lost in the burning hold. Treasure seekers still row out to dig in the ash, and some do not row back.
places.history: Ô Kình Hải gathered pirates on an islet of the southern gulf in 640 and founded Thôn Hải Môn; fishers say the pirate ships lay hidden in the great sea cave. A century and more later his pirates burned the pearl harbour of Châu Lệ Cảng, and soon after they carried off the whole village of Lô Châu. Then Đỗ Tinh Hà of Thiên Xu Tông called the Pirate Purge, and Phượng Minh's and Lạc Hà's fleets sailed under the Pivot's writ, while the watchers on the cliffs of Vọng Hải could see the pirates' sails a day before they landed. In 781 the Purge ended at Thôn Hải Môn: Ô Kình Hải died on his islet, and his sabre Kình Nha was lost in the burning hold. The captives held there were freed and went home to rebuild their villages. The islet has lain in Phượng Minh's land ever since, and no one has settled it.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature of broken verticals: a small rocky islet with dark green trees in blue gulf water, and the signature, a huge black sea-cave mouth at the waterline with a scorched rim and the broken stumps of a log boom standing in the water across it; heaped charred timbers just inside. No roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, deep shadow in the cave. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Phá Quân Môn
places.look: On a high mountain shoulder, a gate arch split clean down the middle still stands, each half leaning away from the other, with seven iron star-studs running across its broken lintel. Behind it, scorched walls and the stump of a watchtower climb the slope. Grass grows in the old parade ground, and little else.
places.lore: Hạ Lang Tinh founded Phá Quân Môn in 720 as a vassal of Thiên Xu, naming it for the Army-Breaker, the Dipper's seventh star. In 870 Hạ Lang Tinh led it against its lord to win by war the land the Compact forbids, and in 874 Thiên Xu destroyed it; Đỗ Tinh Hà took Hạ Lang Tinh's spear. Miners of Dao Quang Lĩnh say the seventh stud on the gate glows on the night of the fall.
places.history: In 720 Hạ Lang Tinh founded Phá Quân Môn in the mountains of Dao Quang Lĩnh as a vassal of Thiên Xu, named for the Dipper's seventh star, the Army-Breaker. It held the high passes for the Pivot and trained hard; within two generations its disciples were drilling at night on nearby Phụ Tinh Phong. In 870 Hạ Lang Tinh led Phá Quân Môn against its lord, to win by war the land the North Star Compact forbids. Thiên Xu laid siege to the fort, and in 872 Cửu Cao's crane riders carried the Pivot's messages over it. In 874 Thiên Xu destroyed Phá Quân Môn; Đỗ Tinh Hà took Hạ Lang Tinh's spear, and Cửu Cao Phái received the rebels' holdings. The fort was never rebuilt, and Thiên Xu keeps the ruin as a warning to its vassals.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of broken verticals on a high mountain shoulder: a stone gate arch split down the middle, its two halves leaning apart, a row of seven small iron studs on the broken lintel, the signature element. Behind it, fire-blackened wall stubs and the jagged stump of a watchtower climbing the slope, a grassy parade ground in front. No intact roofs. Snow and grey rock around. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long shadows through the split. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Kim Cốc Thành
places.look: The burned shell of a merchant city on the bay shore, its walls blackened and its streets choked with ash and weeds. At its heart stands the charred skeleton of a great garden pavilion, a few gold-glazed tiles still clinging to its broken ridge.
places.lore: Kim Cốc Viên, a garden of trade under Lạc Hà Tông, built this city around its gardens in 760 and lost it in a market crash and a great fire in 1003. The pearl Lục Châu was lost in the ashes, and scavengers still sift the old garden for it; they have found only melted coins and broken jade.
places.history: In 760 merchants of Thu Thủy Loan founded Kim Cốc Viên, a garden of trade under Lạc Hà Tông, and built Kim Cốc Thành around it. For more than two centuries its merchants dealt in everything the bay could sell, and its gardens were the wonder of the coast. In 1003 Kim Cốc Viên collapsed in a market crash and a great fire; Kim Cốc Thành burned, and the pearl Lục Châu was lost in the ashes. A year later its merchants were begging in Vật Hoa Thị, where Thiên Bảo Trai hired those who could still count. Within a decade its trade had gone to the new city of Ngũ Cốc Thành. Lạc Hà holds the ruin but has never rebuilt it, and its stewards call the ground unlucky for trade. Rumour holds that the pearl was never lost at all, only hidden.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature on a flat bay shore: a rectangle of blackened, broken grey walls, roofless houses and weedy ash-grey streets; at the centre the tall charred timber frame of a pavilion with a few bright gold tiles on its broken ridge, the main broken vertical. Overgrown garden beds around it. Warm golden light from the top left catching the gold. No text, no people, no intact roofs, nothing outside the walls.

places.name: Vân Môn Thành
places.look: Low grass-grown walls on the river, broken into a rough square, with the stumps of towers at the corners. In the middle stands the one thing still upright: a tall frame of two carved stone pillars and a crossbeam, where the stone chime Vân Môn Khánh hung in the city's hall.
places.lore: Cửu Thiều Cung built Vân Môn Thành in 130 and named it for the Vân Môn music, twin of the Thiều. When Cửu Thiều fell the city emptied within a year, and its people took the music with them to the four coasts. Herders who shelter in the ruin say the empty frame hums a low note in a strong wind, and they will not sleep under it.
places.history: In 130 Cửu Thiều Cung, the palace of court music on the ridges of Thê Ngô Lĩnh, built Vân Môn Thành on the rice plain it had taken under its protection ten years before. The stone chime Vân Môn Khánh was hung in the city's hall, and the city became the plain's centre of music and trade. Its musicians played to the dawn at Triêu Hà Hồ, and the rice of Thủy Điền filled its markets. At the end of the Age of First Gates, Thiên Xu Tông destroyed Cửu Thiều Cung in the War of the Nine Shao. In 341 Vân Môn Thành emptied within a year; its people scattered to the four coasts and took the music with them. Through the Age of Seven Seats its walls fell slowly while wild oxen grazed its streets. Phượng Minh Cung took the plain two centuries later but never resettled the city, and it lies in the Palace's land as a ruin. Whether the chime still lies under the rubble, no one on the plain will say for sure.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature of broken verticals on flat grassland by a river: a rough square of low, grass-grown, crumbling walls with broken tower stumps at the corners and tumbled stones inside. The signature and tallest element is a tall freestanding frame of two carved grey stone pillars with a crossbeam, standing alone in a roofless hall. No roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left casting a long shadow of the frame. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Lôi Trạch Thành
places.look: On a marshy river mouth by the sea, among old forest, stand the broken walls of a city whose stones are fused black and glassy, as if fired in a kiln. Over the old gate rises the shattered stump of a great drum tower, split down its middle. Reeds grow through the streets.
places.lore: Khải Lôi Môn built Lôi Trạch Thành in 170 at the river mouth below its mountains. At the end of the Age of Seven Seats the lightning of Hầu Xuân Lôi's own tribulation burned it, and the next year its people moved up the valley to Không Mông Thành. Its dead lie on the bamboo hills inland, where Thu Phần Các now keeps the graves, and in autumn ghosts are said to sing old poems there.
places.history: Khải Lôi Môn built Lôi Trạch Thành in 170, ten years after Lý Thiên Cổ founded the Gate, at the river mouth below its mountains. It was the Gate's market and harbour, and its great drum tower answered the thunder of the peaks. The city buried its dead on the bamboo hills inland, away from the marsh. Three centuries after its founding Hầu Xuân Lôi, head of the Gate, was struck down by his own tribulation, and its lightning burned Lôi Trạch Thành. In 481 the survivors moved up the valley to Không Mông Thành. Thính Vũ Lâu took the land but never rebuilt the city, and the marsh crept into its streets. Nearly five centuries later Lý Hận Bích founded Thu Phần Các among the city's graves and swore it to Thính Vũ Lâu, and since then the farmers of Ương Ca have heard singing from the graves each autumn.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature of broken verticals on a reedy river-mouth marsh at the sea edge, among dark old trees: fragments of city wall with stones fused black and glassy, and the signature and tallest element, the split, shattered stump of a great round drum tower over a broken gate. Reeds and water in the old streets, no roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left glinting on the glassy stone. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Hồng Vũ Thành
places.look: Burned walls among wild peach trees on the Petal Shore, inland of the bay. In spring the peaches bloom through the roofless halls, and red petals drift down over the black stones like red rain.
places.lore: Lạc Anh Phái built this city on the Petal Shore in 260 and lost it in the war over the shore in 618, when petals and ashes fell together like red rain. Lạc Hà Tông holds the ruin. Every spring, when the peach trees bloom, ghost lights are seen moving through the ruins, and the people of the bay leave them alone.
places.history: In 240 Đào Tân Phân forged the twin swords Phi Hồng and Tàn Hồng from one peach branch hardened by a thousand springs, and decreed that whoever held both would lead the School of the Fallen Petals; the ground where this city would stand was the school's orchard. In 260 Lạc Anh Phái built Hồng Vũ Thành on the Petal Shore. When Đào Tân Phân died early in the Age of the North Star Compact without naming an heir, the two swords parted, and less than a century later the school split and its last head, Khương Vọng Nguyệt, vanished. Lạc Hà Tông and Thính Vũ Lâu both claimed the empty shore, and their disciples fought in the burning orchards. In 618 Hồng Vũ Thành burned in the fighting, and its petals and ashes fell together like red rain. The Pivot's judgement that followed gave the bay to Lạc Hà, and the ruin lies on its side of the line. On the eve of the War of Broken Halberds the founders of Lạc Hà and Thính Vũ met on the Petal Shore they had once fought over. Since 1180 ghost lights have been seen in the ruins every spring when the peach trees bloom.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature on flat green ground: low blackened walls and roofless hall stumps, a few broken wall ends and a fallen gate post as broken verticals, with wild peach trees in full pink-red bloom growing through them and a drift of red petals on the dark stones. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people, no lights, no intact roofs, nothing outside the ruin.

places.name: Vô Định Thành
places.look: A burned city on the dry steppe at the edge of the poisoned plain, its walls broken and its streets empty; of the river that named it, only a dry stream bed under a broken footbridge is left. A grey-green bank of miasma lies against the ruins like fog that never lifts, and above it a charred bell tower still holds its bronze bell, green with verdigris.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông built the city in 600 on the river where three lands meet, and it burned in the battle of 803; the miasma took what was left. Its dead are still dreamed of in the river towns, and those who fled it founded Tân Khẩu Thôn. Children still dare each other to touch the edge of the miasma here, and in 1196 one did not come back. Some say the bell rings on the night of the battle with no one to pull it.
places.history: Lạc Hà Tông built Vô Định Thành in 600 on the river where three lands meet. For two centuries it traded across the borders that met at its gates. When the War of Broken Halberds broke out on the border plain where three sects' lands meet, Thiên Xu Tông under its war marshal Quý Trường Kích stood against Lạc Hà Tông and Thính Vũ Lâu. In 803 the war ended in one day at Chiết Kích Nguyên; Vô Định Thành burned in the battle on the plain, and the miasma took what was left. When the truce left the poisoned plain empty between the three sects' lands, refugees from the city founded Tân Khẩu Thôn at a harbour mouth on the coast. The river that named the city dwindled with it, and only a stream bed and a choked well remain. Its dead are still dreamed of in the river towns. In 1196 children of Tân Khẩu dared each other to touch the edge of the miasma by the ruin, and one did not come back.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature on dry tawny steppe, a dry pebbled stream bed running past it (no river): broken, fire-blackened walls and roofless houses, half swallowed on one side by a low bank of grey-green fog; rising above the fog a charred square bell tower, its roof gone, a verdigris-green bronze bell still hanging in it, the tallest broken vertical. Warm golden light from the top left, dimmed where the fog lies. No text, no people, no intact roofs, nothing outside the ruin's footprint.

places.name: Đông Lưu Thành
places.look: A long stone quay wall runs through an empty meadow, its rusted iron mooring rings hanging over grass where boats once tied up. Behind it stand the roofless stubs of warehouses, and a fresh scar of sand shows where a spring flood has opened up an old paved street. The living river runs past at a distance, along the edge of the bed.
places.lore: Mortal boatmen built Đông Lưu Thành on a great bend of the northern river in 90, long before any sect held this land. They gave the river spirit a pig every spring for safe passage, until the spirit stopped answering; ten years later the river left them, and the city was abandoned in 281. Old boatmen still say all things flow east, and do not finish the saying.
places.history: In 90, in the Wild Age when only hermits and beasts held the land, mortal boatmen built Đông Lưu Thành on a great bend of the northern river. From 100 they gave the river spirit a pig every spring for safe passage, and the city lived well on its boats. Late in the Age of First Gates, Tùng Đào Cung took the river basin, and the city fell under its protection. In 270 the river spirit stopped answering the boatmen's offerings. Ten years later the river left them, cutting a new course across the plain, and in 281 Đông Lưu Thành was abandoned; all things flow east. Some say the spirit itself stayed behind in a pool somewhere on the old course. For more than nine centuries the city lay under silt and grass, until a spring flood in 1198 uncovered its old street on the dry bed, and children found coins of a city no one remembers.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of broken verticals beside a dry, grassy river bed: a long stone quay wall standing in open meadow, hung with a row of rust-red iron mooring rings over the grass, the signature element; behind it the jagged, roofless wall stubs of old warehouses; a short strip of uncovered grey paving in pale flood sand. No intact roofs, only a few fallen grey tiles in the grass. A thin glint of living river along one edge of the footprint. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long shadows from the wall stubs. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Hổ Khiếu Trấn
places.look: Deep in the pine sea, on a river bend, the walls of a small town have sunk under moss and young trees. Its timber watchtower lies toppled across the gate, scored with claw marks as long as a man is tall.
places.lore: Woodsmen founded Hổ Khiếu Trấn where the tigers are, and the tigers ended it. The beast tide that overran it left no one to rebuild, and Tùng Đào never resettled it; its survivors' children live at Thanh Tùng Thôn. Hunters say a tiger still dens in the old magistrate's hall.
places.history: In 380 woodsmen founded Hổ Khiếu Trấn deep in the pine sea, where the tigers are, and lived on timber and pelts. For centuries the town held its palisade against the forest. In 700 a tiger as large as a house was seen near the town; Tùng Đào sent three disciples, and two came back. In 734 a beast tide poured out of the deep pines and overran Hổ Khiếu Trấn, and the tigers' roar was the last thing its people heard. A year later the survivors moved to Thanh Tùng Thôn and planted a green pine for each of their dead. The town was never rebuilt, and the forest has taken back its streets.
places.art_brief: A ruin of broken verticals on a river bend in deep pine forest: low moss-covered walls of a small town, roofless timber houses, young trees growing in the streets. Signature element: a tall timber watchtower toppled across the gateway, its beams scored with huge claw gouges. At the base: a river bend, a collapsed wooden landing. Warm light from the top left through the pines onto the fallen tower. Avoid: text, people, beasts larger than specks, anything outside the old walls.

places.name: Bích Không Cảng
places.look: The empty harbour below Đàm Ảnh Thành: long stone quays running out into blue water, lined with bare mooring posts and not one boat. At the root of the quays stands the roofless shell of a great sail loft, its rafters open to the sky.
places.lore: From here the sails of Cô Phàm Các vanished into the blue, and here the fleet failed to come home. Giang Bích Không made the Viễn Ảnh Châm for this harbour, a needle that always points to the last ship to leave port. The widows left a year after the loss and the quays have faced the empty sea since; fishers will not tie up here, and say the needle, wherever it is now, still points out past the harbour mouth.
places.history: Cô Phàm Các, founded on Cô Vụ Đảo by Giang Bích Không in the Age of Seven Seats, built the harbour of Bích Không Cảng below Đàm Ảnh Thành soon after. In 420 Giang Bích Không made the Viễn Ảnh Châm, a needle that always points to the last ship to leave port, and his sailors read the sea like a scripture. At the close of that age the Strait Oath bound the sect to Lạc Hà Tông, and Lạc Hà's cargoes sailed from these quays too. In the Age of the North Star Compact a storm sank the whole fleet with its head Mã Viễn Ảnh, and the Pavilion of the Lone Sail was lost at sea. In 706 the widows of Bích Không Cảng left the harbour, and the empty quays have faced the blue ever since. Lạc Hà holds the ruin and has never refitted it. What became of the needle is not recorded.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature on a grassy shore: long straight stone quays running out into deep blue water, lined with rows of small bare mooring posts, no boats; at their landward end the tall roofless shell of a timber-and-stone sail loft, bare rafters standing as broken verticals. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people, no intact roofs, nothing outside the quays and the loft.

places.name: Cô Thành
places.look: On a white salt pan that was once a desert lake stands a square fortress, its walls glazed black and cracked by fire. One corner tower still rises to its full height; the rest have slumped. Salt crust creeps up the foot of the walls like frost.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các raised Cô Thành in 520, a lone fortress on a desert lake to guard the caravan road; an old poem says the lone fortress looks far toward the jade gate. In the Desert Road War its garrison held out for two years against Phượng Minh's fire, drinking the lake down to salt, before it fell in 726. Caravans pass it in silence, and some leave a cup of water at the gate.
places.history: In 520 Băng Tâm Các raised Cô Thành, a lone fortress on a desert lake, to guard the caravan road between the desert and the rice plain. For two centuries it kept the road, until Băng Tâm Các and Phượng Minh Cung went to war over the caravan road. From 724 the garrison held out for two years against Phượng Minh's fire, drinking the desert lake down to salt. In 726 Phượng Minh's fire broke Cô Thành; the lone fortress fell and the lake turned to salt. Soon after, the Pivot imposed a truce on the Desert Road and the border stayed where it was; Băng Tâm kept the ruin and never rebuilt it. Much of the trade it once guarded later moved to the sea road through Hồi Lan Thành.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of broken verticals on a flat white salt pan: a square fortress whose walls are fire-glazed black and cracked, one corner tower standing at full height and the others slumped into rubble, the signature element. White salt crust climbing the wall bases, a dry caravan track passing at one side. No intact roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, stark shadows on the salt. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Châu Lệ Cảng
places.look: A curve of low coast where a beach of heaped white oyster shells glitters under rows of charred pier pilings standing in the shallows. Behind them the burned shells of warehouses and a broken harbour wall slope down into the sea.
places.lore: Phượng Minh Cung built the pearl harbour here in 600, and for over a century its divers brought up the pearls of the moonlit sea. In 762 Thôn Hải's pirates burned it; the divers fled, and the pearls in the sea are said to weep. Fishers passing on moonlit nights say the water over the old oyster beds glows faintly, and they do not stop.
places.history: Phượng Minh Cung built Châu Lệ Cảng on its eastern coast in 600, the same year it founded Hoàng Vân Thành, to bring in the pearls of the gulf. Its divers worked the oyster beds off the shell beach, and its pearls went to the Palace's hall and the markets of the coast. A generation later Ô Kình Hải founded Thôn Hải Môn on an islet of the southern gulf, and the pearl harbour lay within reach of his ships. In 762 Thôn Hải's pirates burned Châu Lệ Cảng. The divers fled, and the next year they settled inland at Âu Lộ and never dived again. The pirates were destroyed in the Pirate Purge two decades later, but no one came back to rebuild. The shell beach is all that is left, and the saying that the pearls weep has outlived the harbour.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature on a low grassy coast: a curved beach of heaped white oyster shells, rows of blackened broken pier pilings standing up out of shallow turquoise water, the roofless fire-scarred walls of a few warehouses and a broken harbour wall sloping into the sea. The tallest elements are the charred pilings and a broken wall corner. Warm golden-hour light from the top left glinting on the shells. No roofs, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Thiết Tỏa Quan
places.look: On a forested bluff above the river road stand the broken walls of a fort, its gate towers cracked and one fallen. At the bluff's edge a massive stone anchor-block still holds a great iron ring, snapped open, from which the chain once ran across the river.
places.lore: Thiết Tỏa Quan was the fort of Tùng Đào and Lạc Hà in the War of the Pivot, where they stretched an iron chain across the river road to the heart. Thiên Xu broke it, and the chain sank to the river bed, where the people of Cổ Độ now drag up its links. Tùng Đào holds the ruin but has never rebuilt it, and its elders bring disciples here to see what breaking the peace cost.
places.history: At the end of the Age of Seven Seats, Tùng Đào Cung and Lạc Hà Tông marched together on the heart of the continent, and Kỳ Tùng Ẩn broke the peace of the three days. In 503 the allies raised Thiết Tỏa Quan and stretched an iron chain across the river road to the heart. Through the years of the siege the ferrymen of Cổ Độ kept carrying the chain's iron up the river link by link. In 508 Thiên Xu Tông broke Thiết Tỏa Quan, and the thousand-fathom chain sank to the river bed. The war ended the next year with the allies beaten and no land taken, and soon after the North Star Compact was set at Thạch Kiều Thành. The fort was left as it fell. Nearly five centuries later the links of its chain began to be dragged from the river at Cổ Độ and sold to smiths.
places.art_brief: A ruin of broken verticals on a forested bluff above a river: cracked stone walls of a fort, one gate tower still standing and broken-topped, the other fallen in a heap. Signature element: a massive square stone anchor-block at the bluff's edge holding a great iron ring snapped open, rust-red against the grey stone. At the base: a steep slope down to the river road, pines on the bluff. Warm light from the top left on the anchor-block. Avoid: text, people, a visible chain across the river, anything outside the bluff.

places.name: Thu Phần Các
places.look: On a quiet bamboo hill inland from the ruins of Lôi Trạch, a pavilion of dark weathered wood with two small towers rises above slopes covered in old grave mounds. Between the bamboo, countless thin wooden slips, each brushed with a line of an old poem, hang on strings across the graves and clack softly in the wind.
places.lore: Thu Phần Các is a minor ma đạo sect of soul arts and grave wards, sworn to Thính Vũ Lâu by its founder and head Lý Hận Bích. It keeps the graves of Lôi Trạch Thành, where ghosts sing old poems in autumn. Its disciples copy down the poems the ghosts sing onto the wooden slips and hang them back over the graves. The villagers of Ương Ca stay away.
places.history: The bamboo hill was Lôi Trạch Thành's burial ground from the city's founding in the Age of First Gates, and its graves filled again when the tribulation lightning burned the city. After the survivors left for Không Mông Thành, the graves went untended for centuries and the bamboo grew over them. Mountain folk said that in autumn the dead sang old poems on the hill, and few went near. In 960 Lý Hận Bích founded Thu Phần Các among the graves, a sect of soul arts and grave wards, and swore it to Thính Vũ Lâu. By 962 the villagers of Ương Ca were hearing singing from the graves every autumn, and sang louder at planting to drown it. The pavilion keeps the hill silent in every other season, and its strings of poem slips grow longer with each autumn.
places.art_brief: A minor sect seat miniature, vertical on a low bamboo-covered hill: a dark weathered wooden pavilion with two small stacked-roof towers in dark grey tile, the tallest outline on the hill, above slopes dotted with rounded grass grave mounds.
